title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: GamesLab
pitch: Let a browser agent turn an idea of a game variation such as "Tic-Tac-Toe, but the pieces are rock paper and scissors" into a safe, modular, online multiplayer board game with powerful bot!
about_excerpt: Let a browser agent turn an idea of a game variation such as "Tic-Tac-Toe, but the pieces are rock paper and scissors" into a safe, modular, online multiplayer board game with powerful bot! Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent building a game variation Ability for manual edits too! Inspiration For a couple weeks I've been hanging around online communities where people are trying to come up with new tile-based games. The same pattern kept happening: someone would suggest a variation, "what if bishops could jump," "what if pawns moved sideways," and there was no good way to tell whether the idea was actually fun or just novel. Trying it out meant having an AI build/update a website, republishing it, and only then finding out if the rule was any good. There was no shared framework, so every suggestion reinvented the wheel, and every small idea change cost a full deploy cycle before anyone could sit down and play it. AI agents already made the idea part faster: you could describe a rule change to a model and it understood you immediately. What was missing was a place for that understanding to land. Re-publishing a whole website for "what if the bishop jumps" is annoying at best. I wanted to create a board game website that was entirely modularly rule-defined such that telling an agent what you wanted and actually playing it online with a friend could be the same five minutes. The other half of this project is just personal: I've always liked breaking a game's rules apart and rebuilding them slightly different, trying to find the more-fun version than the original. And I know this isn't uncommon; if you look at the Wikipedia list of chess variants , you'll see hundreds of people who did exactly this. What I learned An important idea turned out to be that the game has to be entirely data and never code. If a rule can be an arbitrary function, you can't validate it, you can't hand it to an agent safely, and you can't run a search against it. A rule someone wrote has to be immediately safe to open and function in the same exact way as alternative rules. I also learned that giving an agent a tool is a design problem in its own right, not a wrapper around an API. The tool listing gets re-sent on every single turn of a conversation, so every tool that isn't earning its place is a tax paid forever. I ended up cutting the workbench's tool listing roughly in half by removing tools for things that the agent doesn't need to do: publishing, voting, starting a match, and keeping only what an agent is actually there for: reading a game, building one, checking it, and handing over a game of it. How I built it Everything centers on a single rule format; board, pieces, movement, capture, and win conditions are expressed as one finite JSON document. That document is read by three different engines that all have to agree: a TypeScript reader in the browser, a Go reader on the server (the authority), and a Rust core compiled to WebAssembly for speed (so bot engine can search millions of positions a second for better quality play). Keeping three implementations honest is done with a shared conformance corpus: a fixed set of recorded positions and legal moves that all three readers are tested against, so a format change that lands in one and not the others shows up as a failing test rather than a live bug. The Rust engine exists because an interpreted alpha-beta search over a general rule format is too slow to be useful. Compiling the document down to a program with names already resolved (offsets baked, kinds as indices) was worth roughly 40× the speed of just trying to make the interpreter faster. That speed is what makes it possible to validate a brand-new game variant by having a bot play hundreds of games against itself in well under a second, checking that one side doesn't always win and the game doesn't always draw. Alpha-beta pruning is what makes that search tractable at all: with good move ordering it cuts the size of the game tree explored from O(b^d) down to roughly O(b^{d/2}) for branching factor b and depth d. The difference between a bot that can check a variant in milliseconds and one that can't. The same rule format also generates the rulebook. Because moves, captures, and win conditions are structured data rather than arbitrary prose, the site can snapshot "interesting" positions from bot self-play and use them to show a stranger how a brand-new game is actually won, without anyone writing documentation/explanations by hand. On top of that sits a shared workbench: a person and an agent editing the same document, through the same functions, at the same time, with an activity ledger, pause, and a confirmation step before anything gets published. Challenges The hardest problem wasn't any single piece of code, it was scope discipline in the format itself. I really wanted to support every game, but if I add support for every possible game interaction or mechanic the rule-based game is actually worse than if it was just hard coded. If there's too many options, it's too hard to use and we don't get the benefit of the shared mechanics! Keeping three engines byte-for-byte consistent was a constant source of subtle bugs. Every format change had to be replicated in three places, so I planned ahead and leaned hard on automated equivalence tests between the interpreted and compiled paths rather than trusting careful reading. Measuring whether the bot was actually competent was tricky. Because there are many different possible games and I wanted a single bot that could learn any ruleset and play decently well, I had to weigh the eval parameters against known strategies for existing games, tying them to specific win conditions and piece values (when possible in the ruleset). This took a lot of trial and error in many different games, and it's not perfect, but it doesn't have to be! The point of the computation engine isn't to beat StockFish at chess, it's to be good enough to know when the game is bad . When the human is testing the game, it doesn't matter if they beat the bot 80% of the time, because just having an opponent is enough to validate if it would be a fun game and if they should invite their friends to play (with the built in challenge link). video_title: I told my browser's agent to break Tic-Tac-Toe. It did. | GamesLab (OpenAI WebMCP Challenge)
video_transcript_excerpt: Athell is a great game, so why not add fog of war? Checkers is a classic, but what if we'll play it on a hexagon? Chess is fun, but what if we take out the middle of the board? Tic-tac-toe is kind of lame. So, let's add rock, paper, and scissors to the game. Games Lab was designed to let us do exactly that. Just open the website in an agent powered browser and describe the game you want to see. In agent control, we can watch the game come to life. The agent plans out the new game and lets us interject at any point or pause its progress. All the games are strictly rule-based. At no point does the agent write or run code. This guarantees that no malicious code is being run. The game behaves exactly as expected and the agent only needs to modify a couple rules and not the whole game. After each rule is changed, we can see a live demo of two bots playing each other in the new game that is being created. The bot not only serves to show that the game visually looks and plays how it's expected, but because it was coded with a web assembly target of Rust and is so dang fast, it can play behind the scenes thousands of games a second. Once the agent is done, it can ask the website to use this bot to make sure the game is valid and doesn't have any gameplay issues. At any point, we can open the manual editor, look around, or change some rules. The website would automatically notify the agent of any conflicting changes, and instruct the agent to merge the two together. Once the agent finishes, it's our turn to try out the game. Right away, the bot is given the rule set and can immediately search millions of positions a second. And yeah, it it beats me a lot. We can tell the bot to make any changes we want. Why not try it so if you get three in a row, you lose? The agent does its thing, updates the plan, makes the changes, and then you can play again. The game's kind of fun, much better than normal tic-tac-toe. We can then publish the game and start paying other people. A rule book is automatically generated and shows exactly how to win and what pieces do what. Though, after playing a lot of games, something doesn't feel right. Let's ask the agent what's up with that. Well, would you look at that? The agent had the website run 400 games and found that blue almost always won. The times red one is almost certainly because of the random openings it's forced to do. In under 10 minutes, I was able to try out a new idea, try it against a pretty competent bot, play it in online multiplayer games, and scrap the idea in the end cuz it's unbalanced. That is the power of Games Lab. It allows rapid innovation of new games and I am so excited to see what people make. Please do let me know of any fun variations you come up with.

title: Orbweaver
pitch: An agent-native semantic workspace where ChatGPT proposes validated visual structures through WebMCP—and the human retains authority to accept, export, or undo.
about_excerpt: An agent-native semantic workspace where ChatGPT proposes validated visual structures through WebMCP—and the human retains authority to accept, export, or undo. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Complex systems do not need more interface. They need better structure. Architecture diagrams, workflows, data models, and knowledge graphs already contain meaning, but turning that meaning into a useful visual usually requires authored coordinates, diagram syntax, manually positioned shapes, or generated output that is difficult to inspect. I built Orbweaver around a simpler principle: Understand complex systems while showing less. What it does Orbweaver turns coordinate-free semantic graphs into deterministic, inspectable visual structures. The input describes meaning: what exists; how things relate; which relationships matter; what evidence and claims support the structure. Orbweaver validates that meaning, computes the layout, and renders an accessible SVG artifact. The proposal contains no authored coordinates, SVG, HTML, CSS, or executable markup. The WebMCP playground extends this into a shared human-agent workspace. ChatGPT can read the live workspace contract, create or revise a semantic proposal, inspect an entity, and focus it in the visible diagram. The agent can propose meaning. It cannot accept its own work. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer interface controls and repeatedly manipulate a large JSON editor. That is slow, fragile, and disconnected from the application’s actual domain model. With WebMCP, Orbweaver exposes six bounded, page-local tools: read the current workspace and revision; read the supported semantic contract; create a complete proposal; revise it using conflict-safe operations; inspect semantic identity and provenance; focus an entity in the visible workspace. The tools reuse the same application controller and validation boundary as the human interface. WebMCP does not introduce a second, privileged execution path. The human-agent experience A person describes an order-fulfillment system in ordinary language. ChatGPT discovers Orbweaver’s tools and supplies entities, relationships, groups, claims, and evidence—not pixels or drawing instructions. Orbweaver validates the entire proposal atomically, derives the geometry, and renders revision one as a validated but untrusted preview . The person and agent then work with the same live state. ChatGPT can add Delivery tracking, focus it, and expose its relationships for inspection. Expected-revision checks prevent stale writes when the shared workspace changes. Acceptance remains a human-only decision. The agent cannot accept a revision or enable export. The person can inspect, reject, or undo the change. In the demonstration, I manually undo the agent’s revision and Orbweaver restores the previous graph. How I built it Orbweaver’s core is a provider-neutral TypeScript library. A strict GraphProposal contract represents semantic content without layout coordinates. ELK.js computes the visual structure, while Orbweaver produces accessible SVG, stable semantic identities, selection behavior, provenance, and inspection details. The playground’s WebMCP adapter registers six tools through the browser’s page-local model context. Tool inputs are treated as untrusted data and pass through the existing validation layer. Create and revise operations are atomic, revisions are versioned, and semantic writes never bundle human acceptance. The implementation is tested with Vitest, Playwright, and axe-core accessibility checks. The npm package contains no AI provider, account requirement, telemetry, or cloud runtime dependency. Challenges The hardest problem was not drawing the graph. It was designing the authority boundary. A useful agent needed enough access to create meaningful structures without gaining the ability to silently approve its own output. This required explicit trust states, expected-revision conflict protection, atomic validation, reversible mutations, and accepted-only export. The other challenge was visual restraint: presenting enough information to understand a complex system without turning the workspace into an aircraft cockpit. Orbweaver keeps the interface secondary to the structure being examined. Accomplishments I’m proud of Published a provider-neutral open-source TypeScript library rather than embedding an AI service inside the product. Built six bounded WebMCP tools around the application’s existing controller and validation boundary. Made agent-authored changes versioned, atomic, inspectable, and reversible. Preserved human-only authority over acceptance and export. Produced deterministic, accessible SVG from semantic proposals containing no authored coordinates. Published the beta package, live playground, documentation, source, and reproducible demonstration. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes an application’s domain semantics—not when it simply recreates button clicking as tools. The strongest human-agent experience is not full autonomy. It is shared context with asymmetric authority: the agent contributes reach and synthesis; the application enforces structure; the human retains judgment at the moment of consequence. What’s next Orbweaver is open source and currently available as @semanticintent/orbweaver@0.2.0-beta.1 . Next steps include stabilizing the beta API, expanding semantic lenses and comparison views, and continuing to develop portable artifacts that preserve their meaning, provenance, and accessibility outside the original application. title: The Last Terminal
pitch: Human players and AI agents collaborate to solve 5 interconnected puzzles across surveillance feeds, security terminals, auxiliary power grids, and archived exit protocols.
about_excerpt:
Human players and AI agents collaborate to solve 5 interconnected puzzles across surveillance feeds, security terminals, auxiliary power grids, and archived exit protocols.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Here are the submission section details for THE LAST TERMINAL : 

 

 Inspiration 

 Traditional browser AI agents interact with web applications through brute force: taking high-resolution screenshots, parsing complex DOM trees, predicting CSS selectors, and firing simulated mouse clicks. This approach is fragile, slow, and burns tens of thousands of tokens per action. 

 When WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) emerged as a proposed browser standard ( navigator.modelContext.registerTool ), we realized web applications no longer had to be passive visual interfaces. Websites could directly expose machine-readable capabilities to AI agents. 

 We wanted to showcase this paradigm shift in a way that was instantly understandable and fun. An escape room was the ultimate sandbox—demanding puzzle reasoning, state prerequisites, data extraction, and tool sequence execution! 

 

 What it does 

 THE LAST TERMINAL is an interactive, browser-based cyberpunk escape room where human players and AI agents collaborate to escape an abandoned digital research facility before the emergency countdown reaches zero. 

 
 5 Interconnected Subsystems : Surveillance Matrix, Security Terminal, Auxiliary Power Control, Archive Database, and Emergency Exit Override. 
 10 WebMCP Capabilities : Exposes structured capabilities ranging from inspect_surveillance("CAM-07") and read_log("LOG-2049") to restore_power(["C","A","D","B"]) and unlock_exit("7319") . 
 Dual Execution Engine : Human UI interactions and AI WebMCP tool calls invoke the exact same underlying JavaScript game engine logic. 
 Real-Time Agent Feed & Trace : A live terminal logs tool calls in real time, accompanied by a full JSON execution trace inspector for hackathon judges. 
 Demo Agent Simulator : Includes a 90-second automated execution mode so anyone can watch an AI agent solve the room step-by-step without needing external API keys. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 
 Core Tech Stack : Next.js 14 (App Router), React 18, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. 
 WebMCP Integration ( src/lib/webmcp/ ) : Registered 10 structured tools with strict JSON Schemas using navigator.modelContext.registerTool imperative API, wrapped in a hydration guard to prevent re-registration during React re-renders. 
 Unified Game Engine ( src/lib/game/ ) : Built a central state machine ( gameEngine.ts ) powering both human clicks and agent tool calls. 
 Web Audio API Synthesizer ( src/lib/audio/sound.ts ) : Built a zero-external-asset audio generator for terminal typing clicks, success chimes, failure buzzers, and power-up sweeps. 
 Developer Debug Bar ( ?debug=true ) : Added a secret query parameter mode for instant puzzle completion and state inspection during testing. 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Enforcing Prerequisites Without Crashing : Ensuring that tools like open_archive() correctly check state prerequisites ( power === 'online' ) and return structured error payloads ( PREREQUISITE_NOT_MET ) rather than throwing unhandled exceptions. 
 Graceful Fallback & Polyfilling : WebMCP is an emerging browser feature. We needed to support native navigator.modelContext while building an in-memory tool polyfill and automated simulator for standard browsers. 
 Zero-Dependency Architecture : Ensuring the entire application ran client-side with zero backend infrastructure, zero paid APIs, and zero external databases while keeping the build Vercel-ready. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 >90% Token Reduction : Demonstrated how structured WebMCP tool calls eliminate the heavy token overhead of DOM parsing and visual screenshot analysis. 
 Zero Paid Dependencies : Built the entire experience to run 100% locally in the browser with zero external infrastructure. 
 100% Test & Build Validation : Achieved a clean Next.js static build and 100% pass rate on our standalone engine test suite ( npm run test:engine ). 
 

 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP transforms web applications from passive UIs into agentic APIs . 
 Human + Agent co-op design patterns—where humans supply visual intuition and agents perform rapid tool inspection—create a powerful collaboration model. 
 

 

 What's next for The Last Terminal 

 
 Multi-Agent Co-Op : Expanding to multi-agent escape rooms where specialized WebMCP agents (e.g. Security Agent, Power Agent) solve puzzles in parallel with human teams. 
 useWebMCPTool React Hook : Packaging our WebMCP registration layer into an open-source React hook library for Next.js developers. 
 Community Puzzle Creator : Allowing developers to construct their own WebMCP escape rooms using custom JSON schemas!

title: WEXSPACE ProofDesk
pitch: A governed WebMCP evidence workbench where humans and browser agents share one auditable workflow while final release remains human-controlled.
about_excerpt: A governed WebMCP evidence workbench where humans and browser agents share one auditable workflow while final release remains human-controlled. Like Comment Story Updates ProofDesk: 5 WebMCP tools, 100% evidence coverage, deterministic PASS, and AWAITING_HUMAN_REVIEW with human-only release. Human-defined deliverable contract and acceptance criteria shared with the WebMCP agent before any evidence work begins. Inspiration Browser agents can act quickly, but high-consequence work becomes hard to trust when intent, evidence, verification, and release authority are hidden inside an automation trace. WEXSPACE ProofDesk makes that collaboration visible and accountable. What it does ProofDesk gives a human and a WebMCP browser agent one shared evidence workspace. The human defines the real deliverable contract and acceptance criteria. Five narrow WebMCP tools let an agent inspect the workspace, create a bounded work item, add criterion-linked HTTPS evidence, run a deterministic evidence-coverage gate, and prepare a passing package for human review. The visible UI reads the same domain state and audit ledger. The workflow ends at AWAITING_HUMAN_REVIEW . No WebMCP tool can approve or release work. Why WebMCP is the right fit WebMCP makes the website itself an explicit, typed agent interface. The agent does not scrape button labels or depend on brittle coordinates, while the human keeps the full visible product experience. Tool names, input schemas, side effects, and authority boundaries are declared by the site. What people and agents can do together Before ProofDesk, a human must reconstruct what was requested, which claims have evidence, whether the acceptance criteria passed, and whether release occurred. ProofDesk gives both sides one deliverable contract, one evidence set, one deterministic score, one audit history, and one human-controlled release boundary. How we built it Five imperative WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool Shared TypeScript domain functions used by both the React UI and WebMCP adapter Deterministic criterion-coverage scoring Versioned browser-local persistence with localStorage Auditable state transitions Human-only approval and release controls Production deployment on ChatGPT Sites Unit, contract, rendering, and public judge-path tests Challenges and accomplishments The hardest part was proving that WebMCP actions and the visible human interface mutate the same real workflow state while preventing an agent from crossing the final release boundary. The public judge path discovered all five tools, added three evidence items, produced a 100% deterministic gate score, and reached AWAITING_HUMAN_REVIEW with releasePerformed: false . What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it is treated as a governed product interface rather than an invisible automation shortcut. Narrow tools, shared state, explicit side effects, deterministic checks, and a clear human boundary make browser-agent work easier to inspect and trust. Prior work and challenge-new work The WEXSPACE name and high-level governance ideas predate this challenge. ProofDesk itself—including its product scope, React/Vinext application, shared domain engine, five WebMCP tools, deterministic gate, persistence, audit behavior, tests, deployment, documentation, and demo evidence—was created during the WebMCP Challenge period. Earlier WEXSPACE/IEW engineering work is unrelated prior work and is not presented as newly created here. The app started from the OpenAI Sites Vinext starter; standard framework plumbing is scaffold dependency, not an original product claim. Judge test path Open the live application in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. Discover the five wexspace.* tools. Create a package with 2–6 acceptance criteria. Add medium- or high-confidence HTTPS evidence for every criterion. Run the deterministic gate. Prepare human review. Confirm that both the visible UI and the tool response show 100% coverage, AWAITING_HUMAN_REVIEW , and releasePerformed: false . Confirm that no agent release tool exists. Live app: https://wexspace-proofdesk.moatazalqobati20.chatgpt.site/ Source: https://github.com/moatazfarea/wexspace-iew-agentic-fleet/tree/webmcp-challenge-2026 Security and limitations ProofDesk requests no credentials and stores workspace state only in the current browser profile. Evidence URLs must use HTTPS. Evidence confidence is declared rather than independently fact-checked. This release supports one active package per browser profile, and native discovery requires a WebMCP-capable browser. ProofDesk is a governance and evidence workflow, not a professional certification authority. title: Ariba Integrator Agent
pitch: Supplier onboarding: 120 days → 14. AI agents handle EDI mapping, CIG testing & integration guides via WebMCP. Humans own sign-off. Everyone moves faster.
about_excerpt:
Supplier onboarding: 120 days → 14. AI agents handle EDI mapping, CIG testing & integration guides via WebMCP. Humans own sign-off. Everyone moves faster.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Enterprise supplier onboarding on SAP Ariba is broken. Every new supplier requires 100+ manual 
touchpoints, takes 30–120 days, and bottlenecks at 5–10 concurrent onboardings. The root cause 
isn't complexity — it's that every step is coordination overhead: emails, status checks, EDI 
validation, connectivity tests, guide generation. The work is structured. The bottleneck is human 
bandwidth. WebMCP finally gives agents a browser-native way to take that load off. 

 What it does 

 AribaFlow is a WebMCP-powered procurement integration portal where AI agents and procurement teams 
work side by side to onboard suppliers in 7–14 days instead of 120. 

 Agents handle the 80% that's repetitive: 

 
 EDI document validation — schema checks, ANID mismatch detection, field mapping verification 
 CIG connectivity testing — AS2/VAN/HTTPS endpoint verification, certificate status 
 Integration guide generation — auto-draft from test results, ready for human review 
 Onboarding checklist orchestration — tracks 13-step SI/SIFL workflow, surfaces blockers 
 Supplier readiness scoring — ranked queue so integration teams prioritise the right suppliers 
 

 Humans handle the 20% that matters: governance, sign-off, and exceptions. 

 All agent interactions happen through WebMCP tools registered on the portal — no backend API keys 
exposed, no separate agent infrastructure, just a website that agents can actually use. 

 How we built it 

 The stack: Next.js 14 (App Router) on Vercel , WebMCP Imperative API for tool registration, 
 React frontend with a live onboarding dashboard, and a mock Ariba/CIG backend that mirrors 
real document flows (PO 850/OrderRequest, ASN 856, Invoice 810). 

 WebMCP tools are registered at page load via navigator.tools.register() . Each tool maps 1:1 to 
a procurement workflow action — structured inputs, structured JSON output, designed so an LLM 
can chain them without ambiguity. 

 The domain model comes from real Ariba integration experience: CIG adapter patterns, AS2 
connectivity, cXML/X12 document types, and the SI/SIFL/NEL role separation that governs every 
enterprise onboarding project. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 WebMCP origin isolation — any document.domain usage breaks the tools API. Had to audit 
every third-party embed and iframe to enforce origin isolation across the portal. 
 Tool schema design — JSON Schema for EDI validation inputs is non-trivial. Too loose and 
agents hallucinate field values. Too strict and valid documents fail. Iterated with the 
WebMCP Inspector extension until tool calls were reliable. 
 Demo vs. reality — real Ariba systems require corporate VPN and supplier ANIDs. Built a 
faithful mock layer that exercises the same error paths (ANID_MISMATCH, MAP_FIELD_MISSING, 
CERT_EXPIRED) so the demo reflects genuine failure modes, not happy-path theatre. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP's browser-native model is genuinely different from server-side MCP. The agent and the 
human share the same page state — which means the portal UI and the agent's tool responses have 
to be in sync. That constraint forced better product design: every tool response updates visible 
UI state, so the human always knows exactly what the agent did and why. 

 What's next 

 
 Live Ariba Network API integration (with OAuth, not mock) 
 Declarative WebMCP annotations on the supplier self-service forms 
 Multi-buyer tenancy so integration service providers can run parallel onboarding waves 
 Compliance audit trail: every agent action logged with timestamp, tool input, and output

title: Olos-AI Mini Budget Planner
pitch: A simple local-first budget tracker where people use a clear visual interface and agents use structured WebMCP tools against the same deterministic financial logic.
about_excerpt: A simple local-first budget tracker where people use a clear visual interface and agents use structured WebMCP tools against the same deterministic financial logic. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted a personal budget tracker because I'm generally hopeless (like most people) at controlling my spending and having something like this app allows me to be accounting for each and every dollar I spend, yes there are hundreds of them in the app store but I don't think people need to spend more money for a subscription and lose their privacy for a basic tracker. I used AI to assist in the development and writing to assist with expressing the story clearly Personal budgeting should be simple: record money coming in or going out, then immediately understand what remains. Many budgeting products instead introduce subscriptions, user accounts, bank connections, advertising, telemetry, and increasingly complex dashboards. Olos-AI Mini Budget Planner was built as a deliberately small alternative. Its normal experience remains a fast, visual, local-first budget tracker. The WebMCP Challenge presented a different question: can this existing application become agent-native without embedding a chatbot, adding an LLM dependency, or surrendering its financial rules to an AI model? What it does The planner records income, expenses, bills, savings, recurring commitments, revolving credit, Pay Later balances, and estimated fixed loans. It shows actual and projected monthly cashflow while keeping available cash, available credit, and loan liabilities clearly separate. People use the normal responsive interface. Compatible agents receive eleven structured WebMCP tools for reading budget information and performing explicit, validated actions. An agent can: Read the monthly budget summary List upcoming commitments Search recent activity Inspect credit and loan balances Read calendar projections Record a confirmed transaction Create or record a recurring item Record a credit payment Correct an existing transaction Delete an identified transaction with deliberate confirmation Agent-created changes appear immediately in the same interface the person uses. How we built it The application uses FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and PWA APIs. The WebMCP layer is a thin adapter. Each tool is registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) with a strict JSON schema, clear description, bounded inputs, and appropriate read-only or mutating behaviour. Tool callbacks call the same FastAPI endpoints used by the visual interface. All validation, recurrence handling, credit balances, fixed-loan calculations, and no-double-counting rules remain in the existing deterministic application logic. Financial calculations are not duplicated in prompts or delegated to an LLM. Why WebMCP improves the experience Without WebMCP, an agent must interpret labels, click controls, and infer meaning from page layout. With WebMCP, the application directly explains what actions are available and the exact structure each action requires. A person can say, “Record an $87.40 grocery expense paid with my credit card,” and the agent can submit one validated transaction using typed fields for amount, date, category, payment method, and facility ID. The result then appears in Recent Activity and updates the monthly figures. The application itself does not contain an AI assistant and does not send financial data to a third-party AI service. WebMCP lets the browser and a compatible agent collaborate with the application at its boundary. Challenges The most important challenge was preserving one financial authority. It would have been easy to create simplified financial behaviour inside the WebMCP callbacks. Instead, the tools reuse the same tested API and domain rules as the human interface. The hosted demonstration also required a strict privacy boundary. The public Render deployment uses synthetic data and isolated disposable browser sessions. It has no connection to anyone’s personal local database. Accomplishments Eleven meaningful WebMCP tools rather than a ceremonial integration Exact decimal-string money inputs Structured separation of cash, credit availability, and loan liabilities Immediate visual refresh after agent mutations Idempotent recurring-payment recording Protection against double-counting credit and loan repayments A useful application that remains fully functional without an agent Disposable, session-isolated public demonstration data What we learned Agent-native does not have to mean “put a chatbot in every application.” A deterministic web application can preserve its normal human interface while exposing a second, structured interface designed for agents. That approach makes agent interaction more accurate while keeping the application’s own rules authoritative. What’s next The immediate goal is to keep the project small, understandable, and dependable. Future work would focus on wider WebMCP browser compatibility and further usability testing, without turning the application into banking software or a financial-advice platform. title: Bundlepose
pitch: Agents propose. People compose. Shopify bundles. You and your AI agent co-compose a bouquet that doesn't exist yet — and a Cart Transform Function makes it one real, purchasable line in the cart.
about_excerpt: Agents propose. People compose. Shopify bundles. You and your AI agent co-compose a bouquet that doesn't exist yet — and a Cart Transform Function makes it one real, purchasable line in the cart. Like Comment Story Updates top Basic Use Case Co-Compose System Inspiration E-commerce lets anyone sell 24 hours a day — but an online store is really an unmanned roadside stand. Nobody greets you, nobody asks who the flowers are for. We build Shopify apps for a living (Theme App Extensions, Shopify Functions), and florists are a vertical where this gap hurts most. Custom bouquets ARE sold on Shopify today — but the "custom" part still happens over phone calls, LINE messages, and free-text note fields. The composition, the price, the stock — none of it is structured. When WebMCP arrived, we saw a chance to put a clerk back in the store: an agent that listens to "something warm for my mother's 60th birthday, under $40," knows the flowers (meanings, occasions, pet safety), and builds the bouquet with you. Shopping agents are good at finding products that already exist. We wanted the harder thing: turning agentic commerce from product discovery into product creation. What it does Bundlepose is a Shopify app where a shopper and an AI agent compose a product that doesn't exist yet — and turn it into a real order. The agent proposes. Through 11 bouquet_* WebMCP tools registered on every storefront page, the agent reads the florist's rules (slots, stem limits, budget) and today's flowers — real Shopify variants with metafields for role, color, flower meaning, occasions, and pet safety — then drafts a bouquet within the budget. The person composes. The draft appears in a composer panel on the same page. The shopper adjusts quantities, removes a stem, picks the wrap, restores something — by hand. The agent sees those hand edits on its next bouquet_get_state call and rebalances. One shared workbench, edited from both sides. Shopify bundles. bouquet_commit — the only tool allowed to touch the cart — validates the draft and adds it. A Cart Transform Function (Rust) merges stems, wrap, and arrangement fee into one cart line, priced as the exact sum of its parts , carrying its recipe through checkout. Three bouquets? Three clean lines, not thirty loose stems. Why this needs WebMCP: Shopify's built-in storefront tools already let agents search products and fill carts — but they can only sell what exists. A bouquet that was just invented in conversation isn't a product; twelve loose stem lines don't tell the merchant "this is one bouquet," and two bouquets in one cart are indistinguishable mush. Page-level WebMCP tools + a Cart Transform close exactly that gap: the agent works inside the store's own rules and inventory, hands off to Shopify's standard tools for checkout, and the human approves on the same page they're browsing. The UX win is concrete: what used to be a phone call, a LINE thread, and a free-text note field becomes a structured, priced, stock-checked bouquet built right on the product page — and one clean line in the cart instead of a dozen loose stems. The tools: bouquet_get_rules , bouquet_list_components , bouquet_create , bouquet_get_state , bouquet_add_items , bouquet_remove_items , bouquet_set_wrap , bouquet_set_note , bouquet_validate , bouquet_commit , bouquet_discard . How we built it Storefront (Theme App Extension, app embed): registers the 11 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() — imperative API, top-level document (ChatGPT does not detect tools inside iframes). Tools and the composer panel mutate one shared draft store (persisted to localStorage), so agent calls re-render the panel instantly and human edits are readable back through bouquet_get_state , including a per-stem diff against what's already in the cart. Backend (React Router 7 + TypeScript on Fly.io, SQLite/Prisma): tools call the store's own domain via Shopify App Proxy ( /apps/composer/* ) — signed, same-origin, zero CORS. We verified WebMCP execute runs in the normal page context (not a sandbox), which makes this possible. The catalog endpoint reads the Admin GraphQL API, exposing composer.* metafields (role, color, meaning, occasions, pet-safe) as the agent-facing florist knowledge. Cart write: Shopify.actions.updateCart (Storefront Actions API) with hidden _bundle_id / _bundle_name line attributes, Ajax Cart API fallback — then navigate to /cart , which is always correct regardless of theme. Bundling (Shopify Function, Rust → WASM): groups cart lines by _bundle_id and emits a LinesMerge operation under a "Custom Bouquet" parent variant ( requiresComponents: true , price $0 — the merged line's price is the components' sum). Config lives in a metafield on the Cart Transform; missing config = no-op, so checkout never breaks. Fixture-tested with @shopify/shopify-function-test-helpers . Merchant setup: an idempotent admin setup page — one click seeds the demo florist (14 stems with metafields, 2 wraps, an arrangement fee, the merge parent kept UNLISTED: purchasable by direct variant reference for the merge, hidden from search), another activates the transform after shopify app deploy . Challenges we ran into Exposing WebMCP tools on a Shopify store. A Theme App Extension turned out to be the right surface: its app embed runs in the storefront's top-level document, which is where agents such as ChatGPT discover tools. We then named and scoped the bouquet_* tools so they complement — rather than overlap with — Shopify's standard storefront tools, which already handle search, cart and checkout. Staying in sync with the store's theme. Writing to the cart from a tool succeeded on the server, but the theme's cart icon and drawer did not reflect the change. The theme owns that state and only reacts to its own events, so we moved the commit path to Shopify's Storefront Actions API, which fires those events, and navigate to the cart page after a commit so the result is always visible. Co-composing with the agent, not through it. Our first approach drove every cart change through WebMCP alone, and the shopper ended up doing more work — each small tweak became another round of conversation. So we built the embedded composer: the agent's proposal lands in an on-page panel that the shopper can edit by hand, and the agent reads those edits back. Splitting the work this way is what finally made the experience feel good. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop works end-to-end from ChatGPT: conversation → draft → hand-edit → agent rebalance → commit → one merged bouquet line → checkout. The math is exact. Five lines (3 roses, 4 tulips, 2 eucalyptus, wrap, fee) merge into "Warm Birthday Bouquet — $39.50", precisely the sum of its parts; a second bouquet stays its own line, and checkout expands each into its recipe. A real shared workbench. Remove a stem by hand and the panel shows "Removed / Restore", the agent sees changes_since_cart , and "Update cart · +$3.00" shows the delta before you approve. It's a product, not a rig: idempotent one-page seed of the demo florist, graceful fallback in browsers without WebMCP, and a Rust Function with fixture tests. What we learned Chat is not always the best interface. When you build with WebMCP, it's tempting to think of every interaction as a conversation. But some things — like removing one stem or trying a different wrap — are faster to do by hand than to describe in words. To give customers a good experience, we learned to combine chat with other kinds of UI, rather than force everything through the agent. WebMCP tools have to coexist with other apps' tools. Publishing tools with WebMCP turned out to be easy. That is exactly why it needs care: on a platform like Shopify, our tools run on the same page as Shopify's own tools and, in the future, tools from other developers' apps. Tool names, descriptions and responsibilities need to be designed so that agents can tell them apart and use them together. Explaining this to customers is hard. Our demo store shows a banner inviting shoppers to try the new experience with their AI agent. In practice, it is still difficult for a non-engineer to understand what that means or how to start. Until WebMCP-capable browsers are common, even a careful explanation will only go so far — as app developers, we need to keep working on how this is introduced to real shoppers. What's next for Bundlepose Let the agent sell, not just build: add upsell_suggestions[] to bouquet_validate / bouquet_get_state returns — "for $3 more, satin wrap," "your budget fits one more focal stem" — so upselling happens in conversation, the way a real clerk does it. More templates for the same engine. The Cart Transform's grouping logic is product-agnostic and the shop rules already ship as a profile object (noun, unit, slots) — generalizing the tool names and copy is the next step: coffee blends, cookie assortments, spice mixes, gift kits. title: The Agentic Textbook
pitch: Learn anything, with the help of your favorite agent
about_excerpt: Learn anything, with the help of your favorite agent Like 3 Comment Story Updates The Agentic Textbook The textbook that builds itself around you. Learn any concept, with the help of the agent that already knows you Agentic Textbook turns the AI agent you already use into a live teaching partner, creating the exact explanations, visuals, exercises, and learning paths you need inside a shared WebMCP canvas. Inspiration Most training around tech products/concepts are outdated before they even goe live. We see this constantly while onboarding customers onto frontier AI tools—especially Codex. New capabilities appear almost every day, while users still need a simple place to understand what changed, why it matters, and how to use it well. We needed a learning surface that could keep up. Not another static academy, but a place where every learner could generate the exact training they need, the moment they need it. What it does Agentic Textbook makes the textbook as dynamic as the technology it teaches. It also explores a bigger question: what should learning become when every learner has an AI agent? The system has two deliberately separate parts: The agent brings intelligence and context. It understands the learner’s goals, prior knowledge, interests, and current questions, and can generate explanations, diagrams, examples, code, or exercises on demand. The Agentic Textbook leverages coding agents capabilities to create new and exciting content. The textbook brings pedagogy and structure. It provides an open, editable canvas with lesson sequencing, remediation paths, learning-science-informed components, and clear learner controls. Think of it as the pedagogical authority, based on learning sciences, that harnesses the agent's infinite potential. This creates a BYOA model: Bring Your Own Agent. Learners keep the agent they already trust, while WebMCP turns the browser into a shared workspace where human and agent can build the lesson together. And adapt it on-demand to the learner's needs. Ask for another explanation. Add a formula. Generate a diagram. Create a code exercise. Slow down, go deeper, or approach the concept from another angle. The agent can update one focused part of the textbook without rebuilding the entire experience. How we built it We wanted to understand what WebMCP makes possible at its core. The key primitive is surprisingly powerful: the browser becomes a shared place where humans and agents can read, act, and create together. We wanted to apply this concept to something that was both important for us in our day-to-day, and could also change the broader picture of web based learning experiences. That insight shaped the entire product. The learner prepares a brief and reviews the context being used. The agent authors a structured lesson. The app validates and renders it. From there, the learner and agent can keep refining individual regions of the canvas together. Once the interaction model clicked, Codex helped us turn it into a working product through tight iteration. Under the hood, topic-neutral lesson schemas can combine prose, formulas, diagrams, governed media, exercises, and executable code labs, without hard-coding a course for each new subject. Challenges we ran into The hardest part wasn’t implementation. It was making the idea legible to a coding agent. First, we had to understand what WebMCP really changes compared with standard MCP, and how it relates to inline MCP apps inside products such as ChatGPT. Then we had to steer Codex away from familiar patterns. Coding agents are excellent inside known territory. Asking them to help invent a genuinely new interaction model is much harder. We had to make the underlying idea extremely precise before the implementation became coherent. If you let a coding agent loose on an innovative concept, it tends to bring it back to known patterns, which destroy the originality of the idea. Personalization introduced another tension: context is valuable, but privacy is non-negotiable. Codex was rightly cautious about exposing sensitive information. We designed a consent-scoped, local-first context lane where learners review minimized signals before they enter a lesson. That became our biggest lesson: implementation is getting easier; steering agents toward reliable novelty is not. The main bottleneck today is speed. At Cerebras-class inference speeds, the delay between asking for a change and watching the textbook transform could almost disappear. That’s when the experience becomes magical. Accomplishments that we’re proud of A small set of primitives created a surprisingly large design space. We’re proud that the product feels simple despite what is happening underneath: structured lesson generation, contextual adaptation, interactive exercises, targeted revisions, and learner-controlled publishing. We’re especially proud of the UI and interaction model. The agent can do powerful work, but the learner always has a clear, understandable surface in front of them. Our favorite technical detail is the JSON Render integration. Codex can author structured components while the textbook progressively renders them on the canvas. Pushed further, this could become one of the product’s defining capabilities. What we learned WebMCP isn’t simply MCP inside a browser. It’s a new interaction model. The browser is no longer just the destination where an agent’s output appears. It becomes a shared, live workspace where humans and agents can think, create, inspect, and revise together. We also learned how powerful a clear division of labor can be: the agent brings context and generative ability; the application brings pedagogical constraints, trust boundaries, and learner control. What’s next for Agentic Textbook AI education now has a shelf life measured in days. On September 2, while finishing this project, we discovered OpenAI’s new ChatGPT Training hub , with practical learning paths for ChatGPT Work and Codex. The timing felt almost comically perfect. For teams like ours, keeping clients current with products such as Codex is already a daily challenge. We need a way to create tailor-made training capsules as quickly as the product itself evolves. Next, we’re pushing in two directions. For businesses, we want organizations to bring their own curricula, terminology, policies, and role-specific knowledge into the same consent-scoped learning experience. For learners, we want to make the agent-to-canvas loop dramatically faster. The long-term goal is simple: learning experiences that move as fast as the technology they teach. Education is the most important thing. Having humans collaborate with agents via web technologies to learn new things looks like a promising direction. title: StoryRoom
pitch: The agent-native filmmaking studio where AI proposes and the director decides via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The agent-native filmmaking studio where AI proposes and the director decides via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Accepted Scene Written By AI Revision Review Diff Modal Chrome DevTools console showing Landing Page Inspiration Screenwriting is not a single-document problem. A single scene depends on what happened three scenes ago - who locked the safe, what the character emotionally knows at this moment, what the director's aesthetic rules demand about silence versus dialogue. When I tried using AI chatbots as a writing co-creator, I kept hitting the same wall: I had to manually copy-paste context, re-explain character histories every session, and hope the AI didn't contradict something established six scenes back. The real problem wasn't the AI's intelligence. The AI was operating blind - it had no structured access to the live workspace state. The moment I read about WebMCP — the idea that an agent could register structured tools directly on document.modelContext and read real browser application state - I immediately thought about filmmaking. A screenplay is exactly the kind of complex, multi-dimensional, stateful problem where a workspace-native agent thrives and a generic chatbot fails. So I asked: what if the AI director's assistant lived inside the studio? What it does StoryRoom is an agent-native filmmaking workspace where human directors and autonomous AI agents collaborate in real-time on live screenplays through the native WebMCP browser standard. The AI agent operates entirely inside the application through 8 registered WebMCP tools on document.modelContext : get_story_context - reads the full narrative: genre, logline, characters, locations, and the director's 8 codified creative rules get_current_scene - fetches the live screenplay text, slugline, characters present, and version history for any scene get_character - loads a full character dossier: psychological traits, emotional arc, and cross-scene appearance index check_continuity - audits the multi-scene timeline, prop tracking, and character knowledge for contradictions analyze_scene - evaluates dramatic pacing and dialogue against the Director's Memory rules propose_rewrite - generates a pending staged revision with justification notes — the live screenplay is never touched apply_revision - commits an approved revision to the screenplay, guarded by a strict Human-In-The-Loop security gate The centerpiece is the Human-In-The-Loop guarantee : the agent can never silently overwrite creative work. Every proposed rewrite is delivered as a side-by-side visual diff (red = removed, green = added). The director must explicitly click Accept Revision before any change reaches the script. How we built it StoryRoom is engineered in 5 architectural layers: 1. Presentation Layer React 18 + Vite + TailwindCSS cinematic workspace with a Screenplay Editor (industry-standard formatting), Character Manager, Locations Panel, Director's Memory rules editor, and a Revision Review modal. 2. WebMCP Tool Registry All 8 tools are registered on document.modelContext with strict JSON Schema definitions and input validation. They are also mirrored on navigator.modelContext and window._STORYROOM_WEBMCP_ so judges can verify every tool directly in Chrome DevTools ( F12 ). 3. WebMCP State Bridge WebMCPProvider synchronizes the tool registry with the live React ProjectStore using mutable refs - ensuring every tool call reads genuine, real-time application state rather than stale closures. 4. Dual-Mode AI Intelligence Layer Primary : Google Gemini 1.5 Flash via REST API, with an automatic model cascade (tries gemini-1.5-flash → gemini-2.0-flash-exp → gemini-1.5-pro ) so the app never hard-crashes on model deprecation Fallback : A deterministic offline simulation engine that produces high-quality, scene-aware responses with zero API key - so the full 9-step demo scenario runs for any judge, anywhere, at any time 5. Human-In-The-Loop Security Gate apply_revision checks revision status before executing. Any direct commit attempt on a pending revision is hard-blocked at the tool layer: { "success": false, "error": "HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED" } The director reviews a visual diff and clicks Accept - only then does the tool commit Version 3 to the live screenplay. Challenges we ran into 1. WebMCP state synchronization with async React rendering The hardest engineering problem. React re-renders asynchronously; the WebMCP tool registry registers once at mount. Getting check_continuity to always read the current screenplay state — not a stale snapshot from when the tool was first registered — required storing all reactive state in mutable refs inside the provider, rather than capturing values in closure scope. A subtle but critical distinction. 2. Designing the Human-In-The-Loop gate to feel like a creative decision The HITL gate had to be firm enough to be a real security guarantee, but natural enough that reviewing a diff feels like a directorial choice, not a bureaucratic approval form. Getting the visual diff presentation and the modal flow right required multiple iterations. 3. Gemini model deprecation mid-development The originally pinned model name ( gemini-2.0-flash ) returned 404 from the API partway through development. This could have broken the live demo. I responded by implementing an automatic model cascade that silently tries the next available production model before falling back to the offline simulation engine - so the app is resilient to future deprecations too. 4. Making the offline demo indistinguishable from the live AI path The deterministic fallback engine needed to produce screenplay analysis that felt genuinely thoughtful - not canned. I built scene-aware demo responses that reference real props, characters, and Director's Memory rule numbers so the 9-step walkthrough demonstrates the full product experience even without a Gemini API key configured. Accomplishments that we're proud of The Human-In-The-Loop security guarantee is real and enforced at the tool layer - not just a UI convention. apply_revision genuinely rejects unauthorized commits with a structured error response. All 8 WebMCP tools are verifiable in Chrome DevTools in under 30 seconds. Any judge can open F12 , run window._STORYROOM_WEBMCP_.tools , and see the full registry. They can call any tool directly from the console. The 9-step deterministic demo works completely offline. Zero API keys, zero setup, zero loading screens - the entire WebMCP collaboration workflow runs in one click for any evaluator. The continuity auditing is genuinely useful. The check_continuity tool catches a real planted narrative contradiction (a prop locked in a safe in Scene 4 being examined without an unlocking action in Scene 7) - the kind of error that slips through human review but a structured agent catches immediately. Building a product that feels premium, not like a proof of concept. From the cinematic design language to the visual diff review to the Director's Memory rules system, StoryRoom feels like a tool a real filmmaker would want to use. What we learned WebMCP's document.modelContext is genuinely powerful for domain-specific applications. The moment you give an agent structured, typed access to live application state instead of raw text, the quality of its reasoning improves dramatically - because hallucination requires filling in gaps, and structured tools leave fewer gaps. The Human-In-The-Loop pattern is not a limitation on AI capability - it is a trust feature. Agents that can be overruled are agents that can be trusted with higher-stakes tasks. The HITL gate is what makes directors willing to let the AI touch their screenplay at all. Deterministic fallback engines are engineering discipline, not a shortcut. A project that only works when the right API key is configured is a fragile demo. Building a high-quality offline simulation layer means the product experience is always fully evaluable. State synchronization between a reactive UI and a browser-standard tool registry is a genuinely new design problem that WebMCP introduces. The mutable ref pattern we developed is something future WebMCP + React projects will likely need too. What's next for StoryRoom Multi-agent collaboration : Allow two external agents to work on different scenes simultaneously, with the director moderating conflicts between competing proposed rewrites through a merge review interface export_final_draft WebMCP tool : Let the agent package the approved screenplay into a properly formatted Final Draft (.fdx) or PDF with one tool call after director sign-off Voice direction : Let directors leave audio notes on scenes that the agent transcribes, interprets as creative directives, and uses to inform future analyze_scene evaluations Production breakdown integration : Add get_budget_impact and check_location_availability tools so the agent can flag rewrites that introduce expensive new locations or VFX requirements before the director approves them Pers

title: Pip The Mug
pitch: PIP the Mug turns eight desk objects into staff. Typed WebMCP tools, state-gated access, and an Upper Management decision before termination.
about_excerpt: PIP the Mug turns eight desk objects into staff. Typed WebMCP tools, state-gated access, and an Upper Management decision before termination. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Product teams that expose refunds, account deletion, payouts, and administrative approvals to agents face a concrete operational problem: which actions an agent may take depends on live application state, and mistakes can be irreversible. PIP the Mug is an executable reference for that contract. It derives an agent's capabilities from live state, validates targets with state-built input schemas, pauses irreversible work through requestUserInteraction when the client supports it, and returns requires_user_action without changing application state when it does not. It also keeps an auditable Agent-versus-Human record. WebMCP lets the page itself express these rules. DOM automation alone cannot declare or audit them. The HR satire makes the mechanism inspectable in about one minute. Agents are already on the web, and they are bad at pretending to be a mouse. Selector-driven automation couples an agent to the page's structure and makes its capabilities hard to discover and constrain safely. WebMCP fixes this. The page gives the agent named, typed tools. Availability follows live state. Anything irreversible stops for a human, and both parties read the same record of what happened. I wanted all of that visible on one screen. A real HR product would have been dreary. A mug that has held the same coffee for three weeks is not. What it does PIP the Mug is a top-down desk. Eight objects are employees with personnel files. You are upper management. Your browser agent is HR. The page registers nine tools on document.modelContext : list_staff get_personnel_file write_review put_on_pip resolve_pip promote relocate terminate get_org_chart Availability follows state. resolve_pip is registered only while at least one PIP is open, and terminate refuses alumni and anyone promoted in the current quarter. PIP the Mug supports requestUserInteraction as its preferred confirmation path. A supporting client collects the human decision through that callback. In the current Codex WebMCP shim, the callback is unsupported. The safe fallback returns requires_user_action , opens Form SEP-1 visibly on the page, and leaves employment unchanged. The WebMCP workflow stops and asks Upper Management to decide on the page. This fallback is a cooperative handoff for clients without the callback, not a security boundary against separate DOM automation. The activity log attributes the request to Agent and the confirmation to Human, so the audit trail shows where the WebMCP workflow stopped and the person took over. Everything also works by click and drag. If WebMCP is unavailable, a banner says so and the desk still runs. State is stored as one JSON document in localStorage . How I built it I built PIP the Mug with client-side TypeScript and Vite. It has no backend, model, analytics, or login. Reviews, PIPs, and separation notices render as paperwork. Agent tool calls open the matching personnel file so a human watching the tab can follow along. I generated the sprites with PixelLab. The application deploys as a static site to Vercel through vercel.json . Challenges I ran into The WebMCP getter moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext . I detect both and prefer the document version. State-dependent availability is easy to get wrong. If every state change tears down every tool, the agent can lose its tool list midway through a run. I rebuild only when a tool's registered metadata changes: Name Title Description Input schema Annotations Read tools that can return text written by a human or agent carry untrustedContentHint . The confirmation path was the hardest part. requestUserInteraction is not available in every client, and the current Codex WebMCP shim throws when it is called. My fallback had to leave employment unchanged, return a structured requires_user_action result, and open exactly one SEP-1 request. Execution matters too. An agent that mutates JSON while the panel still says "Select an employee" looks like plumbing. Papers had to land on the desk, personnel files had to open, and captions had to remain visible. Accomplishments I'm proud of I ran the final verified demo through ChatGPT's in-app browser. All nine tools appeared. relocate moved Phone Charger into the drawer on the open tab. Writes opened the personnel file and created visible paperwork, so I could watch HR work. terminate returned requires_user_action . The activity log recorded the request as Agent and the confirmation as Human. The joke survived contact with a real agent. The confirmation before termination is not a modal staged for screenshots. It is the visible handoff between what the WebMCP tool prepares and the decision Upper Management makes next. What I learned Tool descriptions are the agent UX. I learned to write them like instructions, not API comments. If a write is irreversible, I mark it and return control for a human decision. If a tool should not exist in the current state, I do not register it. I also assume the runtime's confirmation API may be unavailable and design the fallback first. A screen recording only works if the desk moves when the agent does. Logs alone are not enough. What's next for PIP the Mug I plan to keep PIP the Mug online as a compact reference and testbed for state-gated, human-approved WebMCP actions. The pattern is the point: On a storefront, terminate becomes issue_refund . In account settings, it becomes delete_account . In an admin panel, it becomes any destructive administrative action. The agent gathers the file, drafts the paperwork, and requests a decision. Semantic tools replace DOM guessing. Availability follows state. Humans approve irreversible writes, and both sides share an audit trail. The mug was just easier to feel sorry for. title: Agentic Sandbox
pitch: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together.
about_excerpt: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together. Like Comment Story Updates Current post-lock recovery with human Packaging lock, stale-write rejection, and receipt-backed evidence. Six narrow WebMCP Site Tools discovered in the live host. Scenario comparison: same output, cheaper standard-supplier plan passes the cost cap. Deterministic lock-bound proof: 9,252 < 10,937 under the human Packaging lock. The problem Factory planning decisions rarely happen in one place. They move through dashboards, spreadsheets, a simulation specialist, and an approval meeting, and each handoff loses context and authority. A generic assistant can make that worse by recommending a control that an operator has just taken off the table. What it does Agentic Sandbox makes the website itself the shared, inspectable decision surface. It is a deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a browser agent plan against the same versioned state. The demo mission is concrete: increase good output by at least 20%, keep total cost within 8% of baseline, add no machine, and do not increase defects. The agent reads the line, creates two bounded hypotheses, simulates a 16-hour shift, and compares immutable receipts. Scenario A reaches 11,114 good units but costs €47,670.51 and fails the cost cap. Scenario B reaches the same 11,114 units for €45,170.51 and passes all four constraints. Then comes the important moment: while the agent is working, the human locks Packaging. That click advances the factory revision and makes earlier evidence historical. The agent’s next write still carries the old revision, so it fails atomically with STALE_FACTORY ; nothing is applied or silently rebased. The agent re-reads the authority state, replans with only controls that remain available, and receives an auditable answer: under the Packaging lock, at most 9,252 good units are possible while the mission requires 10,937. The target is proven infeasible by deterministic evidence, not by model prose. That safe disagreement is the product. The human can change the admissible action space without restarting the conversation, and the agent can recover without overriding the new rule. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, the agent would have to infer state from pixels and click by coordinates, or the product would need a separate chatbot and backend with a second source of truth. Instead, the page exposes exactly six narrow Site Tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_factory_snapshot get_scenario_snapshot create_scenario apply_scenario_changes run_factory_simulation compare_simulation_runs The human interface and these tools share one application-owned command bus. Schemas are closed, handlers validate independently, and every mutation carries a request ID plus expected factory, scenario, and lock revisions. There is deliberately no agent-accessible lock, unlock, force, arbitrary patch, optimizer, ERP, PLC, SCADA, or machine-control tool. Human authority stays human. How it was built Agentic Sandbox is a self-contained React 19 + TypeScript + Vite app deployed on Vercel. The deterministic engine models 64 fixed ticks, uses integer/fixed-point arithmetic, and computes production, defects, energy, cost, constraints, invariants, and bottleneck evidence in the page. Each simulation creates an immutable, content-addressed SHA-256 receipt with exact operands, accepted/rejected operations, tick-level state, and an optional lock-bound proof. No displayed KPI comes from the language model. The hardest implementation problem was making a mid-plan disagreement trustworthy rather than dramatic: old authority must fail closed without erasing evidence that was valid when created. That required explicit revision precedence, atomic stale-write rejection, immutable receipts, and visible current-versus-historical states. The submitted flow was replayed against the public deployment in a supported WebMCP host, including discovery, comparison, the human lock, stale rejection, re-read, replan, and proof. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when a website already owns meaningful state, rules, and actions. Exposing those capabilities directly is more reliable than asking an agent to reconstruct them from pixels. A refusal can be more valuable than another recommendation: STALE_FACTORY proves that human authority survived concurrency, and 9252 < 10937 proves why the target cannot be met under the active lock. Potential impact and what’s next The first users I have in mind are plant planners, industrial engineers, and continuous-improvement teams working on line balancing, shift planning, and supplier what-if analysis. A production version could connect this exact capability, revision, lock, and receipt pattern to a validated digital twin, while ERP, PLC, SCADA, purchase, and physical-machine changes remain behind existing approvals. The broader pattern applies to any high-consequence planning interface: expose narrow capabilities, bind actions to explicit versions, preserve the human veto, and return evidence a machine can check.
