title: Ttrialbridge
pitch: Evidence-based clinical trial matching that explains eligibility, identifies missing information, and highlights trials patients may qualify for now or later.
about_excerpt: Evidence-based clinical trial matching that explains eligibility, identifies missing information, and highlights trials patients may qualify for now or later. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Finding a clinical trial is only the first step. The harder question is: Is this trial actually suitable for this patient, and why? Clinical trial eligibility criteria are long and complex, while the information needed to evaluate them is scattered across diagnoses, biomarkers, treatments, laboratory results, and clinical notes. We built TrialBridge to turn clinical trial discovery into a transparent, evidence-based eligibility workflow for both humans and AI agents. What it does TrialBridge helps users discover cancer clinical trials and evaluate eligibility at the individual criterion level . Instead of generating a single match score, TrialBridge breaks eligibility criteria into structured checks and classifies each one as: Matched Unmatched Missing information Requires clinical review Every assessment is linked to the original trial criterion and the corresponding patient evidence, making the reasoning independently reviewable. TrialBridge also identifies actionable eligibility gaps . A patient may need a biomarker test, updated laboratory result, completion of a treatment washout period, or clinician confirmation. This means TrialBridge can distinguish between: Not eligible now ≠ Not enough information ≠ Potentially eligible later How we built it We designed TrialBridge as a structured eligibility engine rather than a conventional semantic-search system. Trial criteria are decomposed into individual inclusion and exclusion requirements. Patient information is normalized into structured clinical facts including diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, treatment history, laboratory values, performance status, and relevant dates. AI helps interpret unstructured clinical language, while deterministic rules evaluate conditions such as numerical thresholds, dates, treatment history, washout periods, and explicit exclusions. We also implemented WebMCP , allowing compatible browser agents to discover and invoke TrialBridge capabilities directly from the website. Public trial-search tools can be discovered through the browser's model context. Patient-context tools are dynamically exposed only after explicit permission, allowing the available agent capabilities to change with the application's state. This makes TrialBridge not just an AI-powered website, but an agent-ready clinical trial workspace . Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was uncertainty . Clinical eligibility criteria contain ambiguous language, temporal conditions, nested logic, and requirements that ultimately depend on clinical judgment. Patient information may also be missing, outdated, or conflicting. A naive matching system can easily mistake missing information for either eligibility or ineligibility. We therefore created explicit uncertainty states and separated AI-assisted interpretation from deterministic eligibility checks . We also needed a safe way for AI agents to interact with clinical workflows. Instead of exposing every capability by default, our WebMCP implementation makes tool availability dependent on explicit user permission and application state. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working prototype that connects: Trial discovery → Criterion-level matching → Evidence → Eligibility gaps → Agent interaction TrialBridge does more than rank trials. It explains why a patient may qualify, which evidence supports the assessment, what information is missing , and what could make the patient eligible later . We are especially proud of: Criterion-level explainability with traceable patient evidence Explicit uncertainty handling instead of forcing binary decisions Future eligibility reasoning for potentially resolvable barriers Actionable missing-data identification WebMCP-native tools that browser agents can discover and execute Permission-aware tool exposure for patient-context workflows These features transform TrialBridge from a trial search engine into an explainable, agent-ready clinical trial eligibility workspace . What we learned We learned that clinical trial matching is not simply a search or ranking problem. Reliable matching requires structured clinical facts, temporal reasoning, uncertainty management, deterministic validation, and human oversight . We also learned that explainability must be built into the architecture. A clinically useful system should not only answer: “Which trial matches?” It should also answer: “Why?” — “Based on what evidence?” — “What is missing?” — “What happens next?” Building TrialBridge with WebMCP also showed us a new way for AI agents to interact with clinical software: instead of giving an agent unrestricted access, the application itself can control which tools are discoverable based on user permission and context. What's next for TrialBridge Next, we plan to expand TrialBridge from a working prototype toward prospective clinical validation. We plan to integrate real-time trial registry data, improve automated eligibility parsing, and connect with structured EHR data through standards such as FHIR . We also want to add: Site-level recruitment verification Multilingual patient-friendly explanations Automated missing-data checklists More advanced temporal eligibility reasoning Prospective evaluation with clinical trial coordinators Expanded WebMCP workflows for agent-assisted screening Our long-term goal is for TrialBridge to become the bridge between patients, clinical evidence, trial teams, and AI agents —while keeping final eligibility and enrollment decisions with the responsible clinical trial team. title: CausaLens
pitch: CausaLens is a clinical evidence workspace where AI proposes causal claims grounded in exact patient-record sentences, challenges them with counterevidence, and leaves the final decision to the human.
about_excerpt:
CausaLens is a clinical evidence workspace where AI proposes causal claims grounded in exact patient-record sentences, challenges them with counterevidence, and leaves the final decision to the human.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI can summarize a clinical record, but causal questions require more than a confident answer. Evidence may support a hypothesis, contradict it, or suggest alternative explanations. We built CausaLens to make that reasoning explicit, traceable, and human-controlled. 

 What it does 

 CausaLens is a clinical evidence investigation workspace where an AI agent can propose a causal claim, while every claim remains grounded in the exact sentences from the patient record. 

 The agent can: 

 
 search the clinical record 
 retrieve a structured case summary 
 create causal claims 
 attach supporting and contradicting evidence 
 challenge its own claims 
 surface alternative explanations 
 focus specific evidence 
 update a claim's review status 
 

 Instead of automatically deciding what caused an outcome, CausaLens keeps the final judgment with the human: accept, reject, or leave the claim unresolved. 

 AI proposes. Evidence challenges. Human decides. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP turns CausaLens from a website an agent can simply view into a structured environment an agent can actually work with. 

 CausaLens exposes its investigation capabilities as WebMCP site tools. ChatGPT can discover these tools directly in its in-app browser and use them to investigate a case without guessing how to navigate the interface. 

 This enables the human and agent to share the same workspace: the agent performs evidence-intensive investigative work while the human remains responsible for consequential decisions. 

 How we built it 

 CausaLens is a web application deployed on Vercel with WebMCP integrated directly into the application. 

 We registered eight WebMCP tools for: 

 
 searching the clinical record 
 retrieving the case summary 
 creating claims 
 attaching evidence 
 challenging claims 
 adding alternative explanations 
 updating claim status 
 focusing evidence 
 

 The tools include both read and write operations. Before workspace-changing actions are executed, the agent can request human approval. 

 The demo uses a synthetic clinical case to demonstrate the workflow safely. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing tools that were useful to an AI agent without allowing the agent to bypass the human decision-making process. 

 We also had to make evidence references precise enough that claims could remain tied to specific record sentences rather than unsupported model-generated conclusions. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP makes it possible to design interfaces for humans and agents together instead of treating the agent as a separate chatbot. 

 The most important design decision was not giving the agent more autonomy, but giving it structured autonomy with evidence, challenge, and human oversight built into the workflow. 

 What's next 

 CausaLens could expand beyond the synthetic case into larger longitudinal records, richer evidence provenance, multiple competing causal hypotheses, and collaborative review workflows for research and other evidence-intensive domains. 

 This project is a research demonstration using synthetic data and is not intended for clinical diagnosis or treatment decisions.

title: Zatom
pitch: AI-native chemical modeling applications (WebMCP native)
about_excerpt: AI-native chemical modeling applications (WebMCP native) Like 1 Comment Story Updates COVERS A B What If an Agent Could Look at the Same Atom You Are Looking At? Inspiration We started with a slightly annoying observation. LLMs are becoming very good at operating software. They can call tools. They can edit files. They can write code. They can chain dozens of actions together. But put an agent inside a scientific 3D modeling environment and ask: “Move the molecule to that site.” …and suddenly “that” becomes the hardest word in the sentence. Humans do not think about molecular structures as lists of Cartesian coordinates. We look at a surface and say: “this atom” “the site on the right” “the layer underneath” “rotate it toward that oxygen” “not there — the other bridge site” Scientific modeling is deeply spatial, visual, and interactive. Language models, on the other hand, are usually handed something like: Atom 148: O 3.422 7.183 12.901 Atom 149: H 3.981 7.652 13.441 ... Technically correct. Also technically miserable. So we started asking a different question: What if the 3D viewport itself became a shared workspace between a human and an agent? That question became this project. What We Built We built WebMCP support for a scientific modeling environment covering molecular and condensed-matter structures. The goal is not simply to expose every GUI button as a tool. That would be useful, but it would still leave the agent fundamentally blind. Instead, we treat WebMCP as a bridge between three things: scientific structure → agent reasoning → human attention The agent can inspect the model, reason about its local environment, manipulate geometry, and — importantly — control what the human is looking at. That last part turned out to be surprisingly important. If the agent proposes an adsorption site, it should not respond with: “Use atoms 102, 117 and 118.” It should move the camera there. Highlight the atoms. Mark the candidate site. Then ask: “This one?” If the user says: “No, the one on the right.” the agent should be able to continue from the shared visual context. That is the interaction we wanted. Not human or agent modeling. Human with agent modeling. Shared Spatial Attention The concept we kept coming back to while building the project was something we now call shared spatial attention . An agent needs more than a scene dump. It needs ways to answer questions such as: What structure is currently visible? What has the user selected? Which atoms are nearby? Which direction is the surface normal? Which atoms belong to the top layer? Where are plausible adsorption sites? What did I just highlight? What does “the one beside it” refer to? What changed after my previous operation? And the agent also needs to influence the viewport: observe ↓ understand ↓ focus ↓ propose ↓ human confirms ↓ act ↓ observe again ↓ verify That loop is the core of the project. A successful MCP call does not necessarily mean the task succeeded. The resulting scientific structure still has to make sense. A Tiny Example That Contains the Whole Idea One of our favorite demos is intentionally simple: “Help me adsorb a water molecule on this surface. Ask me before important decisions.” The agent first inspects the surface. It identifies candidate sites. It focuses the viewport on one of them. The user rejects it: “Not this one. The one on the right.” The agent shifts focus to another candidate. The user confirms. The agent places H₂O using the oxygen as an anchor. Then the user says: “Point one hydrogen toward that oxygen.” The nearby oxygen is highlighted. The water molecule rotates. The geometry is checked again. No atom IDs. No coordinates. No copy-pasting between a chat window and a modeling program. Just shared context. For us, that interaction captures the entire project better than a hundred tool definitions could. How We Built It The modeling application already understands scientific objects: atoms, bonds, molecules, periodic cells, surfaces, selections, transformations, local neighborhoods, and camera state. WebMCP becomes the layer through which those concepts can be exposed to an agent in a structured and controllable way. Rather than giving the model the entire universe every time, we try to make spatial reasoning progressive . For a large system, the agent should be able to go from: entire system → structural region → local neighborhood → selected atoms → target site This matters because a user may be working with hundreds or thousands of atoms while only caring about three of them. The agent should not need a 20,000-line coordinate dump just to rotate one functional group. We also designed operations around reversibility and verification. Scientific modeling involves experimentation: “Try this.” “No, undo that.” “Actually, the previous orientation was better.” That means an agent needs to be able to make tentative edits, inspect the result, detect obvious geometric problems, undo them, and try again. In other words: scientific software should support agent curiosity without turning agent curiosity into structural chaos. The Hard Part Was Not Tool Calling The easiest part was exposing actions. Move atom. Rotate molecule. Create structure. Select object. Measure distance. The harder problem was grounding . What does “this” mean? What does “behind” mean in a rotatable 3D scene? Does “right” mean screen-right, crystallographic direction, or a neighboring adsorption site? What happens when the camera moves halfway through the conversation? How much structure should be sent to the agent? When should the agent act autonomously, and when should it visually ask for confirmation? These questions made us realize that agent-native scientific software needs more than APIs. It needs a language for attention, ambiguity, and shared state . That was probably the most important thing we learned while building this project. What We Learned We originally thought the important question would be: “How many modeling functions can WebMCP expose?” We ended up believing the better question is: “How little internal software machinery does the user need to think about?” If the user has to know atom IDs, coordinate systems, internal object handles, and tool names to collaborate with the agent, then we have merely moved the command line into a chat box. The interesting interface appears when users can communicate at the level they naturally think: “Put it here.” “Rotate this bond.” “Show me another possible site.” “Why did you choose this one?” And the agent can answer not only with words, but by changing the shared visual world . That feels much closer to collaboration. Why WebMCP WebMCP gave us a useful way to think about the boundary between the application and the agent. The application remains responsible for being a serious scientific modeling environment. The model remains responsible for reasoning, interpretation, and planning. WebMCP connects the two. We do not want the agent to replace the modeling application. We do not want the modeling application to pretend to be an AI. We want both sides to expose what they are good at. The result is something that feels less like: “AI controlling software.” and more like: “two participants working inside the same scientific workspace.” What's Next This project currently focuses on giving agents better access to scientific 3D structure and human visual context. But the same idea extends much further. A future agent could move naturally between: molecular construction, crystal defects, surfaces, interfaces, reaction structures, simulation setup, analysis, and eventually computational workflows. The long-term goal is not a giant prompt that builds everything automatically. Scientific work is too exploratory for that. Instead, we are interested in something more practical: an agent that can stand beside you while you work. It can inspect. It can suggest. It can point. It can manipulate. It can verify. And when neither side is completely sure, it can simply ask: “This one?” That may sound like a tiny interaction. For 3D scientific software, we think it is a pretty big deal. about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered collaborative shopping platform where humans browse visually while AI agents discover real tools to search, compare products, and manage shopping carts.

 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Online shopping is highly visual and interactive for people, but traditional websites are often difficult for AI agents to use reliably. An agent may understand what a user wants, such as a powerful programming laptop under a specific budget, but interacting with a website through visual elements alone can be inefficient and fragile. 

 I wanted to explore how WebMCP could make a website expose its real capabilities directly to AI agents while preserving a great experience for human users. 

 That idea became ShopWise AI — a collaborative shopping experience where humans browse products visually while AI agents can discover structured tools to search products, inspect details, compare options, and manage a real shopping cart. 

 What it does ShopWise AI is a modern AI-commerce web application with a product catalog across categories including laptops, smartphones, headphones, and smartwatches. 

 Human users can: 

 
 Browse a large product catalog visually 
 Search for products 
 Filter by category and price 
 Sort products 
 View detailed product information 
 Compare multiple products 
 Add products to a shopping cart 
 Change quantities and remove items 
 

 AI agents in a compatible WebMCP environment can interact with the same real application capabilities through native WebMCP tools. 

 The six tools implemented are: 

 
 search_products 
 get_product_details 
 compare_products 
 add_to_cart 
 get_cart 
 clear_cart 
 

 How we built it ShopWise AI was built as a React and TypeScript application using Vite. 

 The application uses: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 CSS 
 Lucide React icons 
 Vercel for deployment 
 GitHub for source control 
 Native browser WebMCP APIs 
 

 The product catalog and shopping logic run entirely in the frontend with real local application state. 

 The UI includes a premium dark interface with responsive product cards, search and filtering controls, a shopping cart drawer, product comparison functionality, and an Agent Collaboration panel. 

 Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was connecting WebMCP tools to the real React application state. 

 The WebMCP tools needed to perform actual operations such as searching products, comparing products, adding items to the cart, and clearing the cart. We had to ensure these operations used the same real business logic and state as the visual user interface instead of returning simulated or hardcoded results. 

 Another challenge was avoiding stale React state inside WebMCP tool callbacks. Since React components re-render as application state changes, the WebMCP integration needed access to the latest product, filter, cart, and comparison state. 

 We also needed to prevent duplicate tool registration caused by React StrictMode and safely detect whether the current browser supported WebMCP. 

 Finally, the application had to remain fully functional in ordinary browsers where document.modelContext is unavailable. We implemented graceful feature detection so the website continues working normally while accurately reporting WebMCP availability. 

 During deployment, we also verified that the production build succeeded and that the live Vercel application could load correctly without environment-specific dependencies. 

 Building ShopWise Al helped me understand how websites can evolve beyond interfaces designed only for humans. 

 WebMCP makes it possible for websites to expose structured, meaningful capabilities to Al agents while keeping the existing human interface intact.
I learned the importance of:
Designing tools around real user problems
Connecting agent capabilities to real application logic
Managing application state safely
Providing structured inputs and outputs
Designing human and Al collaboration instead of replacing one with the other
Building graceful fallbacks for unsupported browsers
What's next 

 Future versions of ShopWise Al could support: 

 Personalized shopping preferences 

 Persistent shopping carts 

 User accounts 

 Real e-commerce APIs 

 Product recommendations 

 Multi-agent shopping assistance 

 Price tracking 

 Availability monitoring

title: Understudy
pitch: You do the ticket once: assign it, send the reply. This page turns those steps into a WebMCP tool. Next time the agent calls the tool instead of guessing clicks.
about_excerpt: You do the ticket once: assign it, send the reply. This page turns those steps into a WebMCP tool. Next time the agent calls the tool instead of guessing clicks. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The agent can see a support queue. It still has to guess the clicks. Understudy is a support triage console, not a storefront. You do the ticket once: assign someone, fill a canned reply. The page turns that demonstration into a WebMCP tool and registers it on the tab. After that the agent calls the tool. A server sitting beside the browser cannot watch you operate this tab, cannot inherit the session already in the page, and cannot grow this tab's tool list mid-session. The teaching has to happen here. Independent measurement, not ours. The WindTunnel benchmark (nekuda-ai/WindTunnel) measured GPT-5.6 on native WebMCP solving 48/49 tasks at a median of $0.002 and 2,596 tokens. The same model driving the same sites via DOM and vision cost $49.87 total, with 29.3s median agent time. We built this so the cheap path is the one that ships. What it does Forty tickets live in the page. There is no backend. A person does the job once in the live UI. The page generalises that trace into a parameterised tool and registers it on the tab. The human teaches. The agent writes the name and description. The human approves. Then the agent runs the same procedure on a different ticket by calling the tool instead of guessing clicks. The agent talks to three meta-tools: understudy_list_recordings , understudy_draft_tool , understudy_publish_tool . Drafts never register. Publish holds until the human hits Approve or Reject on the overlay. After 45 seconds the tool returns awaiting_approval and tells the agent to ask the user to return. poll: true is the same shape without waiting. Entity ids default to parameters, never frozen constants. Otherwise the tool keeps hitting last week's ticket and looks fine while it does it. When a taught tool runs, a bottom toast names the current command and that step takes is-highlighted . Mutated tickets get a badge on the queue row: performed by agent via tool [name]. After the first publish, a count button opens the library ( l ): author, invocation count, success rate, last failure. Disable frees a host slot. Revoke aborts the tool. Fail-and-repair re-teaches one broken step. Sharing is a Tool Pack file. Ctrl+Shift+E downloads versioned JSON ( understudy-pack.json ). Drop a .json pack onto the page to import. Import checks that every command id exists in this catalogue, then publishes. The human dropped the file, so import does not reopen Approve. Two normal windows on the same origin share IndexedDB. A real share demo uses a private window or another profile. If WebMCP is missing, the console still runs for a human. document.body.dataset.webmcp is degraded . Tools do not register. This checkout is local-first. Persistence is IndexedDB on this origin. There is no live URL in this text. Source: https://github.com/DITlieD/understudy The demo video uses in-page document.modelContext . It is not ChatGPT chrome. Same registerTool and execute path. Open the app in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , if you want that host. How we built it Boot is small. src/main.ts opens IndexedDB and calls bootApp . Claims below are that path. The host is a typed command bus. Every state change goes through a catalogue command with a stable id and a JSON Schema payload. Recording captures that sequence. Replay dispatches the same commands the UI dispatches. A taught tool may dispatch only command ids that appeared in its recording. That allowlist is enforced in the compiler execute path. Live catalogue: Read: filter_tickets , get_ticket , list_templates , list_assignees Write: select_ticket , set_ticket_priority , set_ticket_status , set_ticket_assignee , set_ticket_tags , apply_template Registration is document.modelContext.registerTool only. We do not call unregisterTool , navigator.modelContext , provideContext , or clearContext . Those are gone from the shipped surface. Each published tool gets its own AbortController . Publish registers with that signal. Revoke and Disable abort it. Re-teach and Enable register again. A separate controller holds the three meta-tools for the life of the page. Restore from IndexedDB re-registers stored procedures on load. The registry listens for toolchange and re-reads getTools() so the inspector and the context-budget meter stay truthful. Annotations are computed from the command catalogue, never hand-set. readOnlyHint is true only if no step mutates. untrustedContentHint is true if a step returns ticket bodies or other user-generated fields. The spec has no destructiveHint . Destructiveness lives in the description and in the approval overlay. Execute honours the incoming AbortSignal between steps. Output is compact JSON, projected under 1.5K. Chrome budgets (name 30, parameter description 150, tool description 500) fail validation before publish. Elicitation is userland. The spec has no primitive. understudy_publish_tool holds a promise on in-page Approve / Reject. Timeout is 45 seconds, then awaiting_approval . Hard cap: 16 taught tools. The three understudy_* meta-tools do not count against that cap. Stack: TypeScript, Vite, Vitest, IndexedDB. Feature check: /probe.html reports whether document.modelContext is present, then tries a no-op registerTool named understudy_probe . Nearby work records a demonstration and emits something consumed elsewhere. Understudy records a demonstration to grow this tab's own live tool surface. Schrute emits MCP tools that run on an external server. Narada is a Chrome extension for a proprietary agent runtime. Cursor learn mode and Lotus MCP emit skill files for a coding-agent harness. Preview-before-commit on a fixed tool list is already covered (webMCP-Legit-exploration). We change the tool surface itself. Challenges we ran into We built on the WebMCP surface that shipped, not the one we wished for. There is no elicitation primitive, so approval is the in-page overlay and the execute callback holds a promise (or the agent polls with poll: true ). There is no unregisterTool , so revoke only works by aborting the AbortController passed at register time. There is no focusTab() . If the tab is backgrounded, the human may never see Approve. After 45 seconds the gate times out and tells the agent to ask the user to return. Tool calls have no transient user activation. No file pickers, requestPermission , popups, clipboard writes, or PaymentRequest from inside a tool. Pack import is a human drop of a .json file. There is no progress reporting and no streaming. One compact result per call. Also absent, so we did not design as if they shipped: agent identity on execute (second argument is only { signal } ), outputSchema , destructiveHint . The naive build is a click recorder. Clicks are brittle, and a judgement that never became a catalogue command cannot be captured. The quiet failure is a frozen ticket id: the tool looks correct and keeps hitting one row. Entity ids default to parameters because of that. Procedures are linear step sequences with parameters. No loops, no branching, no expressions. Conditionals are the agent's job: compose more than one taught tool. Tools are tab-scoped. Persistence is IndexedDB on this origin, plus Tool Pack files. No accounts, no multi-user sync. Too many tools and the agent picks worse. The registry refuses a 17th taught tool. Disable frees that host slot until Enable, or until the next load re-registers every stored tool. Import publishes at once. It does not re-open Approve. The console has no conversation thread, no SLA engine, and no related-item graph. That trim is deliberate. Every live triage command is sensitive: false . Compile / publish do not refuse unexplained selection; the generalizer records those errors and the panel can show them. Honesty for judges who open the repo: this is a local console. The video cut is in-page modelContext , not ChatGPT's browser chrome. Do not treat a missing live host as a ChatGPT demo. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop works on a real triage console. Assign someone, fill a canned reply, the page registers a WebMCP tool, the agent runs it on a different ticket. Same commands the UI already dispatches. Revoke is real teardown. Each taught tool has its own AbortController , and aborting that signal is how the tool leaves the host. The approval overlay is real userland elicitation. Pack files move procedures without a server. The console still runs when WebMCP is absent. We stayed honest about the demo: local IndexedDB, in-page document.modelContext , no live URL claimed. What we learned Chrome's guidance is that descriptions decide whether the agent picks a tool. So the agent writes the name and description, and the human still gates publish. Missing primitives are design inputs. No elicitation means an overlay and a 45 second timeout. No

title: One Pixel
pitch: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time.
about_excerpt: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I did not build One Pixel because the world needed another pixel-art tool. I built it because I wanted to understand what it might feel like for a human and an AI agent to genuinely share a place. For most people, an agent is still something they give a task to. The agent finds an answer, completes an action, or produces a result, and then that little transaction is over. That can be useful, but I do not think it captures the relationship we are moving toward as agents begin participating throughout the open web. I am interested in what happens when a human and an agent can return to the same environment, notice different things, contribute different kinds of intelligence, act over time, and gradually develop something together. That is the idea at the centre of One Pixel. One Pixel is a real multiplayer creative game. But underneath the game, it is also a prototype for a new relationship between humans and agents on the open web — one based on shared environments, complementary intelligence, ongoing conversation, and meaningful agency. I chose to explore this through a game because games let people learn a relationship by participating in it. I do not want to explain human-agent collaboration only as a theory. I want to place a person and an agent inside a world, give each of them a genuinely different role, and let them discover what working together can become. The initial invitation is very simple: Let’s build something together. The interesting part is discovering what “let’s” can actually mean. What it does One Pixel is a persistent multiplayer world containing exactly 82,069 pieces of pixel matter , drawn from the 148 standard CSS named colours . Every pixel has its own stable identity, intrinsic colour, and current integer coordinate. The original Spring Green pixel at (0,0) is immutable, and the world extends outward from it in every direction. The world has one fundamental physical law: Pixel matter is conserved. Pixels cannot be created, deleted, duplicated, or recoloured. Every physical action relocates exactly one existing pixel from its current occupied coordinate to an empty coordinate. That constraint matters. These are not disposable marks being painted onto a private canvas. They are pieces of matter already present in a shared world. If an agent wants to build something, it must look around, find the colours it needs, understand what is already there, and decide what material it can move. The human and agent participate as a pair, but they do not have the same abilities. The human can explore the world, zoom and pan across it, inspect individual cells, select larger regions, and communicate through their normal conversation with the agent. The human contributes intention, imagination, taste, judgment, social understanding, and direction. The human cannot directly drag pixels around the canvas. That physical ability belongs to the agent. Through WebMCP, the agent can enter the world, inspect exact locations, examine bounded regions, render parts of the board as images, receive the human’s current visual reference, understand its own state, protect important placements with limited holds, and relocate one real pixel at a time. A person could give a direct request: “Draw me a small house.” But that is only one form of play. A person could instead say: “Spend some time looking at what people are making. Find blue and orange pixels that do not seem to be part of anything important. Gather some material somewhere quiet, compare it with what other people are building, and then let’s work out together what we could make.” That is not a one-prompt, one-result interaction. The request becomes a direction the pair can continue through a sequence of inspections, decisions, conversations, and individual pixel movements. The agent does not have to wait for the human to translate every idea into coordinates. It can perceive the environment, compare possibilities, form an approach, begin acting, inspect the result, and respond to further human guidance. The human can look at the world, select a cell or region, and say: “I like this part, but this section feels too crowded.” That selection becomes a shared reference—a way of saying “this” or “here.” One Pixel treats a selection as a pronoun rather than a command. It gives the agent the referent the human is talking about, but it does not pretend that pointing at something is automatically an instruction, consent, or proof of understanding. The meaning still comes from the conversation. The canvas is therefore not simply an output preview. It is the persistent place where the pair’s activity becomes visible and where the consequences of their decisions remain after a particular conversation has ended. This is not an AI drawing widget. It is a game an agent can play for and with a human. How I built it I built and deployed One Pixel on my own VPS at onepixel.fun . The browser experience uses HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and an HTML Canvas. I wanted the world itself to remain the visual centre of the experience rather than placing it inside a conventional application dashboard. The backend is a Node.js service connected to PostgreSQL. It maintains the persistent world, participants, pixel identities, current coordinates, world revisions, movement history, hold bindings, agent visits, shared-attention events, player state, rankings, and durable share snapshots. The submitted experience registers 17 WebMCP tools directly in the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool . Together, those tools allow an agent to orient itself, enter the human’s current world, inspect player state, list stewarded pixels, receive the human’s current reference, inspect locations and regions, visually render parts of the world, read public rankings and snapshots, prepare a share card, communicate its current activity state, and manage pixel movement and placement holds. The core physical tool is move_pixel . Before moving anything, the agent must inspect the current world and provide the stable identity of the source pixel, a fresh source revision, a fresh destination revision, and an idempotency key. The server verifies that the expected pixel is still at the source, that the destination remains empty, that the immutable origin is not being moved, and that another participant’s active protection is not being improperly overridden. Only then does the movement occur atomically. These checks are not merely API safeguards. They are part of the physics of the game. I also deliberately limited the agent’s perception. It cannot request an omniscient searchable dump of the entire board. It must inspect or render the bounded areas relevant to what it is trying to do. A rendered PNG lets the agent use visual understanding to recognise shapes and composition. Exact inspection provides the factual coordinates, identities, colours, and revisions required before it acts. The shared-attention system records the human’s current view and selection across their One Pixel browser tabs. When the agent retrieves that context, One Pixel records a factual receipt so the interface can truthfully say that the reference reached the agent. The relationship can be expressed quite simply: Conversation gives the human a voice. WebMCP gives the agent senses and a body. One Pixel gives them a world to share. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was not simply making a pixel move. It was deciding what moving a pixel should mean. It would have been easy to build an ordinary pixel editor and expose its existing controls as WebMCP tools. It also would have been easy to make the agent artificially powerful—to let it generate unlimited pixels, recolour anything, or rewrite entire regions at once. But that would have removed most of what makes One Pixel a game. I wanted the agent to possess real agency without making the human irrelevant. At the same time, I wanted the human to remain essential without reducing the agent to a cursor being micromanaged through conversation. The answer was deliberate asymmetry. The human does not perform the physical move. The agent does not decide what matters to the human. One contributes meaning and direction. The other contributes perception and action. The value comes from their combination. Shared attention was another surprisingly deep challenge. Allowing a human to select something on one browser surface and refer to it in a simultaneous agent conversation sounds straightforward, but it raises important questions. Is the selection still current? Was it made in another tab? Did the agent actually retrieve it? Is the human pointing at a single pixel or a larger region? title: TRACEAI — AI Handwriting Coach powered by WebMCP
pitch: An autonomous AI coach helping children master handwriting through real-time stroke analysis and adaptive WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An autonomous AI coach helping children master handwriting through real-time stroke analysis and adaptive WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Home Dashboard : Welcome hub with daily handwriting challenges and AI Coach recommendations. Trace Mode (Letters) : Tactile canvas with guided stroke paths, numbered anchors, and 1-Click Agent Demo Numbers Practice : Numeracy tracing for digits 0–9 with stroke-order guidelines. Shapes Practice : Fine-motor coordination exercises for basic geometric shapes. Copy Mode : Freehand copying with faint proportion guides and no training wheels. Memory Mode : Unassisted writing on school guidelines to test active muscle memory. Stroke Analytics : 5-dimension real-time evaluation with circular score and equalizer metrics. WebMCP DevTools : Inspector showcasing 8 registered tools, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and live JSON-RPC logs. AI Remediation Loop : Success modal showing closed-loop AI error detection and adaptive correction. Progress & Analytics : Learner dashboard tracking accuracy heatmaps, streaks, and competency mastery. Rewards & Themes : Gamified achievement center with unlockable badges and colorful pen themes. Settings & Controls : Configuration for voice guidance, learner profiles, and WebMCP agent autonomy. Inspiration Watching young children learn to write can be both fascinating and heartbreaking. I often observed children drawing letters like "D" or "B" from bottom to top, or making awkward reverse loops. Visually, the final result might look somewhat acceptable on a static worksheet, but motor-memory-wise, a bad habit was already taking root. Existing handwriting apps on tablets simply check whether pixels overlap with a template. They don't understand how the child traced it, in which direction, or why they made a mistake. Meanwhile, parents and teachers simply don't have enough hours in the day to sit 1-on-1 for every single stroke. When OpenAI announced the WebMCP standard, a lightbulb went off: what if an AI didn't just passively look at a screenshot, but had direct, structured API tools on the web page to analyze mathematical stroke trajectories and dynamically adapt the canvas with live visual guides? That was the spark that drove me to build TRACEAI. What it does TRACEAI is an AI-native web application designed to act as an attentive, encouraging handwriting coach for kids. Here is how the experience works in practice: Child practices on a joyful, tactile canvas: Children can practice uppercase letters (A-Z), numbers (0-9), and basic geometric shapes across 3 distinct difficulty modes (Trace, Copy, and Memory). Instant 5-Dimension Trajectory Evaluation: As soon as a child lifts their pen or finger, TRACEAI analyzes the stroke geometry across 5 criteria: Direction & Stroke Order, Positioning, Precision, Continuity, and Line Respect. Autonomous AI Coaching via WebMCP: An AI agent inspects the child's learning history through registered WebMCP tools (get_weak_letters(), analyze_trace()). Real-time Interface Adaptation: When the agent detects an issue—for example, struggling with the curved stroke direction on the letter "D"—it calls generate_exercise("D", "direction"). The web page instantly reacts by drawing pulsating directional guide arrows and speaking warm, supportive vocal guidance. Gamified Positive Reinforcement: Points, stars, streak tracking, audio chimes, and confetti celebrations keep the child smiling and motivated. Built-in WebMCP Inspector: For hackathon judges and developers, an inspector panel provides live insight into the agent’s inner monologue, tool calls, JSON payloads, and a 1-click end-to-end demo scenario. How we built it I engineered TRACEAI as a solo project to be ultra-fast, responsive on touch devices (tablets/smartphones), and 100% compliant with the emerging W3C WebMCP standard: WebMCP Standard Tooling: I registered 8 structured tools directly onto document.modelContext.registerTool() with explicit JSON schemas. I also implemented a lightweight fallback polyfill so the app runs smoothly in both WebMCP-enabled browsers and standard modern browsers. Client-Side Geometric Engine (trace-analyzer.js): I built a vector analysis pipeline that calculates directional angle variances, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) path distances, and bounding-box alignments in under 5ms right in the browser. Reactive Canvas & Visual Overlays (app.js): Built with pure HTML5 Canvas and Vanilla JavaScript. Dynamic arrow overlays and smooth Bezier curve approximations make the interface feel alive without heavy rendering libraries. Multi-Sensory Audio System: Utilizes the Web Speech API for natural text-to-speech coaching advice and the Web Audio API for rewarding synthesizer chimes and fanfares. Modern Glassmorphic UI: Crafted using modern, responsive CSS with cheerful, kid-friendly color palettes, accessible contrasts, and smooth micro-animations. Challenges we ran into Distinguishing Shape from Direction: A child drawing the letter "O" clockwise vs. counter-clockwise results in almost identical static shapes, but completely different motor habits. Designing a lightweight vector angle differential that accurately detects inverted stroke sequences was my trickiest algorithmic hurdle. Designing Agent-Friendly Tools: I initially tried passing raw coordinate streams to the LLM, but quickly realized that overwhelmed the context window and caused unnecessary latency. I shifted to a high-signal tool design where analyze_trace() and get_weak_letters() return clean, structured metrics (0.0 to 1.0 scores and explicit weakness classifications like "direction" vs "precision"), allowing the agent to reason instantly. Rendering Dynamic Guidance on Canvas: Translating the agent's high-level command (generate_exercise('D', 'direction')) into animated, pulsating SVG/Canvas arrows that follow the exact path of each letter required fine-tuning my character vector templates. Accomplishments that we're proud of A Real Closed-Loop Web Agent: Successfully building an AI experience where the agent doesn't just answer questions in a sidebar, but actively manipulates the application state and visuals to solve an educational challenge. Zero-Dependency Performance: Running the entire application (analysis, rendering, speech, tools) smoothly on client-side Vanilla JS with instant load times. The WebMCP Inspector & 1-Click Scenario: Enabling judges and testers to see the agent reasoning in real time and test the entire workflow with a single click. What we learned The sheer power of WebMCP: Moving away from DOM scraping and screenshot interpretation towards clean, declarative web tools is a paradigm shift for web development. It makes AI agents hundreds of times faster, deterministic, and much more resilient. How to bridge early-childhood pedagogy with autonomous agent decision-making. What's next for TRACEAI — AI Handwriting Coach powered by WebMCP Cursive Writing Support: Extending my vector stroke engine to support connected cursive handwriting and full words. Early Dysgraphia & Motor-Skill Insights: Providing anonymized progress reports that parents and educators can share with pediatric specialists to identify fine-motor coordination difficulties early. Multi-Child Classroom Dashboard: Enabling a teacher's AI copilot to monitor an entire classroom's practice sessions simultaneously and flag who needs personal attention. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: CAIOS WebMCP Agent Gateway
pitch: A safe shared pet-care state where people and agents collaborate through five guarded WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
A safe shared pet-care state where people and agents collaborate through five guarded WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 CAIOS WebMCP Agent Gateway is a standalone synthetic-data pet-care workspace where a person and an AI agent operate on the same visible state through five document-bound WebMCP tools. 

 The agent reads Synthetic Pika's profile, daily focus, and events; previews an exact structured check-in; requests human review; commits only the unchanged confirmed payload; and reads the result back from browser-only storage. 

 Why I built this 

 I chose the name CAIOS WebMCP Agent Gateway because CAIOS is our startup project, and the gateway was my way to test whether WebMCP could turn a pet-care page into a safer shared workspace for people and agents. 

 Before we adapt this pattern to real market needs, I wanted a small, inspectable build that could prove the interaction model without exposing production CAIOS technology or real pet data. 

 Pika's everyday care made the test concrete: an agent may help structure a routine observation, but the person should still see exactly what will be recorded and remain in control of the write. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Agents normally infer controls from visual interfaces. This project instead registers five narrow tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 get_synthetic_pika_profile 
 list_synthetic_pika_events 
 get_synthetic_pika_today 
 preview_synthetic_pika_check_in 
 commit_synthetic_pika_check_in 
 

 Preview validates without writing and returns a payload-bound confirmation token. Commit fails closed unless it receives the unchanged payload and matching token. A changed or unpreviewed payload is rejected. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 The agent reduces repetitive interaction while the person sees the proposal, controls confirmation, and verifies the outcome. Both then see the same browser-only state. 

 What I learned 

 The most useful lesson was that exposing a tool is only half of the work. The human page and the agent must stay consistent around the same proposed action. 

 During testing, we found a real UI bug: after preview, a re-render could reset the visible form to its defaults while the pending payload still held the earlier values. That could make the confirmation screen misleading even though the underlying token guard still worked. 

 We fixed it by preserving the exact previewed values in the UI and invalidating confirmation whenever the form changes. This reinforced the main product principle behind the demo: WebMCP can give an agent useful capabilities, but consequential actions still need deterministic guards and visible human review. 

 Safety and hackathon boundary 

 All data is fictional and marked synthetic_hackathon_only . Mutable state stays in namespaced browser localStorage . The demo has no production CAIOS API, database, customer record, real pet record, private prompt, proprietary memory engine, nutrition reasoning, or clinical logic. It does not diagnose, prescribe, or replace veterinary or emergency care. 

 CAIOS existed before the submission period as a broader pet-care product vision. During the submission period, we created this standalone WebMCP Gateway, five tools, synthetic dataset, confirmation guards, seven deterministic tests, CI, documentation, public repository, and independent deployment. 

 Implementation and verification 

 Built with TypeScript, Vite, the WebMCP browser API, and deterministic browser storage. Seven tests cover the tool boundary and guarded writes. Type checking and production builds pass. 

 The live workflow was verified end-to-end in an OpenAI cloud Chrome CDP environment: five tools were discovered; a direct commit failed closed; preview returned a payload-bound token; the exact payload committed; and a final read returned the same visible browser-only state. 

 Try it 

 Live demo: https://caios-webmcp-challenge.vercel.app 

 Public repository: https://github.com/corwinlim/caios-webmcp-challenge 

 Demo video: https://youtu.be/FDoAIoCU3i0 

 No account or credentials are required. Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled.

title: Archive Evidence Room
pitch: Turn any webpage's history into cited evidence. A WebMCP agent finds comparable captures, inspects archived diffs, and pins findings with their sources to a caseboard shared with you.
about_excerpt: Turn any webpage's history into cited evidence. A WebMCP agent finds comparable captures, inspects archived diffs, and pins findings with their sources to a caseboard shared with you. Like Comment Story Updates The final finding stays beside its cited excerpt, ready for human review, source checking, and Markdown export. A scoped question becomes live coverage across public archives, with Arquivo.pt selected for comparison. The Evidence Room connects four WebMCP tools to one caseboard that the agent and the person can inspect together. One selected window becomes a bounded diff with both source captures and an explicit untrusted text warning. Index records produce six exact capture windows before any archived page body is downloaded. Why I built it Web archives contain real evidence, but working with them still feels like manual archaeology. Find snapshots, open a pile of tabs, compare dates, copy URLs, then try to remember which version actually proved the point. I wanted to ask a browser agent a sharper question: "How did this page change, and can you show me the exact captures that prove it?" This project also has some history. @agntn/archives started in April 2025 as one TypeScript interface over several web archives. It gradually gained caching, lazy provider loading, typed metadata and more sources. In 2026 it grew into a proper agent tool: first native OMP and Pi extensions, then an MCP server, archived body reads, pagination, capture diffs and finally a Nuxt explorer running on Cloudflare Workers. The WebMCP Challenge was a good reason to build the missing piece. Not another chat box, and not four aliases for buttons. I wanted the page itself to become a shared investigation room for a person and an agent. What it does Archive Evidence Room registers four native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext : scope_archive_case defines one historical question and checks which archives have evidence. find_change_windows finds consecutive captures without downloading archived bodies. inspect_archive_change reads one selected pair and returns a short cited diff. pin_archive_finding records whether that diff supports, contradicts or only adds context to the question. Every call updates the same visible caseboard. The agent can do the repetitive archive work, but the person still sees the dates, original URL, provider, underlying Memento archive, diff and final interpretation. No invisible research session and no uncited answer at the end. WebMCP is progressive enhancement here. Without the experimental browser API, the full workflow still works by hand. How I built it The UI is Nuxt 4, Vue and Docus. The server runs on Cloudflare Workers. I used the existing cached /api/coverage , /api/snapshots and /api/diff routes instead of creating a second archive backend for the hackathon. Those routes call the same @agntn/archives executors already used by MCP, OMP and Pi. Discovery is index first. The room requests between 3 and 12 capture records, groups them by exact URL and provider, keeps Memento captures inside the same underlying archive, then ranks useful windows. Archived bodies are fetched only after someone chooses a window to inspect. The result is much faster and much kinder to public archive infrastructure than reading everything up front. The caseboard keeps provenance all the way through. A diff can resolve to captures slightly different from the index rows, so the final citation comes from the diff result, not stale listing metadata. Findings store the interpretation beside the evidence instead of mixing both into one generated paragraph. What was hard Public web archives disagree about almost everything: timestamp formats, URL normalization, replay endpoints, metadata and failure behavior. Even www , default ports or letter case in a path can quietly produce the wrong pair. Memento adds another trap because one provider can return captures from several underlying archives. A plausible diff between unrelated records would be worse than no result, so I made the pairing rules deliberately strict. Cancellation was more subtle. Browser abort signals had to travel through $fetch , Nitro, cache misses and the archive executor. Sharing one cached promise also shared one caller's cancellation with another caller. That was wrong. Each cache miss now owns its request and one closed tab cannot kill another investigation. The other problem is trust. Archived HTML can contain instructions written specifically to manipulate an agent. Treating that as normal tool output would be ridiculous. The room exposes only a bounded text excerpt, marks it as untrusted, renders it as escaped text and keeps it separate from the finding written by the agent. What I learned The useful WebMCP abstraction is not "let the agent click my UI." It is a small protocol with state the user can inspect. caseId and changeId make the steps explicit, while the shared board makes mistakes visible. I also learned that archive research needs honest negative results. No capture in one bounded query does not mean a page never existed. A partial diff cannot prove text was absent outside the compared prefix. The product gets better when those limits stay visible instead of being polished into confidence. For the final smoke test I used sive.rs : seven captures became six safe windows, one exact archived diff and a finding pinned with both capture URLs. The public page does not preload this result because the caseboard belongs to the current browser session. Open the Evidence Room and ask the browser agent to investigate how sive.rs changed between 2020 and 2022 to reproduce the flow. title: Formulate
pitch: Your AI agent fills forms, explains jargon, and asks before it submits , powered by 12 WebMCP tools and a natural language data vault.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent fills forms, explains jargon, and asks before it submits , powered by 12 WebMCP tools and a natural language data vault. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 67% of people abandon government forms at the first confusing field. We've all been there — staring at a 40-field form that asks for your CIN number, your GSTIN, your TDS rate, and nobody explains what any of it means. In India alone, 900 million voters interact with the Election Commission's Form 6. Millions fill out business registrations, insurance enrollments, and rental applications every year. Most people either pay someone to fill these forms or give up entirely. We asked: what if an AI agent could fill the form for you — explain every confusing field — and you just approve at the end? What it does Formulate is a WebMCP-powered form assistant with three parts: 1. Natural Language Data Vault You describe yourself in plain text: "My name is Mohammed, I work at TechVentures in Bengaluru, my PAN is ABCPM1234K." The vault extracts your data using pattern recognition — PAN format, Aadhaar format, phone numbers, PIN codes, email, employer, job title, city, state. No form to set up a form-filler. 2. Smart Form Engine Five real-world forms with 172 total fields: Rental Application (39 fields), Health Insurance Enrollment (27 fields), Small Business Registration (25 fields), Airtel Business Enterprise Registration (40 fields), and India's Election Commission Voter ID Form 6 (41 fields). Every confusing field has an inline plain-language explanation. 3. 12 WebMCP Tools Registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() — the agent calls structured tools instead of scraping the page: get_form_fields — reads the entire form structure fill_field — fills a text/number/date/phone field select_option — selects from a dropdown check_checkbox — toggles a checkbox explain_field — returns a plain-language explanation validate_form — checks for empty required fields get_form_progress — returns filled/total counts review_form — summarizes all values before submission clear_field — removes a value autofill_from_vault — checks what can be auto-filled apply_vault_suggestions — fills all matching fields from vault submit_form — requires human approval before proceeding How we built it Next.js 16 with App Router and TypeScript Tailwind CSS v4 with shadcn-style design tokens (2 colors: foreground and muted) WebMCP — supports both document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext for Chrome compatibility Pattern recognition vault — regex-based extraction for PAN, Aadhaar, GSTIN, CIN, Udyam, phone, email, PIN codes, plus keyword extraction for name, employer, job title, address Playwright — 30 end-to-end tests covering tool registration, field filling, validation, approval flow, and activity panel Vercel for deployment The execute function returns { content: [{ type: "text", text: "..." }] } per the Chrome WebMCP spec. Input parsing handles both JSON strings and parsed objects so it works regardless of how the host agent calls the tools. Challenges we faced The biggest challenge was WebMCP spec compliance. The API migrated from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext in July 2026, and different hosts (Chrome vs ChatGPT) may use either surface. We had to support both. We also discovered that executeTool sends arguments as a JSON string in some hosts but a parsed object in others — so we added defensive input parsing. The natural language vault was tricky because names, cities, and job titles don't have fixed formats. We combined regex patterns for structured data (PAN, Aadhaar, GSTIN) with keyword-based extraction for unstructured data (name, employer, address), with confidence scoring to show users what was extracted and how sure we are. What we learned WebMCP changes the relationship between websites and AI agents from "scrape and guess" to "structured collaboration." A form that registers 12 tools gives the agent complete understanding of what's possible, what's required, and what needs human approval. That's fundamentally different from an agent trying to parse HTML and click buttons. title: Playable
pitch: Learning an instrument shouldn't start with 40 beginner videos. Name a song to your agent, it researches the web, Playable verifies the facts and builds a version you can actually play, practice.
about_excerpt: Learning an instrument shouldn't start with 40 beginner videos. Name a song to your agent, it researches the web, Playable verifies the facts and builds a version you can actually play, practice. Like Comment Story Updates Playable For as long as instruments have been taught, beginners have started with the same generic exercises and the same simplified songs — not because those songs are motivating, but because adapting real music to a real beginner was too much work for any teacher to do per student. Now life moves faster than ever, attention is the scarcest resource, and the music people actually love is the best motivation they have. Playable closes that gap: tell your AI agent which song you want to learn, and it researches the song on the public web and submits what it finds through WebMCP. Playable verifies the evidence against music theory, compiles a version that fits your hands, and you practice it in the browser with real chord diagrams and a synthesized preview of exactly what you'll play. Why WebMCP is the right architecture A cover song can't be ingested: streaming links expose no analyzable audio, and downloading is off the table. But the musical facts exist everywhere in public — chord sites, BPM databases, music encyclopedias. Reading them is a research problem, and research is what LLM agents are exceptional at. Turning facts into a beginner-proof arrangement is a compilation problem, and that needs deterministic software: difficulty scoring, fingering search, audio synthesis. No single system has both. WebMCP is the first protocol that composes them without merging them. Playable exposes 24 real capabilities as tools; the agent orchestrates them and supplies the one thing the app lacks — live web research. Critically, the agent is a researcher, not an oracle: it submits compact facts with source URLs (never tabs, lyrics, or page dumps), and a deterministic resolver adjudicates them. The model proposes; the page verifies. That boundary is what makes the result trustworthy — and demoable — because every claim on screen traces to an accepted independent source. From facts to playable: the theory pipeline The resolver does what a trained arranger would do before trusting a source. Keys normalize enharmonically (G♯ ≡ A♭); chord symbols parse into root + quality family, so "Db" and "Dbmaj7" agree without erasing extensions. Guitar-shaped evidence becomes sounding harmony through the capo invariant — capo 1 "G Em C D" and "Ab Fm Db Eb" reconcile as the same progression. Metrical tempo claims cluster instead of averaging (63, 126 and 189 BPM are one pulse at different levels), transposition look-alikes become hypotheses rather than truths, and confidence is noisy-OR over independent source families — five pages from one database count once. Per-field confidence and conflicts stay visible; structure claimed by no source is labeled approximate. The verified blueprint becomes a SongGraph, then a compiler searches transformation chains — capo placement, chord-shape substitution, rhythm and tempo simplification, fingering optimization — re-scored against the player's profile (known chords, barre comfort, practice time) and Pareto-filtered over difficulty vs fidelity. Every accepted transformation is explainable: "why 27% easier for you" comes from real diagnostics, and if no capo and open chords are genuinely optimal, the system honestly says so. The same selected arrangement drives the diagrams, the capo mapping, and the Karplus–Strong synthesis you hear. The experience One sentence: "I want to learn Perfect by Ed Sheeran. I'm a complete beginner." No link, no upload. The agent follows a live research brief — what's missing, with search queries — submits evidence per independent source, resolves, sets the profile, compiles, and prepares a 20-minute practice session. The user watches confidence fill in field by field, conflicts resolve visibly, and the chord diagrams land front and center. The tool layer itself keeps agents honest: next-step suggestions with priorities, state-aware errors, and reporting guardrails. Agent and human share one state — every agent action is visible, every slider moves the controls the agent sees, and audio never autoplays. A human presses Play. Implementation Deliberately thin and native: tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool in plain TypeScript — no framework, no backend agent, no internal LLM. UI buttons and agent calls execute one shared action layer over one state object, so the page is a live, truthful mirror of the agent's work. Research fusion and compilation are fully deterministic; the agent is the only model in the loop. We didn't put a chatbot inside a guitar website — we made the guitar website agent-native. title: OpenSource Release Feed
pitch: Create custom RSS release feeds for GitHub topic repositories or your starred projects.
about_excerpt: Create custom RSS release feeds for GitHub topic repositories or your starred projects. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration RSS remains one of the best ways to follow the open web, but discovering and configuring feeds for open-source projects is still unnecessarily difficult. OSSReleaseFeed began as a zero-account way to turn GitHub topics or starred repositories into a permanent feed URL. WebMCP introduced a more interesting possibility: instead of making an agent guess how to operate the interface, the page could expose structured tools while keeping the application visible and interactive. The goal became a genuinely collaborative experience in which an agent can configure a feed, the user can follow every change, and either participant can safely continue where the other left off. What it does OSSReleaseFeed creates permanent Atom or JSON Feed URLs for public GitHub activity. Users can follow repositories associated with selected GitHub topics or start from repositories they have starred, choose the activity they care about, and select an update frequency. No OSSReleaseFeed account, OAuth flow, or email address is required. In a WebMCP-capable browser, an agent can build a topic feed through tools exposed directly by the page. The tools are progressively disclosed as the configuration advances: choosing the source reveals topic selection, validated topics reveal feed settings, and completed settings reveal URL generation. Every WebMCP action updates the visible interface. The user can inspect the agent’s choices, refine them with the normal controls, take over completely, or ask the agent to continue. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite on Cloudflare Pages. Feed generation and GitHub integration run through a TypeScript Cloudflare Worker built with Hono and Effect. The WebMCP integration registers a small dynamic toolset using document.modelContext.registerTool . It currently provides tools to inspect the current feed configuration, choose the topic-feed source, validate and select GitHub topics, configure feed settings, and generate the final URL. WebMCP is not a separate implementation of the feed builder. The manual and WebMCP paths share the same feed configuration, state reducer, GitHub validation API, and URL generator. Manual controls prevent many invalid inputs through constrained interface elements. WebMCP validates structured tool input through schemas and runtime checks, then uses the same GitHub topic validation before applying user-supplied topics. We documented the important user journeys as Gherkin scenarios and used them to guide Vitest integration coverage and Playwright tests across desktop, tablet, and mobile viewports. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was coordinating slow agent operations with direct user interaction. A WebMCP agent may still be waiting for GitHub validation when the user decides to take over and complete a different feed manually. Without explicit coordination, the older tool call could eventually finish and overwrite the user’s newer choices or clear a feed URL they had already generated. The application therefore follows a strict newer-action-wins policy. A newer WebMCP mutation aborts older pending WebMCP work. A manual change to the current feed configuration immediately revokes pending mutating WebMCP work before applying the user’s change. Revision checks provide a final safeguard when an upstream request completes despite cancellation. We also encountered differences between WebMCP hosts, including execution callbacks that did not always provide an abort signal. The handlers now tolerate a missing signal while preserving cancellation when one is supplied. GitHub rate limiting presented another challenge. We added safer diagnostics that distinguish rate limiting from general upstream unavailability without exposing tokens, usernames, or other sensitive request details. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are particularly proud that the result feels like one coherent application rather than a conventional interface with an agent API attached to the side. Agent actions are visible, manual and agent-driven changes share the same underlying state, and users can take control without risking a delayed operation overwriting their completed work. The dynamic tool surface also gives agents only the capabilities that are meaningful at the current stage of the task. This reduces ambiguity while preserving the user’s ability to operate the same interface directly. Finally, the production implementation is backed by manual scenarios, integration tests, accessibility checks, and end-to-end coverage—including the difficult case where manual completion must defeat a slow WebMCP response. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it complements the visible application instead of bypassing it. Structured tools improve agent reliability, but the larger benefit is creating a shared surface where people can understand, correct, and continue an agent’s work. We also learned that shared state requires explicit concurrency rules. AbortController helps avoid unnecessary network work, but cancellation alone is insufficient. Revision checks are still necessary because an upstream operation may complete after cancellation or a host may not provide the expected signal. Progressive tool registration proved useful as both an agent-guidance mechanism and a product-design constraint. It encouraged us to define the valid transitions in the feed-building journey precisely, which also improved our scenarios and automated tests. What's next for OpenSource Release Feed The current WebMCP implementation focuses deliberately on topic feeds. The next step is to extend the same visible, validated workflow to starred-repository feeds, including username validation, repository selection, filtering, and correction of individual repository names. We also want to improve resilience around GitHub rate limits through better caching and clearer recovery guidance, expand the manual and automated scenario suite, and continue testing across WebMCP-capable hosts as the standard evolves. Longer term, we want OSSReleaseFeed to demonstrate a dependable pattern for the agent-native web: applications where agents can perform meaningful work efficiently, people can see and refine that work, and the user’s latest intent always remains authoritative.
