title: Accessibility Repair Studio
pitch: A human-in-the-loop workspace
about_excerpt: A human-in-the-loop workspace Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Small web teams struggle to understand and fix common accessibility failures without losing human design control. Existing tools either automate too aggressively (risking design integrity) or require deep accessibility expertise. We saw an opportunity to use WebMCP's structured semantic context to let AI agents manipulate accessibility intent more reliably than visually clicking unfamiliar pages, while keeping humans in full control of every change. What it does Accessibility Repair Studio provides a four-part collaborative workspace: Left panel : Page templates and component semantic outline Center : Responsive live preview with selectable elements and viewport controls Right panel : Issue list, issue inspector, patch editor, and approval controls Bottom : Keyboard path, screen-reader-style narrative, audit comparison, and agent activity The product loop: audit → inspect an issue in context → stage a constrained repair → preview visual and semantic changes → obtain human approval → apply → test keyboard and narrative behavior → compare audits → export a patch manifest The studio includes a seeded "Field Notes" event-registration page with eight deliberate accessibility issues: unnamed icon-only navigation, skipped heading level, insufficient text contrast, form error without input relationship, positive tabindex changing focus order, ambiguous link text, unhelpful image description, and unannounced registration status. Two clean reference templates are also included. How we built it Tech Stack: React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend framework Next.js for deployment and server-side billing integration axe-core for documented subset of automated accessibility checks Custom deterministic checks for the seeded component model Vitest, Testing Library, and Playwright for comprehensive testing Polar for paywall and benefit entitlements Remotion for demo video rendering Architecture: Typed component schema with safe renderer (no arbitrary HTML) Versioned state reducer with patch history Safe finite repair DSL with 10 allowed operations WebMCP tool registry with state-scoped capabilities Device-local persistence and one-click reset Apple-inspired studio UI with translucent surfaces, careful typography, high-visibility focus rings, and reduced-motion support Safety Model: Preview isolation until human approval Version guards and approval token expiration Rejection of raw HTML, CSS, JavaScript, event handlers, URLs, arbitrary ARIA Finite allowlists for element, content, color, relationship, and ordering values apply_accessibility_patch registered only after visible human approval Challenges we ran into Balancing automation with human control : Designing a safe repair DSL that's powerful enough to be useful but constrained enough to prevent dangerous changes required careful iteration on the operation allowlist. WebMCP integration complexity : Implementing state-scoped tool registration where apply_accessibility_patch only appears when a preview has human approval required understanding the evolving WebMCP spec and handling edge cases like stale approvals. Truthful audit representation : Avoiding claims of complete WCAG conformance while still providing actionable insights meant carefully labeling automated results as partial checks and preserving issues requiring human judgment. Studio accessibility : The interface itself had to be keyboard accessible and pass its own core audit, which required rigorous focus management and testing. Embedded git repository : During initial commit, the studio directory had its own .git folder, which required removing it to properly commit as part of the main repository. Accomplishments that we're proud of Safe collaboration model : Successfully implemented a human-in-the-loop workflow where AI agents can suggest repairs but humans always approve before application Comprehensive tool surface : 11 WebMCP tools covering the full audit-inspect-repair-apply-compare-export loop Truthful limitations : Clear labeling of partial checks, manual-review requirements, and screen-reader narrative as approximation rather than emulator Beautiful accessible UI : Apple-inspired studio design that itself passes accessibility audits with excellent focus management Full test coverage : Vitest, Testing Library, and Playwright tests covering safety, approval, version guards, and keyboard operability Real demo : Three-minute narrated walkthrough showing the complete product loop with real screenshots Production-ready : Polar integration for paid features, admin allowlist, and static deployment configuration What we learned WebMCP's potential for accessibility : Structured semantic context allows agents to understand accessibility intent much better than visual inspection alone State-scoped tool registration : Dynamic tool availability based on UI state is a powerful pattern for safety-critical operations The importance of version guards : Approval tokens must expire on any relevant state change to prevent stale approvals Partial audit honesty : Being transparent about what automated checks can and cannot prove builds trust DSL design trade-offs : Finite operations are safer but require careful selection to remain useful Studio self-auditing : Building accessibility tools requires the tools themselves to be accessible What's next for it Additional repair operations : Expand the safe DSL to cover more common accessibility patterns More seeded templates : Add diverse page types (forms, navigation, data tables) with representative issues Enhanced narrative : Improve the screen-reader approximation with more semantic nuance Real assistive-technology integration : Partner with actual screen reader vendors for validation Team collaboration : Multi-user support with attribution and review workflows CI/CD integration : Export manifests that can be applied to production codebases Advanced analytics : Track accessibility improvements over time across projects Built With webmcp Try it out github.com Submitted to The WebMCP title: Paperwork - a form your agent fills while you watch
pitch: A gnarly insurance form the agent fills from plain language while you watch - pending until you accept, and the legal attestations have no tool that can touch them.
about_excerpt: A gnarly insurance form the agent fills from plain language while you watch - pending until you accept, and the legal attestations have no tool that can touch them. Like Comment Story Updates The renters-insurance form: six steps, one pending layer Tool console: get_form called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: three legal attestations are structurally unreachable by any tool - human-only fields enforced in the data model itself, not by prompt instruction. Inspiration Nobody's brain fails at forms; their patience does. A renters-insurance application asks forty questions, a third of which only appear conditionally, in the form's own order - even though the applicant already knows all of it. What it does Tell the agent what happened in plain language; it drafts answers onto the real six-step form, in front of you. Nothing the agent writes is an answer yet - every draft lands in a pending layer, highlighted, tracked by provenance (empty / human / pending / accepted / uncertain), and only counts once you accept it. Three legal attestations - fraud acknowledgement, an animal attestation, final accuracy - are marked human-only in the data model itself: no tool can reach them, structurally, not by instruction. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript. Every tool writes through the same setField() the inputs commit through via one invoke() chokepoint, so conditional fields, repeaters, and validation behave identically whichever side acted. fill_field / fill_section draft into the pending layer; review_submission is read-only and there is no submit tool at all - Submit is a human-only button. Challenges we ran into An edge case in add_repeater_item : when a conditional trigger (e.g. "any claims in the last 5 years?") auto-spawned an empty repeater row, the tool would add a second row instead of reusing the empty one the UI had already created - a subtle UI/agent-state drift caught by explicit testing of the conditional-field interaction, not the isolated tool call. Accomplishments that we're proud of A form where the agent can genuinely say "I'm not sure" - a flagged, visible uncertainty on a field, not a silent guess - and where three specific legal fields are unreachable by any tool, not merely discouraged by one. What we learned Provenance tracking (who wrote this field, and is it still pending) turned out to be the real product, more than the fill-from-text trick itself - it's what makes it safe to let an agent write into a legal document at all. What's next Multi-document support (a second insurer's form with a different question set) to prove the provenance model generalizes beyond one carrier's application. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: BrowserMatic
pitch: Add WebMCP to any site instantly. No install, no extension simply enter a web address, we analyse the site, and open it in a browser with WebMCP applied in real time.
about_excerpt: Add WebMCP to any site instantly. No install, no extension simply enter a web address, we analyse the site, and open it in a browser with WebMCP applied in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Live browser embedded for co-browsing with ai Architecture Inspiration Every one of these is a tab-juggling exercise: Find the best deal across four stores Book dinner and movie tickets together Plan and price a trip in one shot Fill in council forms and applications Four stores, two booking sites, three travel sites, the same thirty fields on the twentieth government form. None of it is hard. It's just tedious, which is exactly what you'd want an assistant for. They all hit the same wall. Sites are starting to publish a machine-readable list of actions an AI is allowed to take, but those tools only exist on that site's own page. An agent can help you on one store, and that's the whole conversation. Four stores means four conversations, and nobody wants that. What it does Type a web address. BrowserMatic opens it in a browser that installs the API before the site's own code runs, so the site registers its tools and we carry them into your assistant, origin-qualified, across as many sites as you want. Four stores in one conversation. Flights and hotels side by side. And for forms, the same name and address on the twentieth site without typing it again. How we built it A Cloudflare Worker with one Durable Object per session, each with its own Browser Rendering Chromium, consent list and audit log. It also works directly in ChatGPT's in-app browser, no declarative form and no iframe discovery, so tools register imperatively on the top-level page; no session cookie, so a session is a capability URL. Names are origin-qualified because its permission model is per-site, and each tool holds its own AbortController, so granting a fourth store never disturbs the first three. The injection is one line of Playwright's addInitScript, a minimal WebMCP implementation installed before any page script runs. The same Worker also speaks MCP at /mcp over JSON-RPC with OAuth 2.1 and PKCE, verified against the official SDK, so any compliant client can drive the same session headlessly. Challenges A Chrome extension would have been the easy route. We used the hackathon to find out how far embedded remote browsers could go instead, since that's the lower-friction path for users. Most of the pain came from rendering a session a human and an AI can both drive at the same time. We're happy with where it landed in the time we had. We are still getting stuck in some "honey pots" so need to do a better job at detecting and mitigating. What's next A registry of the sites we've driven and the patterns we generate for them, so a success on one visit gets reused on the next. Then usage data for site owners so they can see how agents behave on their pages and improve accordingly, something like Google Analytics / Datadog for agentic commerce. We also want to try Cloudflare's agent payments and pay-per-access content as a business model. title: 8KG
pitch: A carry-on packed by you and the AI that already knows you.
about_excerpt: A carry-on packed by you and the AI that already knows you. Like Comment Story Updates The privacy boundary is explicit before the AI calls WebMCP tools. 8KG turns selected item IDs into a constrained visual carry-on. The AI-packed bag fits the 8 kg limit and the 6 × 8 spatial grid. Inspiration Most “AI personalization” demos are recommendation lists or theme pickers. They ask the user to repeat preferences the assistant may already understand, then return another block of text. We wanted to test a more tangible collaboration: can an AI contribute personal judgment while a website contributes precise domain constraints, without the website receiving the user’s profile? Packing a carry-on makes that boundary immediately visible. The AI can decide what matters for this person right now; the browser knows every item’s weight and physical footprint and can make those choices fit. What it does 8KG is an interactive carry-on shared by a person and their AI. The user copies one short request into the AI connected to the page. Through WebMCP, the AI reads an anonymous item catalog and sends back only accepted item IDs. The browser then packs those items into a 6 × 8 spatial grid while enforcing an 8 kg cabin limit. The result appears immediately as a visual suitcase rather than a text recommendation. The collaboration continues after the first pack. A user can remove an item or mark it Keep this . A later AI repack sees the public bag state and must work around the user’s locked decision. The page protects those locks even if the model omits them. No prompt, identity, destination, conversation history, private facts, or AI reasoning is accepted by the website. There is no application backend or embedded LLM. Bag state lives only in the current tab. How we built it React 19 and TypeScript for the client-only application. WebMCP tools registered through feature-detected document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext . A constrained catalog of 18 items with weight and grid dimensions. A deterministic first-fit packing engine that validates weight, space, unique IDs, and user locks. Six narrow tools: get_available_items , get_bag_state , pack_bag , add_items , remove_items , and reset_bag . ChatGPT Sites for hosting, with no database, API key, analytics, cookies, or server-side profile. The visual controls and WebMCP tools call the same functions in lib/packing.ts . The model never generates HTML, CSS, or JavaScript and cannot bypass the browser’s constraints. Challenges The hardest part was finding a use of AI memory that felt meaningfully different from ordinary controls. A user can manually select items, so the value could not be “AI clicked buttons for me.” The stronger interaction is mixed-initiative: the AI makes a context-sensitive first proposal, the user expresses a hard preference by locking an item, and the AI adapts around that decision. We also had to keep the privacy story technically honest. The page cannot pull ChatGPT memory. The user deliberately asks the connected AI to act, reviews the tool call, and sends only catalog IDs. Tool schemas reject open-ended text and the page stores nothing after the tab closes. Accomplishments that we're proud of One WebMCP call causes an obvious, physical-looking transformation instead of a subtle theme change. The full experience works without an application backend. User locks are enforced by deterministic page logic, not model promises. The interface explains the data boundary before the user copies the request. The same flow works in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and responsive mobile layouts. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when the website and the model bring different capabilities. The model should contribute judgment and context; the page should expose trustworthy state, enforce domain rules, and render the consequence. Narrow tools and shared business logic make that collaboration understandable and testable. What's next for 8KG Airline-specific cabin limits and baggage policies. Trip-length and weather-aware catalogs without sending destinations to the page. Drag-and-drop manual arrangement with AI repacking around pinned positions. A “why this fits” summary generated in the assistant, while keeping reasoning out of the website. WebMCP evals for weight-limit, user-lock, and privacy-boundary scenarios. title: Toolsmith
pitch: An agent can only press the buttons a website gives it. Toolsmith lets it build the one that's missing — and lets you decide whether it keeps it.
about_excerpt: An agent can only press the buttons a website gives it. Toolsmith lets it build the one that's missing — and lets you decide whether it keeps it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration An AI agent can only press the buttons a website gives it — and those were decided by whoever built the site, months ago. When the button you need isn't one of them, the agent does what agents do: it guesses from the DOM, it scrapes, or it hands you a snippet of Python and hopes you run it. Adding a real one today means leaving the conversation entirely: write an MCP server, host it, edit a config file, restart the client. Minutes to days of work, and a permanent new attack surface, for a function you might call once. WebMCP already moved the button surface into the page — where the user's data and session already live, and where a human is already watching. That's enough to close the loop without leaving. (A note on vocabulary: we say "button" in the interface because that's what it is to the person looking at the screen. The spec calls the same thing a tool, and so does our code.) What it does Toolsmith registers five permanent tools on document.modelContext . One of them, forge_tool , takes a name, a JSON Schema and a JavaScript body, and turns them into a real WebMCP tool the same agent can call seconds later — but only after a human grants it. The loop: the agent calls read_workbench to learn your real column names → calls forge_tool to build the button that isn't there → the page renders it as pending , code on screen and editable, not registered → you press Test run to execute it against your real data before it exists → you press Grant it , which calls registerTool with its own AbortController → the agent presses its new button in the same conversation → Take it back aborts that signal and the button leaves the registry immediately. The count in the header — "buttons the agent can press" — is the honest answer to what can this agent do right now? And a person decided every one of them. How WebMCP is used This is not a wrapper around an existing app; the spec's lifecycle is the product. Every built button is registered via registerTool(tool, { signal }) with its own AbortController . Unregistration isn't a side feature here — aborting that signal is the revocation mechanism the entire safety argument rests on. The tool surface is genuinely dynamic and authored at runtime by the agent talking to the page. getTools() and the toolchange event drive the live count in the header. annotations.untrustedContentHint on every built button, because its output is computed by code an agent wrote minutes ago. annotations.readOnlyHint on the two read-only tools. forge_tool accepts the child tool's inputSchema as a JSON string, validates it, and passes it to registerTool as a real JSON Schema object — schema round-tripping through a tool call. Native document.modelContext when present; otherwise a vendored @mcp-b/global polyfill. The header pill says which one you got. A button you didn't read is not a button you granted Self-extension is only acceptable if refusing is as cheap as granting. So: nothing registers before a human approves; the schema and function body stay on screen and editable, with a Test run that executes against real data before registration; each call spawns a fresh Web Worker with fetch , XMLHttpRequest , WebSocket , EventSource , importScripts , storage and navigator deleted from the global scope before the code is compiled (verified: built code sees typeof fetch === "undefined" ); a 3-second leash terminates runaway loops; editing a granted button unregisters it and sends it back for re-approval; reloading returns every button to pending, never to granted; and every call, with arguments and results, lands in the activity log. This is defence in depth, not a security boundary — a Worker shares the origin, and the README says so plainly. It's enough friction that a button written thirty seconds ago can't quietly drain your data while you're still reading the diff. Challenges we ran into The hard part wasn't generating code — it was revocation. A page that lets an agent extend itself is only defensible if taking the capability back is instant and obvious. WebMCP's AbortSignal -based registration turned out to be exactly the right primitive: one controller per button made grant, edit, take-back and page-reload all collapse into the same mechanism. The second hard part was language. Our first build talked about "dynamic tool lifecycles," which is accurate and means nothing to anyone. Calling it a button — something a person already knows they can be given, and can have taken away — made the same code explain itself. What we learned That the interesting part of WebMCP isn't that a page can expose tools. It's that the set of tools is mutable at runtime , and that mutation can be put in a human's hands. Most of the spec's power lives in the { signal } argument that's easy to skim past. What's next for Toolsmith Cross-origin granting via exposedTo , so one page can hand a vetted button to another. Signed button sets, so a team can publish a reviewed collection instead of each person approving their own. And an output schema, so built buttons can declare structuredContent rather than text. title: MCPation
pitch: A browser-native WebMCP gate that lets Codex inspect one explicitly granted workspace, explain drift, and apply supervised, reversible cleanup—without installing an MCP server.
about_excerpt: A browser-native WebMCP gate that lets Codex inspect one explicitly granted workspace, explain drift, and apply supervised, reversible cleanup—without installing an MCP server. Like Comment Story Updates What I built MCPation is a browser-native WebMCP pre-flight gate for Codex. It is a deliberately scoped MVP exploring a new category of agent-native DevTools: many of the useful, structured interactions people associate with an installed MCP can happen directly in a web page, without installing a server, daemon, extension, or API key. The user grants access to exactly one workspace folder, and the agent works inside that visible boundary. Why WebMCP is a good fit Agent configuration tends to grow quietly. Duplicate MCP servers, disabled entries, invalid endpoints, package drift, and layered Codex instructions can make it hard to know what an agent will inherit before it runs. MCPation turns that uncertainty into a shared, inspectable pre-flight step. The first pass is read-only: it reads an allowlisted set of configuration, package, and instruction metadata, then returns a readiness score, concrete findings, and an evidence graph connecting artifacts to those findings. This creates a better experience for both sides. A person gets an understandable report instead of guessing through configuration files. Codex gets a structured tool surface instead of having to click through an unfamiliar UI. They see the same state, while the person stays in control of every write. What the real demo shows The demo workspace is intentionally seeded with reproducible problems so the workflow has something meaningful to solve. The browser flow itself is real, not a mocked result: MCPation scans the selected folder, identifies duplicate JSON server entries, an invalid endpoint, and a disabled server, explains the evidence, and builds a supervised hardening plan. I choose the exact duplicate cleanup, explicitly approve it, grant the browser write permission, and MCPation creates one sibling backup before removing only those selected keys. It then rescans and shows the new readiness score and the restorable snapshot. More complex commands, TOML, policy, and instruction changes remain review items rather than being silently changed. The important collaboration is that a person can decide what is safe while an agent can inspect, explain, and verify the result through the same page. That combination would be difficult with a normal UI-only workflow and risky with an unbounded local tool. How WebMCP is implemented The page registers a concrete document.modelContext surface with tools for scanning the workspace, reading the declared MCP/package inventory, reading the instruction chain, explaining findings, building a hardening plan, requesting a bounded host handoff, submitting a sanitized host snapshot, applying the selected deterministic cleanup, verifying the result, and explaining the exact access scope. Read-only tools are annotated with readOnlyHint; the apply tool accepts only action IDs from the latest plan and requires confirm: true. The visible browser control owns the permission prompt, backup, write, and rescan. When a browser cannot expose native WebMCP, MCPation says so explicitly and shows a local preview instead of pretending that native tools are available. The same app works in Codex's in-app browser and in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Scope and honesty This is a deliberately scoped MVP for a new category of agent-native DevTools, built under a short hackathon deadline. I chose one deterministic, reversible cleanup and a strong evidence trail instead of pretending to support every possible workspace utility. With more time, the same pattern could extend to onboarding, compliance checks, migrations, review gates, and other supervised workflows. The point is that a useful MCP-like experience does not necessarily need installation when WebMCP can publish a scoped page surface and the user grants explicit permission. A note about the English text English is not my native language. I understand and speak it fluently, but expressing myself precisely in written English takes me much longer. I used AI to help draft, translate, and polish this description so it would be clear to the judges; the product decisions, implementation, testing, and claims in this submission are based on the project that is actually running. I am genuinely grateful to be able to participate in this hackathon. I discovered it rather late and would have loved more time to explore richer utilities, but I am very happy to share this concept and what I managed to build. title: Dim Hour
pitch: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page.
about_excerpt: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Dim Hour is a city guide - the places worth your time, scored, not starred - covering more than 19,000 restaurants, bars, hotels, and venues across 24 cities. For this challenge, dimhour.com became agent-native: the page itself registers five WebMCP tools, so an agent browsing the site can search the catalog, read a venue, check what is open tonight, draft an itinerary, and hand back a booking link - without scraping a pixel. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Planning a night out is one of the most common things people already ask an agent to help with, but today the agent scrapes pages and guesses at what the site already knows. WebMCP lets dimhour.com hand the agent its real search, scoring, and booking data as structured tools, in the same tab where the person is browsing. The catalog is the product; WebMCP makes it callable. Because the tools are thin adapters over a production venue API, every agent answer is grounded in live data instead of page scraping. How it creates a better user experience One page, two users. A person browsing the Dallas guide and their agent now work on the same surface. The agent calls the site's own tools and gets back the same scored venues, hours, and booking links the UI shows - no copy-pasting between a chat window and a browser, and no agent inventing hours, addresses, or availability. The person keeps the judgment (taste, swaps, vetoes); the agent does the legwork (searching, filtering, checking, assembling). The site stays the source of truth for both of them, and saving a plan stays a human action - the tools read, they never write. What people and agents can do together Co-plan a night in one sitting, in one page. "Dinner in Deep Ellum for four on Friday, then cocktails within walking distance." The agent searches the scored catalog, filters to what is actually open tonight using the same rule the site's own tonight strip uses, pulls full venue records, and drafts an ordered itinerary with real booking links (Resy, OpenTable, SevenRooms, Tock) while the person watches - then interrupts: "swap the second stop for something quieter," and the agent re-plans around the constraint. Before WebMCP, the agent could read the page but not act through the site's own logic, and the person could use the site but not delegate the legwork. Now both happen at once, and the result is a plan with real reservation links attached, not a list of suggestions. How we implemented WebMCP The WebMCP layer is one feature-detected script, webmcp.js, loaded by the site's index.html. Each of the five tools is a thin adapter that POSTs JSON-RPC tools/call to Dim Hour's existing MCP server (mcp.dimhour.com) and passes the result straight through: search_venues - one strong keyword plus city, neighborhood, cuisine, score floor, and price ceiling filters get_venue - the full record: hours, score, booking path, awards find_open_tonight - venues with a happy hour or late kitchen, best score first, using the same definition the site's own "tonight" strip uses, so the agent and the page agree build_itinerary - an ordered multi-stop plan with why and how to book each stop; saving stays a human action at /trip.html get_booking_link - the reservation platform and direct booking URL for a venue, returned for the agent to present; it never opens or books anything itself The script handles the in-flight standard rename (document.modelContext first, navigator.modelContext fallback) and is a silent no-op where no WebMCP host exists. No authentication; the tools expose only public, read-only catalog data. What predates the hackathon: the venue catalog, scoring pipeline, MCP server, and site. What was built during the submission window: webmcp.js, the tool schemas, and the index.html include - the public repo's README draws that line explicitly, with dated commits. Challenges we hit Search results deliberately do not carry hours - only full venue records do - so "open tonight" meant ranking candidates first, then reading the top few individually rather than filtering a field that is not there. Booking links live in the page's own catalog rather than the API, so the booking tool merges both sources and says so honestly when a city is not loaded. The verification suite now asserts substance (tonight actually finds venues; a booking link equals the catalog's own URL), not just shape - because an early version passed every check while two tools quietly returned nothing. title: DealTable — WebMCP Negotiation
pitch: DealTable: You set the walkaway. ChatGPT calls negotiation tools on the page—not the DOM. Humans approve what agents can't.
about_excerpt:
DealTable: You set the walkaway. ChatGPT calls negotiation tools on the page—not the DOM. Humans approve what agents can't.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 DealTable — WebMCP Negotiation 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 DealTable — WebMCP Negotiation 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 DealTable — WebMCP Negotiation 
 
 1 2 



 
 Video: https://youtu.be/-zPTvL9Deso 
 Live demo: https://dealtable-webmcp.vercel.app 
 Repo: https://github.com/shielyule/dealtable-webmcp 
 Blog Post https://shielyule.co.uk/2026/09/03/the-day-i-outsourced-my-backbone-to-an-mcp-bridge/ 
 ## Inspiration
I've negotiated freelance rates, lease renewals, and vendor terms the slow way — email threads, mental math on walkaway numbers, and no audit trail when things went sideways. When the WebMCP hackathon opened, the fit clicked: **negotiation is exactly the kind of task where an external agent needs structured access to live state**, not a screenshot of a web page.
DealTable is the room I wished existed — you set the rules once (your **mandate**), something role-plays the other side, and ChatGPT can advise by calling tools on the page. The human still owns the lines that matter.

## What we built
DealTable is a mandate-driven negotiation app:
- **You (principal)** set target price, walkaway limit, and concession tolerance
- **Counterparty agent** (rule-based for this build) opens and responds in chat
- **ChatGPT (advisor)** calls seven WebMCP tools registered on the page
- **Human-in-the-loop (HITL)** blocks any offer below walkaway until you Approve or Reject
- **Audit log + closure summary** export transcript and JSON when a deal closes
The core constraint is simple. For any proposed price \(p\):
\[
\text{apply}(p) = \begin{cases}
\text{execute immediately} & \text{if } p \geq w \\
\text{require human approval} & \text{if } p < w
\end{cases}
\]
where \(w\) is your walkaway. Agents can suggest; they cannot silently cross your floor.

## How I built it
**Stack:** Vite + React + Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. No backend API — session state lives in a browser store so judges can run the demo instantly with no login.
**WebMCP:** On load, `App.jsx` registers tools via `document.modelContext.registerTool` in `src/lib/webmcp.js`:
| Tool | Role |
|------|------|
| `get_deal_state` | Read mandate, ask, messages, advisor metrics |
| `set_mandate` | Update target / walkaway / concessions |
| `parse_opening_offer` | Extract numbers from pasted offer text |
| `propose_offer` / `concede` | Send counters (HITL if below walkaway) |
| `accept_term` | Close with approval gate |
| `hold_firm` | Refuse latest concession |
**HITL:** When a tool returns `needsHitl`, a modal opens on the page. The WebMCP tool promise resolves only after the human clicks Approve or Reject — ChatGPT cannot bypass the walkaway.
**Product flow:** entrance → mandate setup → negotiation hub (chat + advisor rail) → optional advisor insights → audit log → summary on accept.
AI coding assistants (Cursor) helped scaffold UI and debug WebMCP flows; the shipped demo is the real app — live URL, working tools, recorded video.

## What I learned
1. **WebMCP changes the integration shape.** Instead of "ChatGPT reads the page," it's "ChatGPT calls typed tools that mutate validated state." That is materially safer and easier to audit than DOM automation.
2. **Split the roles.** One chatbot pretending to be both advisor and counterparty muddies the demo. Separating principal / counterparty / external advisor maps to how real deals work and makes HITL legible to judges.
3. **HITL has to live on the page.** ChatGPT's tool bridge struggled when human approval UI was unclear or nested wrong in tool state. The fix was a prominent modal, a top banner, and a one-click "triggers HITL" demo button in the same browser panel.
4. **Honest scope wins.** The counterparty is rule-based, not an LLM — and that's fine for a WebMCP hackathon entry where the story is the advisor bridge. Saying so clearly beats over claiming.

## Challenges
- **Deploy friction:** Vercel rejected a project name with capitals and spaces; a `# comment` on the same line as `npm run build` broke Vite. Small things that eat time on deadline day.
- **HITL state bug:** Early builds passed the whole `proposeOffer` result into `openHitl` instead of the inner pending object. Approving produced `$undefined/sqft` in the chat. Fixed by unwrapping pending correctly and guarding invalid prices.
- **ChatGPT single-window demo:** Triggering HITL via a WebMCP tool call pauses ChatGPT while waiting for a page click — awkward on video. We split the demo: ChatGPT calls tools for safe moves above walkaway; HITL is triggered from an in-page button in the same browser panel.
- **Three minutes is tight.** The first script was too essay-heavy. The recorded demo front-loads: mandate → WebMCP tool call → HITL → closure export.

## What's next
- Rules-led **LLM counterparty** conditioned on persona behaviors
- Persist sessions and export to contract workflows
- Deeper document parse for opening offers (PDF)

title: OpenQuest
pitch: OpenQuest turns unused AI agent capacity into useful public work through an open WebMCP network.
about_excerpt: OpenQuest turns unused AI agent capacity into useful public work through an open WebMCP network. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenQuest started from a pretty simple idea. A lot of us already pay for capable AI agents and we dont always use all of that capacity. Tokens reset, credits expire, whatever. At the same time there is basically infinite useful public work that could use more intelligence. Open source, research, education, climate, accessibility, science etc. So the question was: what if people could point some of that unused agent capacity at useful open problems? Not donate API keys or send credits somewhere. Just bring the agent you already use. Thats OpenQuest What it does OpenQuest is an open public network where independent AI agents can work together. The structure is pretty simple: Quest → Challenge → Contribution → Review → Result A Quest is a big goal. It gets split into smaller Challenges that are actually manageable for an agent. An agent can come in, see what work exists, pick something useful, do the work and submit a Contribution. Then another independent agent can review it. If the work is good it becomes the Result. If not the Challenge stays open and someone else can improve it. Everything is public so the work doesnt just disappear inside another chat window. Why WebMCP This is probably the most important part. We didnt want to build another platform with our own agent inside it. The idea is that you bring your own agent . WebMCP gives that agent a structured way to understand OpenQuest and actually participate in it, instead of scraping the page or clicking around blindly. OpenQuest currently exposes five tools: observe the network find useful work submit work review work propose new work Humans use the UI. Agents use WebMCP. Both are working against the same shared public state. That felt like a pretty natural use case for WebMCP. How I built it The frontend is React + TypeScript and the backend runs on Cloudflare Workers. Shared state is stored in D1 and we use Durable Objects + WebSockets so the UI updates when agents change something. We also added a simple rule where an agent session cant review its own Contribution. Another session has to do it. It sounds small but this is quite important because otherwise "review" doesnt really mean anything Challenges and what we learned The hardest part was mostly figuring out how little we could build. It would have been very easy to turn this into some huge agent orchestration system with 40 tools and a lot of abstractions. I tried to do the opposite. What is the minimum information an agent needs? What are the minimum actions it needs? What should the server control? How do you keep it understandable for humans and predictable for agents at the same time? One thing I learned from this is that the website itself starts becoming a different kind of thing with WebMCP. Its still a UI for humans, but its also an interface that can explain its capabilities directly to an agent. You dont necessarily need to put an AI assistant inside every product. Sometimes the better model is to make the product legible and usable by the agents people already have. Whats next The bigger idea is that eventually a research lab, open source project, university, nonprofit or whoever could publish useful work as Quests. Then people around the world could point their own agents at parts of that work. One agent contributes, another reviews, another builds on the result and so on. The network doesnt need to own the intelligence. title: Chiptunes.app
pitch: Ask an agent for retro video game music and it'll compose it! 15 WebMCP tools drive a real emulated Game Boy sound chip and a deterministic composer. Works fully offline, and can export a real rom!
about_excerpt: Ask an agent for retro video game music and it'll compose it! 15 WebMCP tools drive a real emulated Game Boy sound chip and a deterministic composer. Works fully offline, and can export a real rom! Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI music tools have the same shape: prompt a remote model, wait, pay for a generation, receive an opaque waveform. Chiptunes has no model and no server. Its deterministic Game Boy composer already runs entirely inside the browser. A song takes about 1.6 milliseconds to generate. Nothing is uploaded. There is no API key, account, quota, or per-generation cost. WebMCP turns that implementation detail into an agent capability: if an agent can open the page, it can compose music. What it does Chiptunes exposes 15 WebMCP tools for composing music and controlling the live instrument. Ask for “a gloomy 40-second dungeon theme with no drums” and the agent can: compose it locally in the tab generate 12 complete alternatives in ~70 ms analyze their harmony, melodic direction, density, and resolution choose between them play them through the interface you're watching make the current song happier, darker, faster, or slower export the result as a share link, MIDI, or a 32 KB .gb ROM that boots on a real Game Boy The agent doesn't need to hear the music to reason about it. chiptunes_analyse measures musical properties such as consonance, phrase direction, chord agreement, activity, and tonic resolution. And because WebMCP calls the same functions as the UI, the agent and human are operating the same instrument . When the agent changes something, the user hears it immediately and sees the action announced on screen. How I built it The WebMCP layer lives in src/webmcp.js and registers 15 tools against the available model-context surfaces. The hardest problem was timing. Some agents enumerate tools before the application bundle runs, so Chiptunes registers tool descriptors before hydration , reconnects them when the application loads, and handles model contexts injected later. The page also adapts when an agent is present. The explainer gets out of the way and leaves the instrument front and center because the agent browser already provides the conversation. Automated tests inject a spec-shaped model context before any page JavaScript executes , invoke every tool, and verify the real application responds. Challenges The most dangerous bugs were cases where the implementation and its test shared the same wrong assumption . I initially registered against the wrong model-context surface. My test used the same surface, so everything passed while a real WebMCP agent would have discovered zero tools. The same thing happened musically. My composer and analyzer shared an incorrect definition of consonance, so each confidently verified the other. Both are now tested against something external: the WebMCP API shape for integration, and measurable musical behavior for composition. Accomplishments I'm proud of 12 songs in ~70 ms. WebMCP lets an agent explore a possibility space instead of spending a costly generation on one answer. The music is measurable. Across test songs, happy vs. sad compositions separate strongly on pitch material, tempo, phrase direction, and consonance. A classifier using the writing itself — excluding the easy signals of mode and tempo — identifies the intended mood 93% of the time . The output can become a real cartridge. The same browser session can produce a 32 KB ROM that boots on original Game Boy hardware. It fails explicitly. Ask for vocals, reverb, a waltz, or an unsupported mode and the tool explains the limitation rather than pretending it succeeded. What I learned WebMCP isn't just “an API without HTTP.” Its more interesting property is that the capability, agent, and human can inhabit the same place . Here, the agent isn't requesting music from a service and describing the result afterward. It's operating an instrument the user is listening to — generating, measuring, comparing, changing, and handing control back in real time. And because the computation was already in the webpage, WebMCP gives the agent all of that without adding a backend at all. What's next Next is live adaptive composition: an agent changing a cue while it plays, so a game developer can hear a boss theme escalate instead of generating separate takes. After that: agent-controlled loop points and adaptive game-music structures built from the composer's existing knowledge of bars and phrases. title: Estro
pitch: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking.
about_excerpt: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Projects Page ChatGPT Browser Window with Estro Before vs After Project Open within Estro Inspiration Everyone has a friend who takes the same photo on the same phone and it comes out like a poster. When you finally ask how, they send you a recipe: exposure +0.95, tint -18, an S-curve, blacks +52. You understood the word "photo." Every editor puts Saturation, Temperature and Tint in front of you and assumes you already know what they mean. Most people don't, so they never touch them, and the picture stays as it came off the phone. That's the gap Estro is for. The sliders were never the problem. The words were. WebMCP fits this problem unusually well because the thing a beginner needs isn't a smarter filter, it's someone beside them who can move the control, say the word out loud, and explain it in one sentence. An agent driving the real editor through the same commands a person uses can do exactly that, and the person keeps the Undo button. What it does Estro is a photo editor that runs entirely in the browser and registers 56 tools with document.modelContext . Open it in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and the agent next to the page can use the editor the way you would. Hand it your friend's recipe and it works through the steps. Every edit lands as a card in the interface naming the control, the value, a plain-language explanation of what that word means, and an Undo button for that one step. Mine and the agent's edits sit in one History, so I can undo its saturation without undoing my crop, and it can see what I did. Where Estro doesn't have a control the recipe names, the agent has nowhere to hide it. There is no Dehaze tool, so it has to say so and tell you what it used instead. Ask it where the contrast slider is and it points at the real control without touching it, so you can drag it yourself. Ask for a before-and-after and it puts the canvas in split view. Ask it to match your other three photos from that evening to this one and each project gets its own Undo, because each keeps its own history. Underneath, it's a real non-destructive editor: layers, groups, crop, transform, masks, curves, levels, colour balance, selective colour, vibrance, sharpen, blur, grain, lens correction, presets, batch export, and a live per-channel histogram that names which channel is clipping. Nothing is uploaded. There is no server and no account. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite on the front. Dexie over IndexedDB for project history, the origin private file system for original photos, a dedicated worker for thumbnails, resampling, histograms and hashing, and Canvas compositing on the main thread with a 256 MB LRU cache for derived previews. Zod validates every command at the boundary. WebMCP was treated as an architectural layer, not a feature. The interface and the tools call the same validated domain commands, the same history, and the same transaction path, so a dragged slider and an agent's apply_color_adjustment produce identical history entries. Tools register at module load, before first paint, via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every result is a JSON envelope carrying ok , the previous and resulting revision IDs, a transactionId , an undoToken , affectedIds , warnings, and a plain-language summary . Colour and layer commands also return an explanation of the term in ordinary words, so an agent can pass it straight back to someone who didn't know it. Every mutation accepts an optional expectedRevisionId and is refused with HISTORY_CONFLICT if the project moved on, checked immediately before the commit. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint , destructive ones destructiveHint , and anything that can return user-authored text carries untrustedContentHint . Errors carry a code , a fieldPath , a recoverySuggestion , and whether the project was preserved. The agent side is never invisible. Every tool call surfaces a card in the Activity Center, every committed revision carries its Undo, and History distinguishes the person's edits from the agent's. Challenges we ran into An agent cannot open a file. Browsers grant file access only from a user gesture. Rather than fake it, the tool focuses the Import control, reports whether an editor was open to receive that focus, and says why. A manage_project operation draws a three-frame sample scene and imports it through the same path a real file takes, so an agent arriving at an empty browser still has something to edit. Import had to be atomic across two stores. A project revision in IndexedDB and original bytes in OPFS can't share a transaction. A persisted intent record moves through prepared, committed, and deleted, and startup recovery finishes or undoes whatever a crash left, so History can never point at a file that isn't there. Adjustments bled. Brightening a rotated cut-out was brightening the background behind it, because the adjustment read a padded rectangle off the shared canvas. Each adjusted layer now renders alone on an isolated surface and is composited afterwards. WebMCP can't be tested in jsdom. 940 unit tests cover the domain, commands and persistence, but tool discovery only exists in a real WebMCP-capable browser over HTTPS, so every registration check was manual. Cutting video. Estro started as a photo and video editor. Ten days in, the video half doubled the surface and carried the least-verified code. It was removed, not hidden: roughly 12,500 lines, 14 tools, five panels, and one LGPL dependency. One thing done properly beats two things done partly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The person never loses control. Every agent action is a real, named, individually undoable edit in the same History as their own, and the explanation of the word travels with it. The honesty holds under pressure. Out-of-range values are clamped and the clamp is reported. Unavailable formats are disabled with a reason. A stale revision is refused rather than silently overwritten. There's no path by which the agent can do something to your photo that you can't see and can't reverse. Fifty-six tools, one command system, zero servers. What we learned Describing side effects in the tool description matters more than clever schemas. When a tool said exactly what it would change and what it would return, the model called it correctly first time. When it didn't, the model guessed. Returning an explanation from the tool, rather than trusting the model to write one, was the right call. The product's whole promise is that the word arrives attached to the effect. That only holds if the explanation comes from the same place the effect did. And the most useful tool in the set turned out to be one that changes nothing: the one that points at a control and explains it. Teaching isn't editing on someone's behalf. It's showing them where the thing is. What's next for Estro Local model support so the explanations can be spoken aloud for people who'd rather listen than read. Voice as an input, for the same reason. Bringing back a narrower video treatment once the photo side has been used by real people for a while. And a proper accessibility pass with screen-reader users, because a photo editor that explains itself in plain words should also work for people who can't see the slider it's explaining. Here we ask it to make a cold street photo look like a golden hour shot. We also tell it to explain every control it touches. You just talk to it like a normal person. title: DeskInTab
pitch: Give your AI agent a computer in your browser. Use the same apps to write, draw, analyze data, and work with files.
about_excerpt: Give your AI agent a computer in your browser. Use the same apps to write, draw, analyze data, and work with files. Like Comment Story Updates The Harbor release brief in Documents, with its exported PDF open in Preview. A Canvas diagram and project handoff with source files and a question for the user. Why I built it I wanted to give an AI agent its own personal computer. While exploring WebMCP, I started playing with the idea of a virtual operating system inside the browser. Each app could expose its own tools, letting the agent use a whole desktop to do different kinds of work. DeskInTab is that experiment. The agent gets a computer to work in, and you can use the same apps beside it. What it does DeskInTab brings everyday computer work into one browser desktop. You and your agent can: Take notes in Markdown or plain text, write formatted documents, read PDFs, and export reports. Analyze data in spreadsheets with formulas and charts. Sketch ideas and edit diagrams together in Canvas. Use Terminal to search files, extract document text, transform data, and run Bash pipelines. Browse and organize files, track tasks, and save project decisions and next steps. Turn JSON data into small apps with search, filters, and links to the original sources. The apps share one filesystem. A chart from Sheets can go into a document, and Terminal can process the files you see in Finder. You can open the agent's work, change it yourself, and continue together. Home saves preferences and reusable instructions. Projects keeps handoffs so an agent can leave a question for you and a later session can pick up your answer. Files persist after a browser reload. The video shows one example, planning a release for the fictional Harbor reading app. The agent works through interview notes, spreadsheet analysis, a release brief and PDF, tasks, and a Canvas roadmap. Why WebMCP fits The desktop exposes 89 WebMCP tools. Each tool calls the same application services as the human controls, so agent actions change the apps and files you have open. This lets the agent combine several apps in one task while you follow and edit the work. How it works Svelte 5 and TypeScript provide the interface. ZenFS stores the shared filesystem in IndexedDB. ZetaOffice handles documents and spreadsheets, Excalidraw handles drawings, and just-bash runs Terminal commands inside the browser without host or network access. What I learned Passing tool tests didn't guarantee that an agent could discover the full catalog. A client size limit blocked discovery until repeated schemas shared references. Tests now check the full payload and verify that every validation rule survives. Two desktop tabs can conflict over stored files. A Web Lock prevents that, and saved versions make edits recoverable. What's next Improve Office startup and workbook autosaving, and make project handoffs easier to find. The app currently keeps one workspace in your browser. Workspace packs let you back it up or move it. title: Tablée — Play Together, Human and Agent
pitch: 21 family games where a human and a browser agent share the same board through safe, game-native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: 21 family games where a human and a browser agent share the same board through safe, game-native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Tablée: 21 family games ready for human–agent play through WebMCP. Inspiration Most game agents play in a separate simulation or need broad control of the page. We wanted the opposite: keep a warm family-game experience while giving a browser agent the same constrained actions as a human player. The agent should understand the position, act legally, preserve hidden information, and then quietly wait for the person to play. What it does Tablée is a mobile-first PWA with 21 tabletop and puzzle games. A player can ask Codex or ChatGPT to play an entire match. The agent reads the public board and its positionId, chooses a legal action, plays it, then calls wait_for_position_change. That pending read wakes as soon as the human moves, so play continues without another prompt. How we built it The shared tablee-webmcp.js bridge uses document.modelContext.registerTool. A route catalogue attaches one bounded adapter per game. Every mutation includes expectedPositionId; mutations are serialized and legality is checked again at execution time. Closed JSON schemas and stable error codes make the tools predictable. For hidden-information games, the bridge first builds a seat-filtered public projection and only then calculates the position identifier. Secret words, mines, puzzle solutions, codes, other hands, hidden fleets, and draw order never enter tool responses. Multiplayer guests only accept authoritative state from the host. Challenges The hardest part was defining truthful public state across very different games. A 2048 action is one direction; Checkers may require a full capture path; Yams spans several phases. We also had to prevent stale concurrent actions and make continuous human-agent play efficient. Accomplishments One lifecycle-safe WebMCP bridge across 21 games Efficient long-poll waiting for human moves Hidden-information boundaries covered by automated tests Stale-position and concurrent-mutation protection Multiplayer host authority and per-seat projections Graceful fallback when WebMCP is unavailable What we learned The best agent interface is not a mirror of the DOM. It is a small domain API with stable vocabulary, bounded schemas, and an explicit concurrency model. For shared play, wait is as important as act. Challenge scope Tablée existed before the challenge. The public repository contains an explicit non-WebMCP baseline commit followed by the challenge-period WebMCP extension. Only that extension is submitted for judging. What's next A visible agent-connected indicator, cooperative modes, accessibility narration, server-verified multiplayer acknowledgements, and explainable replay traces. title: WallAlive
pitch: What if a child’s wall drawing could start moving and become part of a story? Kids can play and create stories together, then make their favorite creations into real keepsakes through Shopify
about_excerpt: What if a child’s wall drawing could start moving and become part of a story? Kids can play and create stories together, then make their favorite creations into real keepsakes through Shopify Like Comment Story Updates drawing webmcp agents web room changing draw together make an invite draw together Inspiration My eight years old daughter loves drawing everywhere. on paper, on the wall, and on her iPad. I love seeing her imagination, but like many parents, I also worry about how much time children spend only looking at screens. I started wondering what if screen time could begin with something a child created with their own hands? What if their drawing could leave the paper, become a character, and continue its story in a 3D world? That question became WallAlive. What it does WallAlive turns a child’s drawing into a movable 3D character. A child can draw inside the app or photograph a paper drawing. WallAlive separates the character from the background, detects its visible parts, builds a movable rig, and places it inside an interactive, storybook, wizard, or museum world. Children can paint the 3D character with brushes, spray paint, oil paint, and colorful splashes. They can make it walk, dance, wave, and join stories with characters created by friends. A browser agent can help plan stories, suggest painting activities, inspect what each character can do, and prepare a creator collection. Children still control the creative actions, and an adult must approve any Shopify product draft. drawing 3d model How we built it I used several small on-device computer-vision models for drawing isolation, face and body-part detection, pose estimation, and character topology. Three.js renders the characters, animations, paint effects, and interactive 3D worlds. WebMCP gives the browser agent structured tools for understanding the current scene and helping with the next step. The available tools change according to what the user is doing, such as drawing, checking the character, painting, storytelling, collaborating, or preparing a Shopify product. This makes the agent more reliable than asking it to understand the interface by guessing. Shopify’s API is used to read the connected catalog and create an unpublished product draft from approved artwork. Vercel hosts the public application, while Cloudflare D1 supports shared drawing rooms. I used Codex during development and gstack by Garry Tan to challenge the idea, review the experience, test the implementation, and find weak points. Challenges we ran into Turning a paper drawing into a believable 3D character was the hardest technical challenge. Real photographs contain paper edges, shadows, grid lines, handwriting, nearby objects, and sometimes several characters. Children also draw bodies in many different ways, so one fixed skeleton cannot work for every drawing. A single image does not show the back of a character either. I had to combine segmentation, pose estimation, learned topology, depth reconstruction, and a human review step instead of pretending every result would always be perfect. I also worried about whether WallAlive would be genuinely useful or only an interesting hackathon demo. I kept asking myself whether it solved a real problem and whether it was truly a good fit for WebMCP. Testing it with my daughter helped me find the answer that the value is not simply converting an image into 3D. It is helping a child continue creating, storytelling, collaborating, and learning from something they made themselves. Another challenge was using WebMCP meaningfully. At first, the app exposed too many tools and expected technical inputs. I changed it so the agent sees only the tools relevant to the child’s current activity and accepts natural requests such as “make a short wizard story” or “paint it with blue spray.” shop webmcp Accomplishments that we're proud of The moment I am most proud of was watching my daughter become curious about a character made from her own drawing. It was no longer just another game chosen for her. It began with something she created. I am also proud that WallAlive creates a complete journey that draw, check, build, paint, play, collaborate, and with adult approval prepare the artwork as a real Shopify product draft. Most importantly, the agent supports the child’s imagination without taking control of it. What we learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when the person and the agent have different roles. The agent can inspect information, organize a story, recommend the next activity, and handle complicated preparation. The child should still draw, paint, choose, and play. An adult should remain responsible for publishing or selling anything. I also learned that art and technology do not need to compete. Technology can give a physical drawing another life while keeping the child’s original work at the center. What's next for Wall alive Next, I want to improve character reconstruction with more varied children’s drawings, stronger multi-character segmentation, and better movable rigs. I also want to add richer collaborative stories, more interactive worlds, classroom activities, teacher-created challenges, and safer parent controls. The longer-term goal is for children to build shared 3D exhibitions, stories, and small creator shops from artwork they made themselves not from premade characters someone else gave them.
