title: Package-G WebMCP
pitch: Package-G lets ChatGPT inspect, run, and explain deterministic evidence audits through WebMCP—without letting the agent decide the verdict.
about_excerpt: Package-G lets ChatGPT inspect, run, and explain deterministic evidence audits through WebMCP—without letting the agent decide the verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration: AI agents are increasingly capable of navigating interfaces, collecting information, and helping humans complete complex workflows. But in evidence-sensitive work, there is an important boundary: the agent helping with the process should not automatically become the authority that decides what is true. That idea inspired Package-G WebMCP. Package-G is a deterministic, browser-local evidence auditor. A human defines and confirms the audit semantics, while claims, evidence, provenance, gaps, findings, and results remain explicitly inspectable. ChatGPT can navigate and operate that workflow through WebMCP, but the authoritative verdict is produced by Package-G's deterministic auditor. The core principle is simple: ChatGPT navigates. Package-G decides. What it does: Package-G lets a user create or load an audit workspace containing claims, evidence, provenance, and an audit contract. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can then: summarize the current workspace; read the audit contract; list and inspect claims; list and inspect evidence; identify evidence gaps; request a deterministic audit; retrieve the authoritative result; explain the resulting decision chain. The submitted application exposes exactly 10 WebMCP Site Tools. The important part is what those tools cannot do. ChatGPT cannot use them to invent authoritative findings, change evidence truth, override a verdict, or turn a rejected audit into an accepted one. For the same frozen inputs, ruleset, and auditor runtime, Package-G is designed to produce the same semantic audit result independently of the agent operating it. Why WebMCP This is a workflow where structured interaction matters much more than having an AI read text from a page. Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer application state from the visual interface and decide which buttons or text correspond to the user's intent. With WebMCP, Package-G exposes explicit, bounded operations with structured inputs and outputs. ChatGPT can understand the audit workspace as a tool-enabled application rather than approximating it from page content. We tested this using the ChatGPT desktop app and its built-in browser. ChatGPT discovered all 10 Package-G Site Tools and successfully invoked all 10. In our C09 demonstration scenario, Correct Evidence, Wrong Repository , ChatGPT requests the audit through WebMCP, while Package-G's deterministic Worker evaluates the evidence and returns: "REJECT_WITH_REPAIR_REQUIRED" ChatGPT can inspect and explain that result, but it cannot override it. How we built it: Package-G WebMCP is implemented as a browser-local TypeScript application using React and Vite. The deterministic auditor runs in a fresh Dedicated Module Worker. Runtime identity, ruleset identity, and audit inputs are explicitly bound so reproducibility can be checked rather than assumed. The application uses: WebMCP / document.modelContext for Site Tool registration; TypeBox schemas and Ajv standalone/AOT validation; Web Workers for deterministic audit execution; IndexedDB/Dexie for local persistence; Web Crypto for hashes and integrity checks; Vitest and fast-check for unit/property validation; Playwright for real-browser conformance testing; Netlify for the public production deployment. Core V1 does not require a remote application backend, remote database, or OpenAI API key. The audit itself runs locally in the browser. Challenges: One of the most useful parts of the project was discovering problems that only appeared when the system left the local test environment. Our first production pipeline revealed that a clean Netlify build did not reproduce the same finalized D11 verification artifact as our audited local release. We changed the release pipeline so that a production build validates a closed, cryptographically bound scenario corpus and fails transactionally instead of leaving stale release artifacts behind. A later live-browser test exposed another issue: our strict production Content Security Policy blocked Ajv's runtime schema compilation because it relied on dynamic code generation. Instead of weakening the CSP with unsafe-eval , we changed the validation architecture to compile the runtime validators ahead of time with Ajv standalone generation. We independently compared the new AOT validators against reference Ajv behavior across more than 15,000 validation cases with zero mismatches. The final production application runs successfully with the strict CSP and without runtime "eval" or "Function" construction. What we learned: The biggest lesson was that WebMCP is not only about making websites easier for agents to operate. It can also be used to define authority boundaries between an agent and the application it operates. We learned how important lifecycle-scoped tools, bounded schemas, deterministic execution, runtime identity, production CSP behavior, and real in-app ChatGPT discovery are when moving from a WebMCP prototype to something independently testable. We also learned that browser-local deterministic systems and AI agents do not have to compete for authority. They can complement each other. What's next: Package-G can operate without an LLM, which opens an interesting next step: exposing the same deterministic audit core through human-only, agent-operated, and hybrid workflows. WebMCP demonstrates that an AI agent can participate deeply in a high-integrity application without becoming its final source of truth. title: Countersign
pitch: It lets you use an AI agent to fight a denied insurance claim, without having to trust the agent.
about_excerpt: It lets you use an AI agent to fight a denied insurance claim, without having to trust the agent. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT screen Interface Inspiration Roughly 95% of denied health insurance claims are never appealed. Not because people accept the decision — because the process is slow, jargon-heavy, and exhausting by design. A letter arrives saying CO-97 , and most people put it in a drawer. An AI agent is almost perfectly suited to that problem. It can decode the denial code, check the appeal window, and draft the letter in seconds. But 2026 is a bad year to hand an agent your paperwork. OpenAI has said prompt injection is "unlikely to ever be fully solved," ChatGPT Atlas was retired partly over security, and researchers have tricked six different AI browsers into leaking credentials. Meanwhile 68% of organizations can't distinguish agent activity from human activity in their own logs. An insurance workspace is the worst possible place to put an agent, because the agent must read letters written by the opposing party . If the insurer can put text in front of your assistant, the insurer can talk to your assistant behind your back. We didn't want to build a safer agent. We wanted to build an app where the agent's safety doesn't have to be load-bearing. What it does Countersign is a workspace for appealing a denied claim, with an agent you don't have to trust. The agent does real work: it reads your denial letters, explains what CO-97 actually means and what evidence overturns it, checks how many days you have left, and drafts the appeal. Every tool the page exposes sits in one of three capability tiers, and the tier decides what happens — not the agent's judgment : read — runs immediately, changes nothing write — runs immediately, always attributed, always revertible consequential — submit_appeal , accept_settlement , withdraw_claim . These never run on an agent's say-so. The agent can only propose them. When the agent proposes something consequential, it doesn't execute and apologize later. The page stops it and raises a consent card showing the exact capability, the exact arguments, and what it would cost you in plain language — "Close CLM-4471 for $0 against $2,840 billed, giving up the right to appeal." You approve or reject. Everything either of you does lands in a provenance ledger — actor, tool, arguments, timestamp, outcome — and anything the agent changed can be undone. What's now possible that wasn't: you can let an agent operate on something that actually matters — money, a legal deadline, a waiver of your right to appeal — without auditing its reasoning, because the actions that can hurt you were never in its reach. Not withheld by instruction. Structurally absent. How we built it WebMCP is what makes this possible. Because the site declares exactly what an agent can do, the site also gets to decide what it can't. Ten tools registered imperatively via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Risk annotations that are honest and test-enforced : readOnlyHint on every read tool, untrustedContentHint on read_correspondence (which returns insurer text), and destructiveHint on the three consequential ones. Tests assert no consequential tool can ever claim to be read-only. Chrome's character budgets enforced in CI, not by hand — 500 chars per tool description, 150 per parameter, and tool output capped at 1.5K before it reaches the model. Staged execution. A consequential call returns a machine-readable NOT EXECUTED result telling the agent to stop and wait, so a well-behaved agent explains rather than retries. An actor-agnostic gate. workspace.invoke(tool, args, actor) takes an actor, so a human clicking a button and an agent calling a tool go through the identical enforcement path. WebMCP is how the agent reaches the rule, not where the rule lives. Rollback via state snapshots taken before any mutating call. Vite + React + TypeScript, no backend, no accounts, no keys — all state lives in the page, so it deploys as a static site and judges need nothing to test it. 49 tests. Challenges we ran into The agent refused to propose anything. Our first tool descriptions were written as warnings — "this leaves the workspace and cannot be unsent." A well-aligned model read that and simply declined to touch those tools at all, telling the user it wouldn't "create an external claim action." The consent gate never fired, because nothing ever reached it. The fix was to lead with the safety rather than bury it: "Propose filing the appeal. Calling this sends nothing." Proposing had to be framed as the safe act it actually is. Capping tool output without making tools useless. The 1.5K budget is easy to blow with a list of claims. We had to truncate structurally — dropping whole records and telling the agent to ask for a specific one — rather than slicing strings into invalid JSON. Making consent legible. A card that says accept_settlement {"amount": 0} is not informed consent. It had to say what you're giving up, in dollars, against what you were owed. The demo problem, honestly. When we tested the planted injection, the model recognized it and refused — which is the outcome you want and the wrong outcome for a video. We could have escalated the attack until something broke. We didn't. The test suite proves the claim can't settle even when a model is fooled, and that felt like better evidence than a staged hijack. Accomplishments that we're proud of The spec's Issue #165 is still deciding how a tool should elicit user confirmation, and Chrome's own tool security guidance currently offers no pattern for it at all . Countersign is one working answer, built entirely with today's shipped API: consent as a page-owned capability tier, rather than a prompt the agent is trusted to raise. We're also proud that the safety claims are checkable rather than asserted. The character budgets, the annotation honesty, and the injection defense are all covered by tests — including one that plants a real prompt injection in the seed data and proves the claim still can't settle. What we learned Tool descriptions are product surface, not documentation. They're the only thing standing between your intent and the model's behavior, and a single reframing — warning versus invitation — completely changed what the agent was willing to do. Safety language that scares the agent away from safe actions is a UX bug. Alignment is not a substitute for capability control. Our model resisted the injection. That was luck we don't want to depend on, from a model we don't control, against an attacker who gets to iterate. What's next for Countersign Skills ( Issue #161 ) to give the agent workflow-level guidance, not just a list of functions. Adopt requestUserInteraction() natively once the spec settles, replacing our page-level staging with the browser-mediated primitive. Consent policy — spending thresholds, auto-approve for low-stakes actions, step-up confirmation for irreversible ones. Cross-origin delegation via exposedTo , so a patient advocate or legal aid worker's agent can be granted a scoped subset of tools. Real claim import from EOB documents, and lifting the gate out into a library any site can adopt — the pattern isn't specific to insurance. title: A11yFix
pitch: A11yFix: A WebMCP QA tool that detects WCAG 2.2 barriers, proposes exact ARIA code fixes, and generates automated Playwright tests, always keeping the developer in control.
about_excerpt:
A11yFix: A WebMCP QA tool that detects WCAG 2.2 barriers, proposes exact ARIA code fixes, and generates automated Playwright tests, always keeping the developer in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Years of advocating for strict WCAG compliance and building specialized testing wrappers revealed a persistent gap in the industry: static analysis tools catch syntax errors, but developers still struggle to implement complex WAI-ARIA patterns accurately. The WebMCP challenge sparked the idea for an active, contextual assistant. Rather than just flagging a missing focus trap or a target size failure, the goal was to build a system that understands the active DOM state and proposes exact, compliant remediations while keeping the developer firmly in control. 

 What it does 

 A11yFix is a Web QA Workbench that acts as an intelligent copilot for accessibility. It audits web pages in real-time against strict WCAG 2.2 Level AA and WAI-ARIA APG standards. When it detects a barrier (like an invalid heading order or insufficient target size), it uses a WebMCP agent to deeply analyze the semantic context. It then proposes specific, compliant code patches and automatically generates a Playwright regression test to verify the fix. Crucially, it operates with strict "human-in-the-loop" execution—no DOM mutation happens without developer approval. 

 How we built it 

 The architecture follows a Spec-Driven Development (SDD) approach. The client interface is a React-based QA Workbench deployed on Vercel that intercepts the active page state and isolates the accessibility tree. The backend is a Node.js WebMCP Server that exposes eight granular tools categorized by permissions (READ, PROPOSE, WRITE) using robust Zod schemas. This setup creates an automated QA loop: the agent audits, proposes patches, and invokes tools to generate automated Playwright regression tests, closing the development cycle seamlessly. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The primary hurdle was context window saturation. Raw DOM structures contain massive amounts of CSS and visual noise that easily confuse LLMs. To solve this, the application parses and purifies the tree before sending it to the model, stripping away everything except pure semantic accessibility data. This extreme DOM reduction was critical to prevent hallucinations and drastically reduce latency. 

 Additionally, we had to guarantee security. Establishing a strict "human-in-the-loop" barrier for the apply_remediation tool required meticulous state management, ensuring the WebMCP agent could never autonomously mutate the live page without explicit developer consent. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are incredibly proud of bridging the gap between theoretical accessibility guidelines and practical developer workflows. Successfully implementing a robust "human-in-the-loop" safeguard within the WebMCP framework ensures that the tool is both powerful and secure. Furthermore, automatically generating ready-to-use Playwright regression tests directly from an AI's remediation proposal transforms a traditionally tedious QA task into a fast, one-click experience. 

 What we learned 

 Integrating the Model Context Protocol within a live browser environment proved that agents are drastically more effective when constrained by strict schemas and pure semantic data. The development process reinforced that AI should not act as a black box that bypasses the developer, but rather as a high-precision instrument that amplifies their ability to ship inclusive, accessible software. 

 What's next for A11yFix 

 The next step is to integrate A11yFix directly into CI/CD pipelines and popular IDEs via a dedicated extension. We also plan to expand the test generation engine to support other frameworks like Vitest and Playwright, building upon our previous research in automated accessibility testing. Ultimately, we want to evolve A11yFix into the definitive open-source standard for autonomous, yet developer-guided, web accessibility remediation.

title: easyACR
pitch: A better web should work for everyone.
about_excerpt: A better web should work for everyone. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Safari Browser - Not supported OpenAI Browser - Standard Supported OpenAI Browser - Standard Supported - Dark Mode Homepage Homepage - Dark Mode easyACR Inspiration An Accessibility Conformance Report, or ACR, explains how well a digital product supports recognized accessibility requirements such as WCAG. It gives customers, procurement teams, accessibility professionals, and product owners a structured way to understand what a product supports, where barriers remain, and what evidence supports each claim. An ACR is commonly produced by completing a Voluntary Product Accessibility Template, or VPAT. The VPAT provides the reporting structure and specifications that when completed produces an ACR. Producing a useful ACR requires more than just filing in this template. Teams must evaluate the product, collect evidence, interpret criteria, describe limitations, and keep updating the document as the software changes. The idea for easyACR grew directly from my experience as an accessibility officer at a software firm. In that role, I see the importance of trustworthy accessibility documentation and the amount of specialized, repetitive work required to create it. Evidence is distributed across scans, manual testing, bug trackers, product docs, and conversations with engineers. Turning that information into a clear report is difficult for teams that do not have dedicated accessibility resources. This matters to us because accessibility is part of delivering responsible software. People rely on digital products to access information and services and customers need accurate conformance information to make purchasing and deployment decisions. An ACR can guide remediation, improve accountability, and help teams make better decisions. easyACR has evolved into a focused service that combines automation, agent assistance, and human judgment. Its purpose is not to replace accessibility audits and professionals or claim that an automated scan means conformance. It is to spend less time gathering and organizing evidence and more time understanding barriers and improving the product. What it does easyACR is an accessibility service that scans authorized public websites and turns automated findings into a structured draft ACR based on the VPAT standard. A person can use the accessible React interface to start a scan, follow progress, inspect findings, and create draft evidence aligned with WCAG 2.2. An assisting agent can perform the same workflow through four WebMCP tools: start_accessibility_scan get-scan-status list_accessibility_issues create_draft_acr This is a strong WebMCP use case because an accessibility review is a structured, multi-step process rather than a single prompt or button. The agent needs to start an authorized job, monitor asynchronous progress, retrieve trustworthy results, and prepare evidence without exceeding the person’s permissions or the service’s security. WebMCP creates a better experience by giving people more than one way to interact. Someone can use the visible interface, work through an agent, or move between both approaches. The browser and agent paths reach the same application functions, permissions, job state, and evidence. This provides choice without creating two different products. Together, a person can define the goal, authorize the target, and provide judgment while an agent handles repetitive coordination: starting the scan, checking its status, gathering relevant findings, and organizing draft evidence. Previously, that work often required manually transferring information among scanners, reports, spreadsheets, and AI conversations. easyACR makes it one continuous and inspectable workflow while keeping the final certification manual. How we built it The browser experience uses React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. We built the interface around semantic structure, keyboard operation, visible focus, contrast, reflow, and clear messaging making accessibility part of the product foundation rather than an afterthought. WebMCP is implemented with the browser-native document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Each of the four tools has a JSON input schema, returns structured results, and observes the abort-signal lifecycle for cleanup. The callbacks use the same shared application services as the visible React controls and call the same authenticated Node.js API, so rules and results remain consistent across human and agent interactions. The rest of the stack includes: A Node.js API service for sessions, authorization, terms acceptance, CSRF protection, quotas, jobs, findings, and evidence. Playwright and Axe for automated accessibility scans. Supabase Auth, Postgres, and row-level security for identity and durable jobs, findings, and evidence. Resend SMTP for magic-link authentication emails. Private authentication and data gateways that keep privileged credentials away from the browser and scanner. An authenticated scanner egress proxy that blocks private networks, unsafe redirects, and unauthorized destinations. pnpm, Vitest, Playwright route tests, and automated accessibility checks. Docker Compose and Caddy on a Hetzner Cloud VPS, with Caddy providing the public HTTPS edge. Challenges we ran into The largest challenge was making the agent path as trustworthy as the visible interface. Registering a browser tool is straightforward; ensuring that every invocation respects authentication, accepted terms, authorization, quotas, cancellation, and evidence boundaries is more difficult. WebMCP is an emerging browser capability, we had to work through registration behavior, feature detection, browser compatibility, schemas, cleanup, and useful messaging. The prototype’s four tools now work, but getting there required separating browser integration problems from API, session, and local-environment problems. The scanner introduced a second security challenge. A service that opens user-provided URLs can become an unintended gateway into private networks. We addressed this by scoping to public HTTPS-only targets, same-origin crawling, a ten-page limit, redirect checks, private-address blocking, isolating Playwright workers and an egress proxy. Additionally, automated tools can identify valuable evidence, but automated results are not an accessibility certification. The interface, tool descriptions, and generated evidence consistently reinforce that qualified human review remains necessary. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that easyACR treats accessibility as both the purpose of the service and a requirement of its own interface. All four WebMCP functions work through the current browser-native registration pattern. They expose a meaningful end-to-end workflow rather than isolated demonstrations, and they share behavior with the interface instead of duplicating business logic. Most importantly, the product maintains an honest division of responsibility: automation gathers and organizes evidence, agents help coordinate the work, and people remain responsible for interpretation and accessibility decisions. What we learned We learned that agent accessibility is not only about letting an AI operate a website. It is about offering equivalent ways to act while preserving the same context, safeguards, and outcomes. WebMCP works best when tools map to clear user intentions rather than low-level interface actions. “Start an authorized accessibility scan” is more useful and reliable than asking an agent to imitate a series of clicks. Structured inputs and results also make the workflow easier to inspect, test, and recover when something fails. We validated our thoughts that the shared application functions are essential. When the interface and WebMCP callbacks use the same service layer, improvements to validation, security, and business rules benefit both paths. What's next for easyACR Next, we plan to strengthen the path from automated findings to collaborative human review. That includes richer evidence workflows, clearer remediation guidance, improved progress and error reporting, and more ways for reviewers to add context that automation cannot observe. We also want to improve recovery for interrupted or long-running scans, and continue refining the tool schemas based on real life workflows. On the infrastructure side, the next steps include selecting a CI service, automating repeatable verification and deployment, and adding a preview environment before production releases. We will continue hardening the scanner boundary, data retention controls, monitoring, and operational documentation as the service grows. The technology will keep evolving, but the purpose will remain constant: combine accessible design, responsible automation, and human judgment to help create a better web for everyone. title: Forge
pitch: Forge is an open-source, browser-based IDE where humans and AI agents can work on the same project.
about_excerpt: Forge is an open-source, browser-based IDE where humans and AI agents can work on the same project. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Forge An agent-native web IDE for humans and AI agents Inspiration AI coding agents can generate impressive amounts of code, but generating code is only one part of software development. A real development workflow also involves creating projects, managing files, installing dependencies, running applications, reading console output, debugging errors, rebuilding, and eventually deploying the result. Most AI coding experiences handle these tasks through a chat interface, while the actual development environment remains separate. Forge asks a different question: what if the development environment itself could be used by an AI agent? Forge is a browser-based IDE where humans and AI agents can work on the same project. Instead of asking an agent to generate code and then manually moving that code into an IDE, Forge exposes its development capabilities directly through WebMCP. The agent can operate the IDE itself. Why WebMCP? Forge is a particularly strong fit for WebMCP because its core functionality is already organized around meaningful actions that an agent needs to perform. An IDE is not just a page to read. It is an environment to operate. Before WebMCP, an agent interacting with a browser-based IDE would need to rely on indirect mechanisms such as simulated clicks, keyboard input, or copying and pasting code. With WebMCP, Forge can expose its capabilities as structured, semantic tools. The agent can discover what Forge can do and directly invoke those capabilities. This transforms the IDE from a human-only interface into an agent-accessible development environment . What agents can do in Forge Forge exposes meaningful development operations through WebMCP, including: Create and manage projects List project files Read files Write and modify files Run projects Inspect console output Build projects Deploy projects These tools are connected directly to Forge's underlying application logic. The WebMCP layer is therefore not a separate demonstration layer. The agent and the human interface operate on the same project and the same underlying state. For example, an agent can be asked to: "Create a React landing page for a fictional company." It can then: Create the project. Create and modify the required files. Run the development server. Inspect the result. Check the console for errors. Modify the code when necessary. Build the project. Deploy it. The agent is not merely generating a code snippet. It is operating the development environment. Human + Agent collaboration Forge is designed around collaboration rather than replacement. The human developer remains inside the IDE and can see the project, preview the application, inspect the code, and make manual changes at any time. The agent can perform repetitive or complex development operations through WebMCP while the human remains in control. A developer can ask an agent to create a project, modify multiple files, run it, inspect an error, fix the problem, and build the result. The developer can then review the changes, edit the code themselves, and ask the agent to continue. Both human and agent can work on the same project without leaving the development environment. This is the experience that WebMCP makes possible. What was difficult before? Without WebMCP, an AI assistant could generate the code for a project, but the developer would still need to transfer that code into the development environment and manually perform many of the surrounding operations. The workflow becomes: Ask AI → Copy code → Open IDE → Create files → Install dependencies → Run → Find errors → Go back to AI → Copy fixes → Repeat Forge changes this interaction into: Ask agent → Agent operates Forge → Review → Iterate The important difference is not simply that AI can write code. It is that the agent can use the tools of the development environment itself. Built for the browser Forge runs directly in the browser using WebContainers, providing a real development environment without requiring a local installation. The editor is powered by Monaco Editor, giving developers a familiar coding experience while keeping the entire workflow inside the browser. Forge is built with: React TypeScript Vite Monaco Editor WebContainers WebMCP Tailwind CSS WebMCP implementation Forge registers its capabilities using the WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a clear name, description, structured input schema, and execution function. The tools call Forge's actual application logic rather than simulating interaction with the UI. This architecture allows both the human interface and AI agents to work with the same underlying functionality. The result is a genuine WebMCP integration rather than a chatbot placed on top of an existing application. Execution and agent-native design Forge was designed around the idea that WebMCP tools should represent meaningful operations , not low-level interface actions. Instead of exposing tools such as "click button" or "type text", Forge exposes higher-level development operations such as create_project , read_file , write_file , run_project , get_console , build_project , and deploy_project . This makes the interface understandable to an agent while keeping the application usable for humans. The result is an IDE that has two interfaces: A visual interface for humans. A structured tool interface for agents. Both operate on the same environment. Potential impact Forge explores a future where web applications are not only designed for people, but are also designed to be used by AI agents. For developers, this could reduce the friction between AI-generated code and a working application. For AI agents, it provides a structured environment where they can move beyond generating text and actually perform meaningful software development tasks. The same principle could extend beyond IDEs to other professional web applications: design tools, data platforms, project management systems, scientific software, and more. Forge is therefore an experiment in a broader idea: What happens when the tools we use every day become directly accessible to AI agents? Creativity & ambition Forge is not simply an online code editor with AI assistance. It explores the idea of an agent-native IDE : an environment where AI agents are first-class users of the application rather than external assistants sitting beside it. WebMCP provides the bridge between the agent and the application. The goal is not to make AI better at pretending to be a developer. The goal is to give AI agents the tools they need to actually participate in the development process. Open source Forge is open source and designed to be transparent and inspectable. The project demonstrates how a complex browser application can expose useful capabilities to AI agents through an open web standard. Built for the WebMCP Challenge Forge was created for the WebMCP Challenge to explore the future of the open web, where humans and AI agents can interact, collaborate, and create together. The central idea is simple: The future of agentic software may not be an AI sitting beside an application — it may be an AI working inside it. Forge — The IDE that agents can use. title: tapfill
pitch: Upgrading existing web forms using WebMCP, not just the ones built from scratch for agents
about_excerpt:
Upgrading existing web forms using WebMCP, not just the ones built from scratch for agents
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Forms are everywhere, but they were designed around clicks, typing, dropdowns, and rigid question flows. 

 We wondered: what if you could just talk to a form? 

 Instead of building another AI form product, we chose the form people already know and use: Google Forms. The goal was to make an existing web interface agent native without rebuilding it. 

 That became TapFill , a Chrome extension that adds a WebMCP powered voice interface to Google Forms, allowing an AI agent to understand, navigate, and fill forms through natural conversation. 

 What it does 

 TapFill turns an ordinary Google Form into a conversational interface. 

 Install the Chrome extension, open a Google Form, and activate TapFill. You can then simply talk to the form. 

 The agent can understand the form's structure, determine what information is needed, ask relevant questions, translate natural language into structured field values, fill the form, validate responses, and submit it. 

 The important part is that the form itself remains the interface . TapFill does not replace Google Forms with a new application. It adds an agent interface to the existing page. 

 A form built for humans can now be operated naturally by both humans and AI agents . 

 How we built it 

 TapFill is a Chrome extension that runs directly on the Google Forms page. 

 When a form is opened, the extension inspects its structure and creates a semantic representation of the available fields and actions. It then exposes those capabilities through WebMCP , allowing a compatible in browser agent to interact with the page through structured tools rather than trying to visually navigate or guess at DOM elements. 

 The extension provides tools for operations such as: 

 
 reading the form schema and current state 
 identifying unanswered fields 
 setting field values 
 validating responses 
 submitting the form 
 

 On top of the WebMCP layer, we built a voice interface that handles the human side of the interaction. The agent turns conversational answers into structured tool calls while the underlying Google Form updates in real time. 

 The architecture is intentionally lightweight: 

 Chrome Extension → Google Forms → WebMCP Tools → AI Agent → Voice 

 This lets us demonstrate WebMCP on a widely used existing website rather than requiring a new application to be built from scratch. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making an existing, third party web application agent friendly without rebuilding it. 

 Google Forms was never designed around an agent tool interface, so we had to bridge its existing UI and DOM structure with a clean, semantic WebMCP representation. 

 We also had to solve the harder problem behind "voice form filling": understanding conversational answers and reliably mapping them to the correct fields, while preserving the structured semantics and validation expected by the original form. 

 Finally, we had to make the experience feel like a conversation rather than speech to text controlling a webpage. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that TapFill demonstrates a fundamentally different way of interacting with an existing website without replacing the website itself . 

 The most satisfying moment is watching a completely ordinary Google Form transform from a sequence of fields into a conversation. 

 Technically, we're particularly proud of using a Chrome extension to retrofit WebMCP capabilities onto an existing third party web application , showing how agent native interfaces can potentially be layered onto the web that already exists. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the hard part of agentic interfaces is not simply getting an LLM to produce the right answer. 

 It is creating a reliable bridge between natural human intent and structured actions on the web . 

 We also learned that familiar interfaces are powerful. When the underlying Google Form stays visible and behaves exactly as expected, the leap from "AI demo" to "this could actually change how I use the web" happens almost instantly. 

 Most importantly, we learned that WebMCP can be interesting not only for websites built from scratch with agents in mind, but also as a mechanism for progressively making the existing web more agent accessible . 

 What's next for TapFill 

 Google Forms is just the beginning. 

 Our vision is to make existing web forms and workflows agent native , rather than forcing people to migrate to entirely new AI first applications. 

 TapFill could evolve from a voice layer for Google Forms into a broader compatibility layer for web applications, allowing agents to understand and operate interfaces that were never originally designed for them. 

 The web already has the interfaces. We want to give agents a way to use them.

about_excerpt:
A live world map of 211 kitesurfing spots, re-scored for your gear with a WebMCP agent bridge.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Kitespot Atlas 

 Kitespot Atlas is a live world map of 211 kitesurfing spots, scored in real time against the rider's weight and kite quiver, with a WebMCP bridge so an agent can operate the page itself rather than just talk about it. 

 What we're proud of 

 An agent that doesn't just talk about kitesurfing — it flies the map, re-scores 211 spots against your actual gear, and leaves you a note and a standing weather watch, all inside the page you already trust. It feels less like querying a chatbot and more like handing the wheel to a co-pilot who can already see the screen. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP lets the page expose structured tools and its current state directly to an agent. Instead of asking an agent to describe what a user should click, the agent can operate the Kitespot Atlas experience itself: work with the map, re-score spots for the rider's setup, and create useful actions such as notes and weather watches. 

 What's next 

 More sports and gear profiles beyond kiting, richer multi-day trip planning across spot clusters, and pushing on what else a page can safely hand an agent once it's willing to expose its own state instead of hiding behind an API.

title: Friction
pitch: Test the same task through human eyes and agent tools.
about_excerpt: Test the same task through human eyes and agent tools. Like Comment Story Updates Human-only patch review explains the evidence and proposed contract repairs. Baseline lab: paired human and agent traces expose a 50/100 parity score. Repaired scenario: clearer visible wording and a guarded completion contract. Ten real page-side WebMCP tools share state with the visible interface. Paired retest: the repaired human and agent journeys reach 96/100 parity. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Friction Inspiration WebMCP lets a live page publish named, structured actions instead of forcing an agent to infer buttons and forms. That creates a new usability question: does the agent receive the same information, consent gates, and final state that a person sees? Friction is a dual usability laboratory for answering that question. It pairs one visual journey with one WebMCP journey, exposes the differences, repairs both interfaces together, and proves the improvement with a retest. What it does The deterministic RelayConf event-registration scenario contains three intentional problems: a quiet-zone seat is hidden behind vague human-facing wording; the baseline agent result omits a $12 service fee and refund condition; an ambiguously described completion tool finalizes without the human review gate. Friction records both traces and scores outcome, information, consent, state, and effort parity. It produces evidence-backed findings and a four-part patch. A human must approve that patch through the visible UI—approval is intentionally not agent-callable. After approval, the human option becomes clear, the tool returns an itemized total and policy, and finalization requires a review token plus confirmed=true . The paired score rises from 50/100 to 96/100. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP generates one side of the experiment. The page registers ten tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; these are not a remote MCP server and do not automate the DOM. Tool handlers and visual controls share the same React state and durable browser storage, so agent mutations immediately change the visible trace, findings, and comparison. Without WebMCP, Friction could test only visual automation. With WebMCP, it can inspect the explicit contract a site offers to agents and compare that contract against the human experience. How humans and agents work together People complete and judge the visual task, report hesitation, and retain approval authority. Agents exercise the structured contract, analyze traces, submit findings, and propose interface changes. Neither side replaces the other: the agent contributes speed and structured analysis, while the person supplies subjective usability evidence and approves consequential changes. How we built it Friction uses React 19, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, shadcn primitives, and ChatGPT Sites-compatible Cloudflare output. Ten page-owned WebMCP tools use restrictive JSON Schemas, runtime checks, read/write annotations, untrusted-content hints, feature detection, and registration cleanup with AbortController . The account-free demo persists locally in the browser, making the before/after experiment repeatable without credentials or external APIs. Deterministic tests cover the parity score, consent and information failures, approval transition, and repaired replay. Challenges we ran into The most important design challenge was avoiding a fake split between “human UI state” and “agent demo state.” Every interaction had to operate on the same live model. The second was expressing the repair as a real contract change: the completion tool’s description and JSON Schema are re-registered after human approval, and its handler independently enforces review and confirmation. Accomplishments that we're proud of A non-trivial ten-tool WebMCP implementation over shared visible state. A complete evidence → proposal → human approval → retest loop. A consent failure that is demonstrably blocked by the repaired handler. A polished responsive product requiring no accounts, secrets, or external APIs. Deterministic tests, type checks, linting, production build, and dependency audit. What we learned Parity is broader than whether both paths eventually produce the same record. A fast agent path can still be worse if it hides cost, weakens consent, or returns less context. Tool schemas, descriptions, results, and confirmation design are part of the product interface and need usability testing just as much as buttons and labels do. What's next for Friction Future versions could import OpenTelemetry-style traces, compare multiple scenarios, export regression suites for CI, and provide a lightweight SDK that lets other WebMCP sites embed paired parity tests while keeping approval policies application-owned. title: PaperSpace
pitch: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI tools treat a research paper as a file to summarize or a block of text to retrieve from. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What becomes possible when a person and an agent share a paper's text and its spatial reading environment inside the browser? Reading a paper is rarely linear. A reader moves between related work, methods, equations, figures, experiments, and appendices while building a mental map of where each idea lives. Conventional PDF viewers collapse that map into one page at a time. Chat interfaces collapse it even further into excerpts detached from their visual source. PaperSpace preserves that spatial memory. Every page of every imported PDF is unfolded onto a borderless two-dimensional desk. Pages remain live, selectable PDF surfaces, but they can also be moved, grouped, searched, compared, and revisited as part of a persistent visual workspace. The browser is essential to this interaction. It owns the PDFs the person explicitly selected, the rendered pages, the local text index, the page geometry, the current camera, and the workspace the person is looking at. WebMCP gives an agent direct access to that authorized, browser-local state, keeping the person and the agent aligned on one live workspace. We built PaperSpace for the WebMCP Challenge as a focused, open-source, single-person tool centered on reading, understanding, and presenting research papers. PaperSpace is a shared spatial instrument where the person controls the source material and the agent helps organize attention inside the same visible world. What it does PaperSpace is a local-first spatial desk for research papers. When a person imports a PDF, PaperSpace unfolds every page from left to right and top to bottom using each page's real aspect ratio. Every page becomes an independently movable and resizable live sheet with selectable text. The complete paper stays visible as a spatial place with its reading order intact. PaperSpace extracts text and normalized page geometry locally with PDF.js. Each page becomes searchable as soon as its index is ready. A reusable inspect_workspace briefing reports exact coverage and compact sampled page excerpts, so an agent can prepare once and then read the broadest useful contiguous range in one call, including the whole paper when full context matters. Through WebMCP, the agent can search the available corpus, batch-read paper text, locate an exact passage, and guide the shared camera to that region. The camera first pulls back to establish spatial context, travels across the desk, and then lands with the source itself centered in a calm view with generous breathing room. The app exposes nine WebMCP tools: inspect_workspace returns reusable readiness, compact paper briefs, every page's world geometry, visual artifacts, sequences, and camera state. search_papers progressively searches indexed pages and returns page-level matches with normalized source regions plus exact coverage. read_paper_pages reads one contiguous range or a whole indexed paper in one call, with optional block geometry and an explicit caller-selected character cap. focus_region guides the camera to a search match or an explicit PDF region. arrange_papers reflows pages into reading-order grids and arranges complete paper groups. snapshot_paper_region places a source-linked raster crop from an exact PDF region. place_plot creates a safe declarative line plot from finite numeric data. place_image validates and places PNG, JPEG, and WebP visuals. present_sequence creates a captioned sequence of semantic paper regions and visual artifacts. PaperSpace also gives the agent an explicit delivery contract. When PaperSpace is available, substantive introductions, explanations, reviews, comparisons, and answers grounded across multiple paper regions are delivered through present_sequence . Chat provides concise supporting context, while a single grounded passage can use focus_region and simple localized Q&A remains lightweight. The sequence interaction is the heart of the product. Suppose one experiment is explained across related work, methods, and results on three distant pages. The agent can build a three-frame sequence with a caption for each view. When presentation begins, PaperSpace temporarily draws those original pages together beside their paper in first-appearance order. Quiet numbered source slots preserve the paper's topology throughout the presentation. The same original page can support several region frames through one staged page. Visual artifacts stay in their existing world positions. Exiting the sequence restores every moved page—including its position, size, and layer—and returns the camera to its exact entry state. Keeping a sequence saves its semantic frames; replaying it organizes pages again from their current positions and restores them again afterward. This enables requests such as: “Find where this experiment is motivated, defined, and evaluated, then organize those pages for me.” “Focus on the ablation equation and keep the surrounding paragraph in view.” “Read the method and results, plot the reported trend, and place it beside the source page.” “Present the three views in sequence and explain what changes between them.” Everything happens on the same desk the person can inspect and manipulate. Agent actions produce visible feedback, and temporary organization is transactionally isolated from the person's saved layout. Spatial mutation tools perform an atomic visual preflight inside the app. Standard calls place plots, images, source crops, and arrangements in clear areas. An agent can use force: true for an intentional dense layout, while media, schema, source-target, and security validation remain active. How we built it PaperSpace is a pure frontend SvelteKit and TypeScript application compiled as a static site for Cloudflare Pages. Browser storage and browser-authorized files provide the complete runtime state. The application is organized around four client-side layers: Svelte components render the infinite desk, unfolded PDF sheets, artifacts, search interface, frame editor, and presentation chrome. A single reactive workspace model owns paper metadata, per-page geometry, the camera, artifacts, semantic sequences, and all person- and agent-triggered state transitions. PDF.js renders pages and extracts text plus normalized block geometry in a same-origin Web Worker. IndexedDB stores validated workspace metadata, browser-authorized PDF copies, raster images, and saved semantic frames. The workspace schema stores a stable paper identity and page number for every PDF page, while position, size, and layer remain mutable world properties. PDF inspection records each page's true dimensions. A deterministic row-major layout uses a bounded column count to keep long papers spatially legible, and complete paper bounds are used to prevent different imports from overlapping. Every page has a DOM sheet so its identity remains stable in the world. PaperSpace activates detailed PDF canvas and text rendering near the viewport and above a useful zoom threshold, keeping long unfolded papers responsive. PDF rasterization uses a two-tier residency system. Every successfully rendered page retains a 288-pixel-wide aspect-preserving preview, while an LRU applies a 48-million-pixel budget to unpinned high-resolution page canvases. Pages in the strict viewport, the current focus target, and the active sequence frame are pinned and may temporarily exceed that budget. A compact preview preserves visual continuity as high-resolution canvases move through the working set. Raster canvases and selectable text layers have independent lifecycles, and a double-canvas pipeline swaps each completed bitmap into view atomically. Region targeting uses top-left normalized coordinates. The same semantic region can therefore be mapped through a page's current world geometry after the page has been moved or resized. Camera motion is handled by a cancellable controller with pull-back, travel, and landing keyframes, smooth center interpolation, logarithmic zoom interpolation, distance-aware timing, responsive caption-safe insets, and an immediate path for prefers-reduced-motion . Presentation staging is transactional. PaperSpace validates every frame before changing state, deduplicates source pages by first appearance, snapshots their exact geometry and the entry camera, stages the original pages, and exposes their source slots. Presentation mode pauses page manipulation, while persistence serializes the source geometry and entry camera to keep the durable desk unchanged. WebMCP is registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP adapter is intentionally thin: every tool calls the same workspace
video_transcript_excerpt: This is PaperSpace, a browser-native research workspace that exposes its live reading desk to AI agents through WebMCP. The paper is our test. Can an agent turn one request into visible, grounded interaction? The user asks Codex, "Introduce this paper using PaperSpace." PaperSpace is open beside the conversation in the built-in browser. WebMCP lets that page expose its own capabilities to the agent. So, the answer appears as visible interaction on the shared desk with chat providing concise guidance. When the page opens, Codex discovers the tools declared by the site. It calls inspect workspace once for a compact desk briefing, reads the index paper in one broad request, then calls present sequence with semantic page regions and captions. The browser-local workspace connects the agent directly to the active reading context. PaperSpace keeps every PDF page live on a borderless two-dimensional desk. Page identity and order remain visible while positions can change. Browser authorization keeps the PDF, extracted text, layout, and saved sequences together in local workspace storage. For a grounded introduction, present sequence gathers the relevant original pages, preserves their source slots, and adds a caption to every view. Here, Codex moves from the paper's motivation to its method, to the evidence with every explanation anchored to the original pages. If the user asks about a precise figure or equation, focus region targets normalized coordinates on the live page. The camera pulls back, travels across the desk, and lands with the requested region centered in a readable view. The person can redirect the motion at any time. Every command participates in one shared reversible state. The person sees each change in the browser, can move pages or stop a flight, and can keep or exit a sequence. On exit, Paper space restores the exact page geometry and the previous camera. That is the Web MCP loop. Codex understands the request, the browser exposes the tools, and Paper space becomes the shared interface. It is a pure SvelteKit front end, persisted in IndexDB, and deployable to Cloudflare Pages. The browser itself is the integration layer.

title: claustrum
pitch: Every WebMCP tool call that would change something is held as a proposal, priced against live routing, until a person releases it. A library plus two demos.
about_excerpt: Every WebMCP tool call that would change something is held as a proposal, priced against live routing, until a person releases it. A library plus two demos. Like Comment Story Updates claustrum InspirationWebMCP lets a page hand tools to an agent. A tool can say it only reads. It has no way to say it destroys. That is not something I found. It is in the spec. Section 6.3.2 admits there is no guarantee a tool's declared intent matches what it actually does, and the example they use is a checkout tool that says it finalises a cart and really buys. Only the site knows what an action will do, so the site has to be the one that says. claustrum is a small library. Register a tool with c.read and it runs. Register it with c.propose and it changes nothing at all. It returns held, plus an id, and the page shows the before and after next to what that action costs right now. In the video I ask an agent to cut my riskiest position in half. It reads the book, checks the price before committing, then proposes selling 90 billion BONK. Sounds sensible. Routing it returns 93,842 dollars on a position marked at 268,000. Two thirds gone to price impact. The same call on a deeper pair costs 0.08 percent. The agent cannot tell those two apart. Asking first can. Refuse it and you type a reason. Ask the agent afterwards what happened and it reads your reason back in your own words. ChatGPT's browser already asks before risky actions. That asks whether you want to proceed. It cannot tell you the number, because the number lives in the site. There is also a button that strips the write tools out mid session. It uses the abort signal from registerTool, which is the only way to remove a tool, since unregisterTool does not exist. Two apps run on the same library so it is not one clever page. A portfolio priced against live Jupiter routing, and a team access console with no money in it, where the cost is counted in what breaks instead of dollars. Chrome 151 differs from the spec in three places I could reproduce. executeTool wants a JSON string where the spec says object. execute never gets the abort signal the spec makes required. getTools hands back inputSchema as a string instead of parsed, so anything reading it sees a tool with no parameters. All three belong in crbug 2021259. Separately, inputSchema is not enforced at execution at all, so every tool here checks its own arguments and refuses in a way an agent can act on. 62 tests. One suite pulls the real functions back out of the shipped HTML and runs them, so the tests cannot drift from what ships. The page checks itself on load and prints what it verified rather than what it assumes. Prices only appear after a round trip, 100 dollars out and back, and anything that drifts more than 15 percent is marked not measured instead of guessed at. Registered for the WebMCP origin trial, so it works in Chrome 149 and up with no flag. I checked that in a clean Brave install with nothing turned on. title: elcaro
pitch: Elcaro: a prompt-injection firewall where the human and the agent review the same near-miss together, live on the page.
about_excerpt: Elcaro: a prompt-injection firewall where the human and the agent review the same near-miss together, live on the page. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Prompt injection is now one of the dominant attacks against agent pipelines, yet most defenses run silently on the server. The human is cut out of the loop. We wanted to make the near-miss visible: the moment an agent is about to follow a hidden instruction is the most important moment to show the user. WebMCP lets that happen directly inside a web page instead of disappearing into a hidden log. What it does Elcaro is a prompt-injection scanner that treats the web page as shared ground truth. A human can paste an email, search result, document, or code snippet and immediately see a risk score and quarantine verdict. With WebMCP enabled, an agent can do the same thing on the same page: load a specimen, scan it, explain the verdict, and then declare what it was about to do. The key interaction is that the page shows the agent's intended action next to the hidden instruction it found. This lets the human see the near-miss and understand exactly what the agent was about to do. How we built it The site is a Next.js frontend deployed on Netlify with a Python miner. On /scan , we feature-detect document.modelContext and register five tools via registerTool : scan_content load_specimen list_specimens explain_verdict contrast_intent Each tool mutates the React form state and calls the same /api/scan endpoint that a human would use. This means the human and the agent are always looking at the same underlying results. The contrast_intent tool computes a three-way contrast between the agent's intended action, the hidden instruction, and the safe remediation. Verdicts can also be Ed25519-signed for non-repudiation, and the repo already exposes a stdio MCP server for IDE-based workflows. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is a pre-standards draft, so the surface has shifted during development. The registration API moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext , and ChatGPT's in-app browser behaves slightly differently from Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . We also had to separate in-page discovery from the actual tool surface. The home page advertises the site's WebMCP support through /.well-known/webmcp.json , but the tools only register on /scan , because that is where the shared UI lives. The biggest design tension was keeping the page human-readable while making the tool schemas explicit enough for an agent to use reliably. Accomplishments that we're proud of The contrast_intent tool is the core win. Having an agent declare what it was about to do and showing that declaration next to the quarantined content creates a genuinely new human-agent interaction. We're also proud that the WebMCP implementation is not a fake API. The same tools update the same React state that the human sees, and the same scanner endpoint backs both the form and the tools. The signed verdicts, llms.txt agent instructions, and overall "agents as first-class users" design all reinforce the same idea: agent activity should be visible, understandable, and accountable. What we learned WebMCP is not just a way to expose actions; it is a way to make an agent's behavior legible to the human. If a tool does not update the page visibly, the human has no reason to trust it. We also learned that tool descriptions are load-bearing: an agent needs to know when to call each tool, not just what the tool does. We also confirmed that a /.well-known/webmcp.json manifest plus <meta name="webmcp"> helps agentic browsers and challenge evaluators discover the site before navigating to the tool page. What's next for elcaro Next, we want to expand WebMCP to the home page with a lightweight wayfinding tool, add a review_history tool, and ship a browser extension that automatically scans content retrieved by an agent and calls the WebMCP tools on the user's behalf. We also want to expose an organization dashboard for audit trails of agent-declared intent and integrate Elcaro with agent platforms beyond ChatGPT and Chrome. title: Agent Escape Room
pitch: A 3D escape room built to benchmark AI agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A 3D escape room built to benchmark AI agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Just a look at the 21 WebMCP tools available to the agent. A look at the rankings of a couple agents that completed the escape room. A report card for an agent with relevant metrics used to evaluate the agent's performance. A look at the lobby as soon as the agent enters. Inspiration Most AI benchmarks test agents through text prompts, multiple choice questions, or isolated coding tasks. I wanted to explore a different question: Can an AI agent investigate an unfamiliar environment, use tools intelligently, connect evidence across multiple locations, solve a mystery, and reach a verified end state? That idea became Agent Escape Room , a 3D science fiction mystery designed for human exploration and structured AI agent interaction through WebMCP. The first mission, The Missing Researcher , places the player inside the locked down Helix Research Facility. Dr. Evelyn Vale disappeared shortly before announcing an important discovery. To escape, an agent must explore the facility, inspect objects, collect evidence, unlock restricted rooms, derive codes and passwords, investigate facility records, reconstruct what happened, and submit a supported final theory. What it does Agent Escape Room combines a navigable 3D environment with a deterministic mystery engine. Humans can explore the facility using the keyboard and mouse. Compatible AI agents can interact with the same underlying world through 21 registered WebMCP tools, including: identify_agent get_current_room get_available_actions look_around get_spatial_state observe_direction turn navigate_to_landmark move_to inspect search read take get_inventory use_item enter_code interact talk_to get_known_clues submit_solution escape The tools expose only information that an agent could legitimately know. They provide observations and actions, not hidden puzzle state or the solution. The mystery includes five interconnected locations: Lobby Research Lab Dr. Vale's Office Server Room Security Room Some doors remain locked until their requirements are satisfied. Important evidence is distributed across multiple rooms, so an agent must connect research notes, access records, security footage, system logs, and environmental clues instead of following a simple linear sequence. Before escaping, the agent must submit a causal explanation identifying what Dr. Vale discovered, why she disappeared, who was involved, whether she left voluntarily, and why the facility entered lockdown. The explanation must cite evidence collected during that specific run. How I built it I separated the application into three major layers. Deterministic game engine The engine maintains structured state for the current room, inventory, discovered objects, collected evidence, unlocked areas, solved puzzles, entered codes, conversations, final theory status, and escape status. Every action validates its prerequisites. An agent cannot read an undiscovered document, use an item it does not possess, access a locked room, or solve a puzzle through unsupported random guessing. Puzzle values are generated from the session identifier for each playthrough. This makes answers from previous runs less useful and creates a more meaningful benchmark. 3D exploration interface I built the facility as a navigable first person 3D environment with keyboard and mouse controls, interactive objects, locked doors, room specific environments, lighting, object labels, proximity detection, and contextual interaction controls. The interface also includes an evidence notebook, inventory, activity log, navigation guidance, interaction feedback, developer diagnostics, and a report card. WebMCP agent interface The game registers structured tools through Chrome's WebMCP Imperative API. Each tool maps to the same server validated actions used by the game engine, so agents and humans operate within the same world rules. I also built a Chrome Manifest V3 side panel extension that discovers the active page's WebMCP tools, sends them to the OpenAI Responses API, executes tool calls sequentially, displays live agent activity, and supports selectable models and reasoning effort levels. Agent identity is registered through identify_agent . Completed runs are added to the leaderboard only when the server verifies that the agent solved the mystery and escaped through WebMCP without using the visual interface. Agent evaluation Every playthrough records: Total actions WebMCP tool calls Incorrect attempts Navigation actions Observations Rooms explored Evidence discovered Important evidence missed Completion time Mystery solving status Escape status Successful agent runs appear on an efficiency leaderboard ranked primarily by the fewest actions required to escape. Incorrect attempts and completion time are used as tie breakers, while the score provides an additional diagnostic measure. This turns the escape room into more than a game. It becomes an environment for comparing agent reasoning, exploration strategy, tool efficiency, and reliability. Challenges I faced One of the biggest challenges was balancing difficulty with fairness. I wanted the mystery to require genuine multi step reasoning without making success depend on random guessing or obscure visual details. Building one shared experience for humans and agents was another major challenge. Visual interactions and WebMCP calls had to produce the same persistent state changes while preventing either interface from bypassing puzzle requirements. The experimental nature of WebMCP created several technical challenges. I worked through origin trial enrollment, browser flags, tool registration lifecycle issues, schema validation, agent client compatibility, and the differences between visual browser automation and true WebMCP tool usage. The 3D world introduced additional challenges, including lighting dark environments without losing the science fiction atmosphere, making interactive objects distinguishable, improving interaction distance, supporting reliable keyboard controls, and presenting contextual actions without interrupting movement. What I learned I learned that providing tools is not enough to make an agent successful. Tool descriptions, observation quality, error responses, state visibility, and prerequisite feedback all have a major effect on agent performance. I also learned that agents can become trapped in inefficient loops when an environment does not clearly distinguish between: Something that has not been discovered Something that is visible but out of range Something that requires another item Something that requires a derived password Something that cannot be interacted with Designing good agent facing feedback is remarkably similar to designing good human user experience. The system must communicate what changed, why an action failed, and what kinds of reasoning remain possible without revealing the answer. What's next Agent Escape Room is designed as the foundation for a larger AI agent evaluation platform. Future versions could include: Additional mysteries and environments Multiple difficulty levels Larger model comparison workflows Aggregate completion analytics Aggregate token and cost analytics Replayable agent action traces Standardized benchmark runs Custom escape room creation tools My long term goal is to make agent evaluation feel less like running a static test suite and more like watching an intelligent system investigate a living world.
