title: spool
pitch: Turns messy CSV migration into a deterministic, agent-driven workflow with phase-aware WebMCP tools, validation, recovery, and verified export
about_excerpt: Turns messy CSV migration into a deterministic, agent-driven workflow with phase-aware WebMCP tools, validation, recovery, and verified export Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it doesSPOOL SPOOL is a local-first, agent-assisted data migration system designed to turn messy CSV files into validated, structured, database-ready outputs without forcing the user to manually supervise every transformation. The user provides a source file and selects the desired outcome. SPOOL then runs a deterministic workflow that profiles the data, infers field types and mappings, creates a transformation plan, dry-runs it, identifies unsafe ambiguities, executes the migration, verifies the result, and produces an export. Its key WebMCP innovation is Temporal WebMCP. Instead of exposing every tool to an AI agent permanently, SPOOL dynamically exposes only the capabilities that are valid for the current workflow state. For example, planning tools are available only after profiling is complete, execution tools appear only when the migration is ready, and stale capabilities disappear when mappings or source state change. This means the website—not the model—owns workflow correctness. SPOOL uses constrained deterministic transformations rather than arbitrary AI-generated code. It includes typed schema inference, data validation, revision-aware mappings, dry runs, Worker-based execution, recovery after refresh, violation reporting, and spreadsheet formula-injection protection. The product is designed around a simple experience: Add data → choose outcome → run Autopilot → resolve only genuine ambiguities → receive verified output. The broader idea behind SPOOL is that complex web workflows should expose agent capabilities contextually rather than giving agents a permanent toolbox and expecting them to manage application state correctly themselves. title: MyProvence Agent-Ready
pitch: The official Provence tourism catalogue, rebuilt as a shared stage where you and your agent explore a real destination together, and you watch it happen.
about_excerpt: The official Provence tourism catalogue, rebuilt as a shared stage where you and your agent explore a real destination together, and you watch it happen. Like Comment Story Updates The trip becomes an artifact: a three-day carnet built only from the visitor's kept choices, downloadable as PDF. Tonight in Marseille: distance-ranked events, the town filter set by the request, and the demand panel logging the calls. Agent results with photos and map, plus the Invisible Demand panel printing every real tool call. Inspiration The problem, seen from both sides of the screen. As a traveller: tourism websites are cluttered. MyProvence holds 2,798 places, 3,605 dated events, 232 official routes, plus filters, categories and pages of details. Nobody has time to read that any more. So we stopped reading and started asking an assistant instead. As the destination: MyProvence watches its traffic shrink every day, and it is not alone. Clicks nearly halve when Google shows an AI summary (8% vs 15%, Pew 2025). Tripadvisor's CEO told investors about "ongoing declines in flyby visitors... due to the rise of AI overviews". 56% of US travellers used AI for a trip this year, up from 33% a year earlier (Phocuswright). And a third of website visits already come from agents, not humans (Agentic Web Index). Both sides point at the same conclusion. Nobody HAS to visit a destination website any more. With ChatGPT and AI Mode, they never will have to again. The solution: give people a reason to WANT to come back. Easier access to the information: one wish, in any language, and the answer appears. A website that is alive and personalized: it transforms in real time before your eyes, the masthead becomes YOUR wish over the photos of what was found, the map moves for you, every pin waits for your yes or no. A site that reacts to you, not to anyone else. And an experience unique enough that you come back for it, and talk about it. The MyProvence team's own question showed us the way in: "What if, instead of asking AI agents to figure out how our tourism website works, we explicitly told them what they can do with it?" WebMCP is what makes the whole idea buildable: the agent and the human on the same live page. We are not replacing the site with AI. We are making the site worth visiting again, for humans and agents together, and every record links back to its canonical myprovence.fr page. What it does Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP. A destination catalogue is exactly what agents fail at today: 6,403 records behind JavaScript filters, interconnected facets, a map, and a human with opinions standing in front of it. Scraping sees none of that, and a headless API loses the human. WebMCP is the only channel where the agent's actions and the visitor's reactions share one live surface. That shared surface is the whole product here. What a human and an agent can now do together that they could not before: Before: you asked ChatGPT about Provence, got a text list scraped from stale copies, then retyped it into the real site. Now: "a quiet seaside village, a hotel with parking, something happening locally" is ONE send_scouts call. Two to four scouts visibly fan out across the map, plant evidence flags from the official catalogue, and the masthead becomes your wish written over the real photographs of what was found. Before: your taps meant nothing to the agent, because a human gesture had no API. Now: you tap GARDER or ECARTER on any pin, padlock a result, right-click the map ("more like this here", "avoid this"), or answer the agent's question cards. The agent reads every one of them as a decision through get_scout_reports and get_visitor_signals. Dismissed is never re-proposed. Before: "what am I looking at?" was unanswerable, because a viewport is just numbers. Now: get_visitor_view hands the agent the TOWNS your zoom frames, ranked, with the dominant one named. Zooming on Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer means Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer even with every filter on "all towns". "What's on tonight near me" is one distance-ranked call. Before: the agent's plan lived in the chat and died there. Now: your choices (kept flags, locked cards, the accepted pin) compose the carnet de voyage: a print-ready pack with one section per request you explored, real photographs, canonical links, downloadable as PDF. Plus the postcard from day 3 of your future trip. The agent can only reference ids you actually chose; unknown ids are refused. Zero hallucination in the factual layer, by construction. Why the experience is better, not just automated. The page answers the CURRENT question: a new search retires the old mission banner and takes the masthead itself, and the town dropdown shows the city you explicitly asked for. The agent's pin is an unmissable marker with its popup open, never a claim in chat you have to trust. Every agent action has visible, verifiable theatre. And every zero-result agent search feeds an anonymized (k>=3) "demand pulse" the destination reads back as its product roadmap: the demand its catalogue misses, measured instead of guessed. Trust, because agents need it. An independent audit (Trustwright) read the 20 tools, ran 35 automated checks, and signed the surface (Ed25519). The badge in the hero re-verifies the live toolset against that audit on every page load. How we built it 20 tools registered at module evaluation via document.modelContext.registerTool, synchronously, so an agent that lands and calls getTools() immediately sees the complete list. One client-side engine (inverted indexes over the full catalogue, sub-millisecond queries) and ONE shared view store consumed by both the React UI and the tools. The agent and the human literally cannot diverge, because they act on the same state. Beyond the basics, three mechanics that push on the spec: pin_visible_place: its input schema is an ENUM of the place names currently on the visitor's screen, re-registered (AbortSignal unregistration) as the view moves. An off-screen place like "pin the Ritz Paris" is invalid BY SCHEMA, not by a polite refusal. read_visitor_wish: WebMCP has no push channel, so we built the closest spec-legal thing. The tool APPEARS mid-session when the visitor acts, and its description is rewritten with the live page state on every change. Description as heartbeat: at its next turn the agent already knows what you typed, what ran and what you kept, before making a single call. Hybrid elicitation: ask_visitor puts a real question card in front of the human, blocks 45 seconds, then degrades into a pending ticket the agent redeems later with get_input_result. Synchronous when possible, async when the human is slower than the agent. Plus the unglamorous parts that make it production-shaped: abort signals honored around every await, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations throughout, and strict Zod schemas shared between the page tools, the remote MCP endpoint and the public GET APIs. One contract, four surfaces, so they cannot drift. We also rewrote all tool descriptions to the vendor-documented selection pattern after learning the hard way that "ALWAYS use this instead of web search" is the exact tool-poisoning signature safety scanners flag. 280 unit tests and 46 Playwright e2e tests, including tests that drive the tools through document.modelContext itself. Field-tested against ChatGPT desktop site tools, Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and claude.ai as both MCP connector and fetch-only agent. Challenges we ran into Field-testing against real driving agents WAS the project, including live sessions with the MyProvence team, whose bug reports shaped half the build. ChatGPT hands tool input as a JSON string, may omit the options bag, re-reads the tool list every turn, and freely prefers web search. Each quirk became a design rule: the wish box as a guaranteed mailbox, the heartbeat tool, context-anchored descriptions. claude.ai's fetcher follows links but cannot compose a query string. It answered "family activities near Marseille" with Cassis hotels because our /agenda published no leisure example to click. Every cluster now has a real parameterised link, and paging goes to 100 per call. Agents SAY things they did not do ("I pinned it"). Every action now has unmissable, verifiable theatre, and the on-page demand mirror prints every real tool call, so a false claim is visible to the visitor. Honest geography is hard: GPS-less events used to answer "tonight near Marseille" from 70 km away. They now ride their town's centroid through the radius check, or drop out. Not a toy dataset. Real ChatGPT sessions chained send_scouts, get_scout_reports and get_visitor_signals unprompted, and our telemetry logged 5 distinct tools in one day of field testing.  💡 Inspiration
Managing multiple medications shouldn't require patients to become pharmacology experts. A single new medicine can introduce an interaction that's easy to miss.
We built SafeDose AI — RegimenGuard to turn complex medication information into understandable safety insights — and with WebMCP , allow AI agents to work directly with structured medication context. 

 
 The agent investigates. SafeDose provides context. The human decides. 

 🛡️ What it does 

 SafeDose is an agent-native medication safety workspace that helps users: 

 
 💊 Manage their current medication regimen 
 ⚠️ Detect potential drug interactions 
 📊 Understand an overall regimen safety score 
 🔴 Distinguish critical risks from cautions and safer combinations 
 🔎 Search structured medication information 
 👥 Support caregiver and medication-management workflows 
 
 

 🤖 Powered by WebMCP 

 SafeDose exposes three focused, read-only agent tools :
 search_medication 🔎 — Find medication information
 get_current_regimen 💊 — Understand the user's current regimen
 check_regimen_safety 🛡️ — Check a candidate medication against that regimen 

 Instead of repeatedly copying medication lists into an AI conversation, compatible agents can work with SafeDose's structured capabilities directly. 

 Agents investigate — they don't prescribe or modify medications. 

 🛠️ How we built it 

 SafeDose combines:
 React + TypeScript ⚛️ → application 
 WebMCP 🤖 → agent-native tools 
 Medication/FDA data 💊 → drug information 
 Google AI Studio ✨ → AI-assisted development 
 GitHub 🐙 → source control 
 Vercel ▲ → live deployment 

 We also built an Agent Activity interface to make WebMCP capabilities visible and understandable. 

 🧩 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge was bridging two worlds:
 Human UI ↔ WebMCP ↔ AI Agent 
We worked through evolving WebMCP browser APIs, tool registration, deployment, agent discovery, and medication-data integration. 

 Healthcare also raised an important design question: How much authority should an AI agent have? 
Our answer was deliberate — read-only tools and human-controlled decisions. 

 🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're especially proud that SafeDose isn't simply “another healthcare chatbot.” 
We transformed an existing medication-safety experience into an agent-native web application , while preserving a polished interface for traditional users. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP addresses a genuinely contextual problem: 

 
 It's not only “What does this medication do?” 
It's “What does this medication mean alongside everything I'm already taking?” 
 

 🧠 What we learned 

 WebMCP showed us that the future of AI on the web isn't necessarily putting a chatbot on every website. 

 It's about making websites themselves understandable and actionable to agents. 
And in healthcare, powerful AI doesn't always mean maximum autonomy.
 Good agents also know where their authority ends. 

 🚀 What's next for SafeDose AI — RegimenGuard 

 Next, we envision:
💊 Medication reconciliation 
👨‍⚕️ Pharmacist-review workflows 
👨‍👩‍👧 Caregiver collaboration 
📅 Smarter medication planning 
♿ Improved accessibility 
🤖 Expanded WebMCP capabilities with human approval 

 Our goal is simple: 

 SafeDose AI — Your regimen. Your agent. Safer decisions. 🛡️ 

 Disclaimer: SafeDose is a prototype decision-support tool and does not replace professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.

title: DONE / PROVEN
pitch: Agents can challenge the definition of done. Humans keep authority. Proof stays current when reality changes.
about_excerpt: Agents can challenge the definition of done. Humans keep authority. Proof stays current when reality changes. Like Comment Story Updates Done is a claim. Proof is a state. AI agents are getting very good at producing work and increasingly good at reporting that the work is finished. The remaining trust problem is deeper: did the agent prove the right definition of success, did it have authority to act on that definition, and is that proof still valid after the world changes? DONE / PROVEN is a proof-carrying work layer for humans and agents. A human owns the mission and the semantic authority to decide what success means. An agent can inspect the mission and acceptance contract through WebMCP and can attack that contract by submitting a concrete counterexample: an outcome that appears to satisfy the current definition of done but should still count as failure. The system evaluates that counterexample deterministically. If the unacceptable outcome would pass, DONE / PROVEN surfaces a false-green contract defect to the human. The agent cannot rewrite the contract, approve its own fix, or impersonate the human decision. After the human admits a corrected contract, execution evidence can earn PROVEN state. If a dependency later changes, DONE / PROVEN invalidates only the proof that depended on the change. Unrelated evidence remains valid, and the system produces a minimum re-proof plan. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns the page from a dashboard into a structured human-agent collaboration surface. The release exposes seven tools that let an agent read the mission, inspect authority, inspect the candidate contract, list known contract risks, inspect evidence state, request a bounded human decision, and submit an adversarial counterexample. The key tool is submit_counterexample . It lets the agent actively pressure-test the human-owned definition of done while keeping semantic authority with the human. Better human-agent UX The point is not to make people write longer specifications. The system concentrates human attention on the few decisions automation cannot safely settle, gives the agent a typed way to expose loopholes, and keeps deterministic code responsible for evaluation and proof state. A later dependency change reopens only evidence that actually depended on what changed rather than discarding all prior proof or trusting a stale green checkmark. What people and agents can do together The agent can inspect mission, authority, candidate acceptance criteria, contract risks, and proof state; request a bounded human decision; and submit a concrete adversarial counterexample. The human owns unresolved meaning and admission. Deterministic code owns evaluation, proof validity, dependency impact, and minimal re-proof. Demo The demo begins with an agent claiming a landing-page task is DONE. The initial acceptance contract is deliberately wrong in two directions: False green: it forgets to require the waitlist signup to actually persist. False red: it requires one exact headline even though the human said wording does not matter. The agent submits a broken-waitlist counterexample. The deterministic engine returns EXPOSES_FALSE_GREEN , records the visible challenge, and leaves the active contract unchanged. The human resolves the genuinely semantic admin-privacy question, the corrected contract is admitted, and five requirements earn evidence-backed PROVEN state. Then a dependency changes. Exactly two of five proof receipts become STALE while three remain PROVEN. Re-running only the affected checks restores 5/5. WebMCP implementation Seven imperative tools register through the current document.modelContext surface when available, with the older navigator path retained only as compatibility fallback. submit_counterexample uses a narrow JSON schema, additionalProperties: false , runtime size/type validation, and an untrusted-content hint. It is non-read-only only because it records a visible challenge. It has no capability to edit or admit the acceptance contract. Evidence boundary This project does not claim that AI can automatically infer arbitrary human intent, that acceptance contracts themselves are novel, or that every verification problem is solved. The demonstrated contribution is narrower: an agent can adversarially falsify the human-owned definition of done without becoming the authority, and proof can remain dependency-aware after reality changes. The final licensed release passes 38/38 deterministic tests , TypeScript typecheck, static build, responsive browser verification, seven-tool WebMCP current-API harness registration, adversarial counterexample execution, agent-content injection probes, deployment-header verification, and zero unauthorized contract mutation. Existing-project disclosure Existing project, meaningfully extended during the challenge. The underlying contract-adequacy and continuous-validity research began before August 25. During the WebMCP Challenge submission period, the project was materially extended with the responsive human product surface, authority reconciliation, seven WebMCP tools, the agent-submitted counterexample mechanism, WebMCP trust boundaries and runtime validation, current-API harness verification, deployment-origin and permissions hardening, browser/mobile/injection verification, public-release packaging, and challenge-specific testing/documentation. Dated commit history and release evidence preserve that distinction. title: UMBRA DRIFT
pitch: A WebMCP shadow theatre where human state changes invalidate stale agent plans—safely, visibly, atomically.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP shadow theatre where human state changes invalidate stale agent plans—safely, visibly, atomically. Like Comment Story Updates A shared shadow theatre for one human and one browser agent, with Reality, Agent Belief, and Human Authority kept visibly separate. The recovery proof: one human override, one rejected stale write, zero partial mutations, and SAFE_RECOVERY. The human moves the lamp; the page rejects the stale plan with LAMP_SEQUENCE_CONFLICT and zero partial mutations. Inspiration Browser agents often act as if a page will wait for them. Real people keep dragging, editing, approving, and revoking. Most demos hide that race condition. We wanted to make it impossible to miss. What it does UMBRA DRIFT is a shared shadow theatre and a reproducible WebMCP recovery trial. A human controls the lamp and temporary capability grants. An external browser agent controls a four-piece rig through typed page tools. If the human moves the lamp after the agent observes the scene, the old plan is rejected atomically, without partial changes. The agent must read the live state again, measure the new projection, and recover. A successful run produces a visible dragon, a SAFE_RECOVERY verdict, and an exportable evidence capsule derived from the page's event ledger. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the coordination layer, not an integration added beside the experience. The state that matters is live, transient, and owned by the current browser tab. UMBRA exposes typed tools tied directly to that state instead of asking an agent to guess through pixels or DOM controls. The agent can observe, measure, request, plan, and commit. It cannot move the human-owned lamp, grant itself permission, bypass a revision check, or provide its own verdict. What becomes possible A person and an external agent can work in the same changing page while retaining separate authority. The human sees every capability request and can revoke control. The agent receives structured measurements and actionable conflicts. The site—not the model—enforces the boundary. How we built it UMBRA DRIFT uses the imperative WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool, closed JSON Schemas, vanilla JavaScript, SVG, and CSS. Each mutation is checked against the observed lamp sequence, rig revision, and capability revision. Batched rig changes are all-or-nothing. A bounded deterministic event ledger produces the final recovery verdict. The UI exposes Reality, Agent Belief, and Human Authority as separate live states. The public app has no backend, account, API key, remote model call, database, telemetry, or external runtime dependency. The Apache-2.0 source includes the engine, tests, security contract, provenance, and reproduction instructions. Potential impact UMBRA is a playable reference pattern for editors, design tools, dashboards, workflow products, and other live applications where humans and agents share changing state. It makes five reusable ideas tangible: explicit ownership, scoped grants, optimistic concurrency, atomic mutation, and recovery after human intervention. Challenges and learnings The hardest problem was making the agent necessary without hiding the whole solution in a tool response. We learned that a tool schema is also an authority contract, and that structured failure is part of the human-agent experience, not merely an implementation detail. What's next Additional seeded trials, reusable conformance fixtures, CI adapters, and evaluations across different browser agents.
